items.quote: every groundhog has to look different
items.paragraph: - “Groundhog Immortal” (Marmot Spirit): A new supporting character that stood out in Ne Zha 2 is the so-called “Groundhog Immortal” – essentially the leader of a marmot-demon clan that Nezha encounters in the first trial. This character did not exist in earlier Nezha films or the original legend, and serves primarily as comic relief with a thematic purpose. The Groundhog Immortal is portrayed as a chubby, humble rodent spirit wearing tattered clothing[[34]](https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/26165005345#:~:text=%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%922%E3%80%8B%E6%98%8E%E6%98%8E%E5%9C%9F%E6%8B%A8%E9%BC%A0%20). He and his community of marmot demons live in an underground village and initially appear to be troublemakers that Nezha must defeat. However, much like Shiji, they are later revealed to be relatively benign beings labeled as “demons” simply because they don’t fit into the heavenly order. Ne Zha 2 uses the Groundhog tribe to inject humor – for example, these creatures are wide-eyed and silly, providing laughs in their interactions – but also to offer social commentary. Chinese viewers noted that the groundhogs symbolically resemble a “refugee camp” or marginalized community, forced into hiding and poverty[[36]](https://news.qq.com/rain/a/20250211A04NJB00#:~:text=%E9%80%9F%E6%88%B3%EF%BC%81%E4%BA%8C%E5%88%B7%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%922%E3%80%8B%EF%BC%8C%E5%8D%87%E4%BB%99%E8%80%83%E6%A0%B8%E7%9A%84%E4%B8%89%E5%A4%A7%E5%A6%96%EF%BC%8C%E7%AB%9F%E8%97%8F%E7%9D%80%E8%BF%99%E4%BA%9B%E2%80%9C%E7%A5%9E%E9%9A%90%E5%96%BB%E2%80%9D%EF%BC%81%20%E5%9C%9F%E6%8B%A8%E9%BC%A0%3D%E9%9A%BE%E6%B0%91%E8%90%A5%EF%BC%8C%E7%94%B3%E6%A0%A1%E9%95%BF%3D%E6%95%99%E5%9F%B9%E4%B9%B1%E8%B1%A1%EF%BC%8C%E7%9F%B3%E7%9F%B6%E5%A8%98%E5%A8%98%3D%E8%BF%87%E5%BA%A6%E5%8C%BB%E7%BE%8E). The Groundhog Immortal himself just wants to protect his people. When Nezha defeats them rather easily, Wuliang’s disciples swoop in to capture the marmot demons, hinting that the trial was a pretext to round up these “undesirables.” This is a sharp deviation from traditional Nezha tales, which generally did not feature such creatures or this kind of moral ambiguity. By including the Groundhog Immortal, Ne Zha 2 adds a layer of sympathy for the “little people” of the myth world. In design terms, the animators gave each groundhog a distinct look (the film painstakingly ensured “every groundhog has to look different” to make the crowd scenes lively)[[37]](http://www.ecns.cn/cns-wire/2025-02-17/detail-ihenxmvs7429875.shtml#:~:text=Audiences%20who%20have%20watched%20the,and%20over%204%2C000%20Chinese%20animators). The plump, buck-toothed marmot leader ends up being more lovable than menacing. His inclusion is an innovation that enriches the story’s world-building and reinforces the theme that not all “monsters” are evil – some are just victims of a biased system. The Groundhog Immortal character thus serves as both a lighthearted element for the audience and a narrative device to challenge the black-and-white morality of old Nezha stories.

items.quote: The blues was really important – this is your healing and love in the music
items.paragraph: “History of Jazz” tree diagram (1977) designed by Mary Lou Williams (drawn by David Stone Martin). This pedagogical poster visualizes her concept of jazz history. One of Williams’s most famous teaching tools was her “Jazz Tree” diagram – a large illustrated poster she used in lectures to chart the lineage of jazz styles[[25]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=As%20Williams%E2%80%99%20popularity%20grew%2C%20she,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it). The structure of the Jazz Tree vividly encapsulates her historical perspective. At the base of the tree, Williams wrote the single word “SUFFERING” in bold letters[[26]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=held%20conviction%20about%20the%20origin,of%20the%20music). This represents the deep roots of jazz in the suffering of African American slaves, out of which arose the spirituals – the first musical expressions that fed into jazz[[26]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=held%20conviction%20about%20the%20origin,of%20the%20music)[[25]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=As%20Williams%E2%80%99%20popularity%20grew%2C%20she,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it). From these roots, a “strong trunk” grows straight upward, marked in ascending order with what Williams considered the four major eras of jazz development[[27]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=Down%20into%20the%20earth%20of,On%20these%20dead%20sticks)[[28]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=Up%20from%20suffering%20grows%20a,jazz%2C%20beginning%20with%20the%20spirituals). The lowest segment of the trunk is labeled “Spirituals”, above which comes “Ragtime”, then “K.C. (Kansas City) Swing”, and at the top of the trunk “Bop” (bebop)[[29]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=which%20Williams%20called%20SUFFERING%2C%20the,magic%2C%E2%80%9D%20%E2%80%9Cmere%20exercises%2C%E2%80%9D%20and%20%E2%80%9Cclassical)[[28]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=Up%20from%20suffering%20grows%20a,jazz%2C%20beginning%20with%20the%20spirituals). These four are the core lineage of jazz as Williams defined it – each era emerging from the previous one in a direct line. Notably, blues is not given as a single trunk era; instead, Williams painted the blues as a continuous life-giving force running up both sides of the trunk through every stage[[30]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=tree%20grows%2C%E2%80%94thick%20and%20straight,the%20vital%20musicians%20in%20whose)[[31]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=After%20the%20spirituals%20come%20ragtime%2C,a%20couple%20dead%20branches%2C%20marked). In her diagram, the word “blues” winds alongside each era (from spirituals and ragtime on up), indicating that blues is integral to every branch of jazz and “originating in the roots” of the music[[30]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=tree%20grows%2C%E2%80%94thick%20and%20straight,the%20vital%20musicians%20in%20whose). As Williams would often say, “The blues was really important – this is your healing and love in the music”, the thread of feeling connecting all jazz styles[[32]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=music%20the%20blues%20flourish).

items.quote: Women using zo may sound rough,
items.paragraph: Specific examples from teaching guides include Genki's grammatical notes stating "boku is normally used by males," without examples of women or non-binary individuals using it for assertiveness, potentially correcting students based on perceived gender and causing distress. In Nakama, particles are taught as "masculine" or "feminine" with warnings about social reactions to mismatches, e.g., "Women using zo may sound rough," reinforcing stereotypes without discussing queer or fluid uses. Research up to 2020, including a 2019 analysis of learner perspectives, showed this rigidity led to "linguistic failure" for LGBTQ+ students, who faced barriers in self-expression and risked misgendering or unwanted disclosure. For instance, non-binary students using boku might receive stares or corrections, as reported in classroom experiences, highlighting how such teaching overlooked intersections of gender and sexuality.[asset.library.wisc.edu](https://asset.library.wisc.edu/1711.dl/QXNZN2B3JOQSC82/R/file-ed6b9.pdf)+更多 2

items.quote: established order won’t allow it, we will together change the world
items.paragraph: In summary, Ne Zha 2 retains the rebellious spirit of the Nezha legend – Nezha is still defying “heaven’s rules” – but it modernizes the themes to be more nuanced and socially resonant. The individual rebellion against a father or a dragon king has transformed into a collective uprising against injustice, fueled by friendship, trust, and love. The film upholds the core message of “fate can be changed” (as in the famous line “My life is determined by me, not by Heaven” from the first film) and extends it: if the “established order won’t allow it, we will together change the world”[[49]](https://www.chinawriter.com.cn/n1/2025/0206/c404076-40413506.html#:~:text=%E5%85%89%EF%BC%8C%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%922%E3%80%8B%E4%B8%AD%E7%9A%84%E4%BB%96%E5%A7%8B%E7%BB%88%E4%B8%80%E8%BA%AB%E6%AD%A3%E6%B0%94%E3%80%81%E5%BF%83%E6%80%9D%E7%BB%86%E8%85%BB%E3%80%81%E6%9E%81%E5%85%B7%E9%A2%86%E8%A2%96%E6%B0%94%E8%B4%A8%EF%BC%8C%E5%9C%A8%E9%BE%99%E6%97%8F%E9%9D%A2%E4%B8%B4%E5%8D%B1%E9%99%A9%E6%97%B6%E6%AF%AB%E4%B8%8D%E9%80%80%E8%AE%A9%EF%BC%8C%E9%9D%A2%E5%AF%B9%E5%AD%A9%E5%AD%90%E6%97%B6%E5%8F%88%E8%83%BD%E5%B1%95%E9%9C%B2%E6%9F%94%E6%83%85%EF%BC%8C%E4%BB%8E%E4%B8%8D%E4%BB%A5%E8%80%81%E4%B8%80%E8%BE%88%E7%9A%84%E7%BB%8F%E9%AA%8C%E6%8D%86%E7%BB%91%E4%BB%96%E4%BA%BA%E3%80%82). This collaborative, compassionate, and balance-seeking thematic stance distinguishes Ne Zha 2 as a truly contemporary retelling of the Nezha myth.

items.quote: viewers embraced a steady stream of foreign-language dramas
items.paragraph: 1. Global Popularity Timeline: Both Japanese TV anime and Scandinavian “Nordic Noir” crime dramas rose from niche to global prominence in roughly the same era, albeit with different trajectories. Anime’s international boom began earlier: Japanese animation started making inroads abroad by the 1980s and 1990s – for example, with films like Akira (1988) and series like Dragon Ball Z and Sailor Moon reaching overseas audiences[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_anime#:~:text=Over%20the%20following%20decades%2C%20anime,pop%20culture%2C%20known%20for%20its). By the late 1990s and 2000s, anime had become a global phenomenon, bolstered by fan conventions, home video, and later internet streaming. The “anime wave” in North America and Europe accelerated in the late 2000s as online platforms (Crunchyroll, etc.) made series widely accessible, and anime moved from a cult following to mainstream youth culture. In contrast, Nordic Noir’s breakthrough on the world stage came in the early 2010s. While Scandinavian crime novels (e.g. Stieg Larsson’s Millennium trilogy in 2005–2007) had garnered international readers, it was the subtitled TV series that truly popularized Nordic Noir globally. The pivotal moment was the Danish series The Killing (Forbrydelsen), which originally aired in 2007 in Denmark and was later broadcast in the UK on BBC Four in 2011 – “The Killing was the breakthrough” that introduced international audiences to the style[[24]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=,of%20Communication%20and%20Media%2C%20says)[[25]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=But%20it%20didn%27t%20break%20through,at%20Aarhus%20University%20in%20Denmark). This was swiftly followed by Sweden/Denmark’s The Bridge (2011) and others; by the mid-2010s, Nordic Noir dramas had gained a dedicated global viewership. In the UK, for example, “viewers embraced a steady stream of foreign-language dramas” after the success of these Nordic series, with The Bridge drawing nearly 2 million viewers on BBC4[[26]](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2016/jan/02/foreign-tv-drama-bbc-channel4-netflix#:~:text=I%20t%E2%80%99s%20not%20only%20Faroese,only%20by%20BBC1%20and%20ITV). To summarize, anime’s global rise was more gradual (spanning late 20th century into 2000s) and initially fan-driven, whereas Nordic Noir’s export success was more sudden around 2010–2012, catalyzed by strategic broadcasting (notably BBC4) and the post-2000 appetite for high-quality international TV drama[[25]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=But%20it%20didn%27t%20break%20through,at%20Aarhus%20University%20in%20Denmark)[[26]](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2016/jan/02/foreign-tv-drama-bbc-channel4-netflix#:~:text=I%20t%E2%80%99s%20not%20only%20Faroese,only%20by%20BBC1%20and%20ITV). Both forms became internationally prominent within a few years of each other, essentially “globally consumed niche media almost concurrently” by the late 2000s and early 2010s (to borrow an observation from academic commentary).

items.quote: boosted motivation and fostered self-regulated learning,
items.paragraph: 2. Self-Regulated Learning Behaviors:AI-integrated scaffolding can deeply influence students’ self-regulation – their ability to plan, monitor, and reflect on their writing. Several studies indicate that AI tools can encourage self-regulated learning behaviors by providing timely feedback and metacognitive prompts. For instance, an AI writing assistant that gives immediate error highlights prompts learners to monitor their writing quality continuously and revise proactively. This kind of constant feedback loop was shown to promote habits of self-correction and iteration[[14]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391778385_English_as_a_foreign_language_EFL_secondary_school_students'_use_of_artificial_intelligence_AI_tools_for_developing_writing_skills_unveiling_practices_and_perceptions#:~:text=match%20at%20L1806%20active%20learning%2C,In%20other%20words%2C%20AI%20medi)[[15]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391778385_English_as_a_foreign_language_EFL_secondary_school_students'_use_of_artificial_intelligence_AI_tools_for_developing_writing_skills_unveiling_practices_and_perceptions#:~:text=active%20learning%2C%20such%20as%20self,In%20other%20words%2C%20AI%20medi). In classroom trials, students with access to automated feedback engaged more in revising their drafts, often experimenting with multiple edits until the AI indicated no errors – a form of self-regulated goal-setting (aiming for a “clean” draft). AI tools also assist in the planning phase: generative models can help students outline their ideas, which students can then follow and modify, thereby practicing planning strategies. Research in China found that an AI-mediated instruction platform led students to use a wider range of learning strategies (e.g. setting writing goals, checking their work against model answers), significantly more than peers without AI support[[16]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955/full#:~:text=Results%3A%20Quantitative%20analysis%20revealed%20that,regulated%20learning)[[17]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955/full#:~:text=platform,motivate%20learners%2C%20and%20promote%20autonomy). Interviews revealed that the AI platform’s personalized feedback “boosted motivation and fostered self-regulated learning,” as students took initiative to improve between drafts[[18]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955/full#:~:text=extensive%20utilization%20of%20self,regulated%20learning). However, there are cautionary findings too: if students become too dependent on AI corrections, they might skip important self-regulatory steps. For example, instead of proofreading their work, some might rely on the AI to catch errors at the end – potentially weakening their habit of self-monitoring. One qualitative study noted concerns that over-reliance on AI could make learners less diligent in independent revision and critical thinking (termed a form of “learned laziness”)[[9]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391778385_English_as_a_foreign_language_EFL_secondary_school_students'_use_of_artificial_intelligence_AI_tools_for_developing_writing_skills_unveiling_practices_and_perceptions#:~:text=cerned%20that%20overreliance%20on%20AI,She)[[19]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391778385_English_as_a_foreign_language_EFL_secondary_school_students'_use_of_artificial_intelligence_AI_tools_for_developing_writing_skills_unveiling_practices_and_perceptions#:~:text=from%20thinking%20independently,affected%20my%20thinking%20ability%20negatively). In summary, AI tools can act as catalysts for self-regulated behaviors by scaffolding the process (reminding students to review, offering hints to revise, etc.), but educators need to cultivate students’ intrinsic self-regulation skills alongside, so that the presence of AI strengthens rather than replaces their self-monitoring and reflection.

items.quote: rural areas are relatively closed societies where dignity is the foundation for a farmer and even a family's standing. The evaluations of villagers who see each other daily, and farmers' self-identity, are all related to this
items.paragraph: The issue of dignity is particularly acute in South Asia's close-knit rural communities. As one analysis notes, "rural areas are relatively closed societies where dignity is the foundation for a farmer and even a family's standing. The evaluations of villagers who see each other daily, and farmers' self-identity, are all related to this" [(116)](http://rmfp.people.com.cn/n1/2017/0111/c406725-29014087.html). Accepting welfare assistance often means publicly acknowledging one's poverty and inability to provide for one's family, a stigma that many find unbearable.

items.quote: a sizeable voting bloc in the General Assembly.
items.paragraph: By the mid-1960s, African nations had constituted "a sizeable voting bloc in the General Assembly." This bloc voting transformed General Assembly resolutions from consultative instruments into expressions of Global South political will. While Security Council permanent members retained veto power, the General Assembly's moral and political authority increasingly reflected decolonized majority interests.[^34][^35]

items.quote: being underprepared to meet this moment
items.paragraph: In light of these challenges, a consistent theme in the literature is that proactive measures are needed alongside AI adoption. Successful integration of generative AI will require improving the technology (to be more reliable and unbiased), investing in people (skills, training, change management), and updating institutions (policies, laws, ethical norms). Researchers often conclude that without thoughtful intervention, we risk “being underprepared to meet this moment”[[57]](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/generative-ai-the-american-worker-and-the-future-of-work/#:~:text=What%20is%20at%20stake%3F) – but if challenges are addressed, the technology’s benefits can be realized while minimizing its harms.

items.quote: away from thinking of … survival and healing
items.paragraph: What makes Husanović’s perspective particularly forward-looking is how she connects this witnessing to a “politics of hope.” In her view, simply recounting trauma is not enough; the goal is to use the act of witness to imagine and build a better future. She argues that Bosnia (and societies like it) should move “away from thinking of … survival and healing” as the only paradigms and towards “reimagination and transformation.”[[41]](https://manifold.umn.edu/read/humanitarian-violence/section/9c685530-467b-4426-b692-d653cdb353eb#:~:text=96,risks%20being%20engulfed%20in%20the) In plainer terms, instead of just aiming to cope with past trauma (by surviving or by therapeutic healing of individuals), there should be a collective project of re-envisioning society and politics in a more just, inclusive way. This is where “hope” comes in – hope not as naive optimism, but as a radical political principle. Husanović posits that through witnessing, people can find the seeds of hope: by openly confronting wounds, communities can also identify desires for justice, for solidarity, for change. She talks about developing a politics that is hopeful in its orientation – not stuck in mourning or in narratives of endless victimhood, but oriented to preventing recurrence and building a different kind of social relations. For example, Bosnian feminist activists, by publicly speaking about rape camps or concentration camps, were not only testifying to what happened but also implicitly demanding a politics of equality and solidarity that transcends ethnic divisions and gendered silences. Husanović often invokes the concept of “equaliberty” (equal freedom) as a foundation for hope in the face of a post-war society fragmented by identitarian politics[[42]](https://www.iash.ed.ac.uk/profile/professor-jasmina-husanovi%C4%87-pehar#:~:text=Professor%20Jasmina%20Husanovi%C4%87%20Pehar%20,and%20solidarity%2C%20governance%20of)[[43]](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9781315795379-8/governance-life-femininity-bosnia-herzegovina-jasmina-husanovi%C4%87#:~:text=Refl%20www,and%20lootings%20in%20Bosnia). The idea is that through witnessing trauma, citizens can collectively critique the systems of power that led to that trauma and thus find common ground to envision an emancipatory politics beyond those divisions.

items.quote: when the model says BUY, how often is that profitable or correct?
items.paragraph: The proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive: \ \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives + False Positives}} \. In a trading signal context, if “positive” means a predicted buy signal, precision answers “when the model says BUY, how often is that profitable or correct?” A high precision means few false alarms. Precision is crucial when the cost of false positives is high (e.g. false buy signals could lead to losses). Researchers might report, say, precision of 0.90 for buy signals – meaning 90% of the time, a buy signal was indeed a winning trade[[41]](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/5/4/101#:~:text=The%20use%20of%20reinforcement%20learning,where%20trading%20bots%20autonomously%20adapt).

items.paragraph: Section 9(3) provides that "in the case of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work which is computer-generated, the author shall be taken to be the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work are undertaken". Section 178 defines "computer-generated" to mean works generated by a computer where there is no human author.[^32]

items.quote: hated rock 'n' roll as a commercial evil
items.paragraph: **Rock Music**: Williams **"hated rock 'n' roll as a commercial evil"**. She distinguished sharply between jazz—rooted in African-American suffering and spiritual traditions—and rock, which she associated with commercial exploitation and spiritual emptiness. This criticism reflected her broader concern about **commercialization that severed music from authentic spiritual and cultural roots**.[^18]

For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river" [(104)](https://anabaptistworld.org/8927-2/). This passage creates a powerful image where God's people nurse from God's breast, receiving both physical nourishment and spiritual comfort.

items.quote: Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is food for the sinful, like murky oil, it boils within bellies,
items.paragraph: For instance, Surah Ad-Dukhan (44:43-50) depicts the tree of Zaqqum: "Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is food for the sinful, like murky oil, it boils within bellies," creating disturbing imagery that viscerally impacts readers, evoking physical revulsion for ethical awakening. Surah Al-Waqi'ah (56:41-56) intensifies this with "scalding water" and "black smoke," functioning as a cruel spectacle to purge worldly illusions, promoting repentance. Applications note this as apocalyptic art, connecting to Artaud's views on van Gogh, where cruelty reveals metaphysical truths, though debates exist on whether this aligns with the Qur'an's merciful intent.[yaqeeninstitute.org](https://yaqeeninstitute.org/read/paper/perspectives-on-islamic-psychology-healing-of-emotions-in-the-quran)+更多 2

items.quote: could still, if he wanted to, play ‘within the tradition.’
items.paragraph: At the same time, Mary Lou Williams did acknowledge positive qualities in some modern developments – as long as they still “spoke the language” of the tradition. She remained, in her own way, an experimenter and was proud of not being “corny” or “hidebound” by the past[[57]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=Yet%20something%20in%20Taylor%E2%80%99s%20music,had%20happened%20since%20her%20reemergence). For example, she wrote new sacred music blending jazz and gospel, and even attempted an olive branch to the avant-garde by performing with Cecil Taylor (more on that below). Williams believed jazz could continue to evolve, but only by re-rooting itself in its origin. She pointed out that even John Coltrane, whose later work ventured far out, “could still, if he wanted to, play ‘within the tradition.’”[[58]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) That is why she accepted Coltrane’s explorations more than those of lesser players – because Coltrane had mastered blues and bebop fundamentals first. In short, Williams’s historiography held that the “core spirit” of jazz was the fervor of the spirituals and blues – a gift from God and the African-American experience – and that every great jazz style kept that spirit alive in new forms. Styles that retained swing, blues feeling, and creative improvisation on song forms (from New Orleans through swing to bop and some post-bop) earned her approval as legitimate continuations. Styles that abandoned those elements (atonal free jams with “no beat” or slick commercial tunes with no depth) she saw as aberrations. As a living bridge between the 1920s and 1970s, Mary Lou Williams championed an inclusive but values-driven view of jazz history: inclusion of any innovation that carries the flame of the blues and spiritual uplift, and exclusion of anything that douses that flame[[19]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=The%20importance%20of%20the%20blues,technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling)[[59]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=Williams%20herself%20explained%20it%20this,%E2%80%9D). Few artists have so passionately articulated the moral and spiritual narrative of jazz’s story as Williams did in her later years.

items.quote: organisations upon which commercial undertakings have decisive influence allowing them to exercise control because of structural situations, such as through their quality of shareholder or member, which could result in preferential access to the research results, should not be considered research organisations
items.paragraph: The directive defines "research organisation" as any entity whose primary goal is to conduct scientific research, including universities and their libraries, research institutes, and hospitals conducting research. Critically, the definition specifies that research organizations must act on a not-for-profit basis or in pursuit of a public-interest mission recognized by the state. Conversely, "organisations upon which commercial undertakings have decisive influence allowing them to exercise control because of structural situations, such as through their quality of shareholder or member, which could result in preferential access to the research results, should not be considered research organisations".[^17][^18]

items.quote: Option A has a higher chance of curing the disease (an estimated 80% success rate) but also carries a risk of severe fatigue. Option B is less likely to cure the disease (around 60%) but has milder side effects.
items.paragraph: - Generative AI (Natural Language Generation): A generative AI (often powered by large language models) in the AI-SDM framework plays the role of a communication and explanation engine. Its job is to take the predictions and evidence from the other AI components and turn them into clear, narrative explanations or educational material for the patient and clinician[[11]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2022.1016366/full#:~:text=importance%20of%20broadening%20the%20view,interaction%20with%20the%20systems%20available)[[22]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=algorithmic%20transparency,through%20Rapid%20Contextual%20Design%20methodology). For instance, a generative model could produce a patient-friendly summary of the pros and cons of each option: “Option A has a higher chance of curing the disease (an estimated 80% success rate) but also carries a risk of severe fatigue. Option B is less likely to cure the disease (around 60%) but has milder side effects.” It might also answer patient questions in real-time, or create visual aids or analogies to clarify complex information. Essentially, the generative AI ensures that information is presented in an understandable, tailored way – adjusting language to the patient’s health literacy level, translating raw statistics into meaningful terms, and even providing “narrative justifications” for recommendations (similar to the AI reasoning concept above) rather than just numbers[[8]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=users%20actually%20seek,this%20gap%20is%20not%20only)[[16]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=recommendation%20might%20generate%3A%20,while%20maintaining%20good%20pressure%20control). This makes the decision process more interactive and personalized.

items.quote: represents a role, sings, recites, declaims, interprets or executes an artistic work, or who directs it or engages in a similar creative activity
items.paragraph: - Coverage: The law covers performing artists in music, dance, and theater, as well as technicians in related creative trades[[67]](https://www.gub.uy/ministerio-trabajo-seguridad-social/comunicacion/noticias/seguridad-social-para-los-artistas#:~:text=Actualmente%20dentro%20de%20estos%20beneficios,Certificadora%2C%20seg%C3%BAn%20establece%20la%20ley). An artist is defined broadly (drawing from the Rome Convention definition of performers[[68]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=22%20En%20el%20art%C3%ADculo%201,El%20mismo)): it includes anyone who “represents a role, sings, recites, declaims, interprets or executes an artistic work, or who directs it or engages in a similar creative activity”[[67]](https://www.gub.uy/ministerio-trabajo-seguridad-social/comunicacion/noticias/seguridad-social-para-los-artistas#:~:text=Actualmente%20dentro%20de%20estos%20beneficios,Certificadora%2C%20seg%C3%BAn%20establece%20la%20ley). Importantly, it explicitly includes backstage creative workers (“oficios conexos”) such as set designers, costume designers, makeup artists, stage lighting and sound technicians – provided their work involves a creative process and is directly connected to a performance[[67]](https://www.gub.uy/ministerio-trabajo-seguridad-social/comunicacion/noticias/seguridad-social-para-los-artistas#:~:text=Actualmente%20dentro%20de%20estos%20beneficios,Certificadora%2C%20seg%C3%BAn%20establece%20la%20ley). This means not only actors and musicians, but also the crew who contribute artistically, are recognized as workers under the statute. (The law gives a committee the power to certify and add other related occupations over time[[69]](https://www.gub.uy/ministerio-trabajo-seguridad-social/comunicacion/noticias/seguridad-social-para-los-artistas#:~:text=cualquier%20forma%20una%20obra%20art%C3%ADstica%2C,Certificadora%2C%20seg%C3%BAn%20establece%20la%20ley).) Initially, literary authors and visual artists were not covered, but policymakers noted the need to extend social protection to those groups in the future[[70]](https://www.gub.uy/ministerio-trabajo-seguridad-social/comunicacion/noticias/seguridad-social-para-los-artistas#:~:text=como%20parte%20del%20per%C3%ADodo%20de,los%20escritores%20y%20artistas%20pl%C3%A1sticos). As of 2012, about 1,800 cultural workers had registered, skewed towards middle-aged performers, indicating many artists were beginning to formalize their status[[71]](https://www.gub.uy/ministerio-trabajo-seguridad-social/comunicacion/noticias/seguridad-social-para-los-artistas#:~:text=Por%20su%20parte%2C%20Brenta%C2%A0anunci%C3%B3%20una,supera%20los%2060%20a%C3%B1os).

items.quote: Why have you made a breach?
items.paragraph: The name given to Perez carries profound theological meaning: *Perez* means "breach" or "one who breaks through." The midwife's exclamation—"Why have you made a breach?"—transforms an obstetrical anomaly into a declaration of divine breakthrough. This difficult birth produces the ancestor in the line of David and ultimately Jesus, positioning the anomalous childbirth as a moment when God's redemptive purposes break through normal human structures of succession and expectation.[^16][^17]

items.quote: The Politics of Gender, Witnessing, Postcoloniality and Trauma: Bosnian Feminist Trajectories,
items.paragraph: Jasmina Husanović, a Bosnian scholar working at the intersection of gender studies, postcolonial theory, and trauma studies, approaches memory and historical violence through what she terms the "politics of witnessing" coupled with what might be called a "politics of hope." Her work, particularly her 2009 article "The Politics of Gender, Witnessing, Postcoloniality and Trauma: Bosnian Feminist Trajectories," addresses how trauma, gender violence, and postcolonial subjugation become sites for political and cultural intervention.[^20][^21]

items.quote: from January 1, 2015, only voluntarily donated organs from citizens will be used in transplants.
items.paragraph: The December 2014 announcement stated that "from January 1, 2015, only voluntarily donated organs from citizens will be used in transplants." On the surface, this appeared to be a definitive policy change ending the use of executed prisoner organs. However, the true meaning of this statement must be understood within the context of the March 2014 semantic reframing.[^17]

items.quote: The food of the sinners is only from the tree of Zaqqum. It is like murky oil that churns inside their bellies, like the boiling of hot water. One will be seized and dragged into the middle of the Hellfire, where scalding water will be poured over his head.
items.paragraph: The Qur'anic depictions of hellfire in Surah ad-Dukhan (Chapter 44) exemplify the Artaudian assault on sensory consciousness. Verses 43-59 describe the fate of the deniers in relentless, graphic detail: "The food of the sinners is only from the tree of Zaqqum. It is like murky oil that churns inside their bellies, like the boiling of hot water. One will be seized and dragged into the middle of the Hellfire, where scalding water will be poured over his head." This passage does not present abstract theological concepts but creates a multisensory nightmare scenario—the texture and taste of poisonous food, the sensation of internal churning, the experience of being violently seized and dragged, the shock of boiling water poured over the head.[^26]

items.quote: Did I conceive all this people? Did I give birth to them, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a sucking child'?
items.paragraph: The nursing metaphor extends to God's relationship with Israel. When Moses complains to God about carrying the burden of the people in the wilderness, God responds: "Did I conceive all this people? Did I give birth to them, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a sucking child'?" (Numbers 11:12). The passage explicitly identifies God as Israel's mother-figure and nursing caregiver, suggesting that **God's providential care of Israel in the wilderness is conceptually parallel to maternal nursing care**. The manna provided by God during the wilderness wandering is understood in Jewish tradition as functioning like mother's milk—providing complete nutritional and spiritual sustenance adapted to the people's developing needs, just as mother's milk composition changes as an infant grows.[^32][^33]

items.quote: According to clinical guidelines, Option A is recommended for patients with your profile
items.paragraph: - Evidence Synthesis & Recommendation AI: This component pulls in evidence-based recommendations – for instance, guidelines, clinical trial data, or best practices relevant to the patient’s condition. It can be thought of as an AI that combs through medical literature or guidelines to identify what interventions are generally recommended (and why). In AI-SDM, this model would present contextualized evidence to support each option. For example, it might retrieve guideline statements (“According to clinical guidelines, Option A is recommended for patients with your profile”) or compare options based on outcomes from studies. By injecting up-to-date medical knowledge, it ensures the discussion is informed by current evidence and not just the clinician’s memory[[20]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2022.1016366/full#:~:text=Decision%20support%20is%20of%20course,treating%20physician%2C%20but%20even%20for)[[21]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2022.1016366/full#:~:text=considerable%20increase%20in%20epistemic%20opacity,10%E2%80%9312). This component essentially serves as a smart evidence provider, ensuring that the options discussed are grounded in scientific research and that patients hear not only the clinician’s opinion but also what “the evidence says” about each choice.

items.quote: prisoners and other individuals in custody are not in a position to give free consent,
items.paragraph: The international medical community’s response up to 2015 was mixed, balancing cautious optimism with wariness. The World Medical Association (WMA) – which had been one of China’s harshest critics – reacted with reserved approval if the policy were genuine. The WMA has a clear position that executed prisoners must not be used as organ donors under any circumstances[[53]](https://www.wma.net/policy-tags/execution/#:~:text=stresses%20the%20importance%20of%20free,choice%20in%20organ%20donation%20and)[[61]](https://www.wma.net/policy-tags/execution/#:~:text=2,against%20coercion%20in%20all%20cases). Back in 2007, the WMA had extracted a promise from the Chinese Medical Association to adhere to this principle[[62]](https://www.wma.net/news-post/chinese-medical-association-reaches-agreement-with-world-medical-association-against-transplantation-of-prisoners-organs/#:~:text=Medical%20Association%2C%20Dr%20Wu%20Mingjiang%2C,said)[[63]](https://www.wma.net/news-post/chinese-medical-association-reaches-agreement-with-world-medical-association-against-transplantation-of-prisoners-organs/#:~:text=The%20announcement%20by%20the%20Chinese,removal%20or%20transplantation%20of%20organs), only to see prisoner organ use continue. Given that history, the WMA in 2015 was not content with mere proclamations. While welcoming the announcement in principle, WMA officials and ethicists underscored that “prisoners and other individuals in custody are not in a position to give free consent,” so even a so-called voluntary donation by an inmate would violate WMA guidelines[[53]](https://www.wma.net/policy-tags/execution/#:~:text=stresses%20the%20importance%20of%20free,choice%20in%20organ%20donation%20and)[[64]](https://www.wma.net/policy-tags/execution/#:~:text=that%20donation%20is%20in%20line,place%20adequate%20safeguards%20to%20protect). The WMA and other bodies urged China to provide transparency and allow independent scrutiny of its transplant system to ensure no prisoners’ organs were being used under the table[[50]](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(15%2960484-6/fulltext#:~:text=After%20repeated%20unfulfilled%20promises%20from,and%20open%20to%20international%20inspections). Essentially, the international medical establishment took a “trust but verify” approach: they praised the intent of China’s new policy but remained skeptical about its implementation.

items.quote: four months of work in a year will be computed as one year of contributions
items.paragraph: - Mechanisms: The law’s core mechanism is to assimilate performing artists into standard social security by accounting for their discontinuous work as cumulative employment. All short-term contracts are subject to normal payroll contributions (toward pension, health insurance, etc.), and the time worked is credited toward the artist’s social security record. Critically, the law stipulates that if an artist works at least 4 months (or 120 days) in a year, it will count as a full year of service for social security purposes[[55]](https://www.infobae.com/2016/01/27/1785698-que-ganan-y-que-pierden-los-artistas-la-implementacion-la-ley-del-actor/#:~:text=,respectivas%2C%20dentro%20del%20a%C3%B1o%20calendario). In other words, intermittent employment is aggregated: “four months of work in a year will be computed as one year of contributions”[[55]](https://www.infobae.com/2016/01/27/1785698-que-ganan-y-que-pierden-los-artistas-la-implementacion-la-ley-del-actor/#:~:text=,respectivas%2C%20dentro%20del%20a%C3%B1o%20calendario). This addresses the fact that many actors may only get a few engagements per year. (If they exceed 120 days, they still just get one year credit; if they work less, they get prorated credit, which was a point of concern[[56]](https://www.infobae.com/2016/01/27/1785698-que-ganan-y-que-pierden-los-artistas-la-implementacion-la-ley-del-actor/#:~:text=,lleguen%20a%20los%20120%20d%C3%ADas).) The law also ensures performers gain access to all standard benefits: health coverage (obra social), pension (SIPA retirement fund), unemployment insurance, family allowances, and occupational injury coverage, just like any formal worker[[49]](https://fia-actors.com/2015/10/30/adoption-of-the-law-of-the-actor-in-argentina-a-historical-moment/#:~:text=taking%20into%20account%20the%20intermittant,nature%20of%20their%20work)[[50]](https://www.infobae.com/2016/01/27/1785698-que-ganan-y-que-pierden-los-artistas-la-implementacion-la-ley-del-actor/#:~:text=A%20partir%20de%20esta%20Ley%2C,la%20implementaci%C3%B3n%20de%20la%20normativa). For example, an actor will accumulate pension rights and can eventually retire with an actors’ pension, and if between jobs, may qualify for unemployment benefits. Another adaptation is a provision to reconcile gaps: if multiple performance contracts are separated by short breaks, those breaks may still count toward continuity. (The Argentine law sets one year of service credit if 120 work days occurred, whether continuous or not, within the calendar year[[55]](https://www.infobae.com/2016/01/27/1785698-que-ganan-y-que-pierden-los-artistas-la-implementacion-la-ley-del-actor/#:~:text=,respectivas%2C%20dentro%20del%20a%C3%B1o%20calendario).) By mandating written contracts and union oversight, the law also formalized what was often informal gig work, thereby reducing evasion of contributions. Overall, Argentina’s mechanism essentially transforms performing arts gigs into covered employment spells, ensuring that a career composed of many short engagements translates into social security protection over the long term.

items.quote: did little to change her attitude toward the ‘New Thing.’
items.paragraph: That said, Mary Lou Williams did not entirely condemn every musician associated with the avant-garde. She was able to appreciate those who, in her opinion, still had mastery of the tradition. Notably, she had a complex respect for Cecil Taylor, the iconoclastic free jazz pianist. In 1977 Williams herself arranged to perform a high-profile duet concert with Cecil Taylor at Carnegie Hall (later released as the album Embraced). Many were shocked that she would share the stage with perhaps the most “out” pianist of the era, given her past comments[[61]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=Many%20people%20wondered%20why%20Mary,earth%2C%20no%20ears%2C%20not%20even). Williams admitted she initially expected the collaboration to be a “love fest” reconciling two camps of jazz, but it turned out to be an “infamous” and tense musical encounter[[63]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-mother-of-us-all/#:~:text=In%20the%201960s%20Williams%20penned,contributions%20had%20been%20largely%20overlooked)[[64]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=When%20pianist%20Mary%20Lou%20Williams,tells%20the%20story). Part of the conflict was Taylor’s aversion to playing any written or arranged music – he bristled that Williams had written out some duet parts (spirituals and rhythm patterns) for the concert[[65]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=of%20duets%2C%20and%20for%20dramatizing,she%20written%20a%20part%20for). He effectively ignored her planned structure and launched into his own improvisational approach, while Williams tried to find common ground by “play[ing] free and then…jump[ing] back to swinging.”[[66]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=revealed%20frayed%20nerves%20and%20disparate,To%20Mary) The resulting performance was challenging for audiences, and Williams later admitted it was not exactly the harmony she had hoped for. As JazzTimes writer Shaun Brady put it, the duet “did little to change her attitude toward the ‘New Thing.’”[[63]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-mother-of-us-all/#:~:text=In%20the%201960s%20Williams%20penned,contributions%20had%20been%20largely%20overlooked) After the concert, her skepticism of free jazz largely remained – especially toward those avant-gardists who, unlike Taylor, lacked a grounding in earlier styles.

items.quote: Why does this advice make sense here?
items.paragraph: Sources: Transparent AI systems share design/data details openly[[1]](https://www.f5.com/company/blog/crucial-concepts-in-ai-transparency-and-explainability#:~:text=Transparency%20in%20AI%20refers%20to,various%20aspects%20of%20the%20system), while XAI methods provide reasons for specific outputs (answering “Why did the model do that?”)[[13]](https://www.f5.com/company/blog/crucial-concepts-in-ai-transparency-and-explainability#:~:text=Key%20elements%20of%20AI%20explainability,include). However, merely explaining an algorithm’s output is often insufficient for clinical use – hence the push toward more explanatory or reasoning-based AI that delivers context-rich justifications (addressing “Why does this advice make sense here?”)[[4]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=While%20XAI%20answers%2C%20,different%20questions%20requiring%20different%20approaches). The example above illustrates the difference: traditional XAI might list abstract feature weights, whereas an AI reasoning approach produces a human-friendly narrative[[17]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=Consider%20a%20concrete%20example%20illustrating,recommend%20reducing%20the%20patient%27s%20blood)[[16]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=recommendation%20might%20generate%3A%20,while%20maintaining%20good%20pressure%20control).

items.quote: They will abide therein forever, and it will not be lightened for them, and they will be confounded therein
items.paragraph: > "They will abide therein forever, and it will not be lightened for them, and they will be confounded therein"

items.quote: Why is this recommendation sensible here?
items.paragraph: “Why is this recommendation sensible here?” – AI reasoning addresses: Given this patient’s context, why does the AI’s suggestion make sense? It provides a richer justification: tying the recommendation to clinical evidence, the patient’s own data and preferences, and logical reasoning[[4]](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2508.06352#:~:text=While%20XAI%20answers%2C%20,different%20questions%20requiring%20different%20approaches). Essentially, it answers whether the AI’s advice is meaningful and appropriate for the specific scenario (the kind of reasoning a human expert might articulate).

items.quote: You thought there was a real fire and were very scared. But it turned out to be just a practice – next time, we know that if the alarm rings and the teacher is calm, it’s likely just a drill.
items.paragraph: - Teach “Prediction Awareness” and Flexible Thinking: Educators can help students build an awareness of their own predictions and learn that outcomes can diverge from expectations without disaster. One classroom technique is to openly discuss events after they happen: “What did you expect would occur? And what actually happened? Was it as bad as you feared, or different from what you imagined?” This kind of guided reflection teaches the student that not all predictions will be correct, and that’s okay[[23]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=We%20can%20support%20neurodivergent%20learners,by). By labeling surprises and outcomes, the teacher demystifies them – a surprise is no longer a terrifying unknown but an event that can be analyzed and learned from. Over time, the student can internalize that prediction errors are information, not merely threats[[24]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=pathways%20as%20you%20rise%20out,of%20the%20pit)[[25]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Mindset%20and%20Neurodivergent%20Brains). For example, if an unexpected fire drill occurs, later the teacher might gently review: “You thought there was a real fire and were very scared. But it turned out to be just a practice – next time, we know that if the alarm rings and the teacher is calm, it’s likely just a drill.” Such debriefs help update the child’s predictive model of the world, making it more accurate and less anxiety-prone. Additionally, explicitly framing mistakes or surprises as learning opportunities (“errors provide us data to improve our predictions”[[24]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=pathways%20as%20you%20rise%20out,of%20the%20pit)) can reshape a student’s mindset. They begin to see that if something unexpected happens, they can adapt rather than panic, fostering cognitive flexibility.

items.quote: you need something to quell them…if jazz doesn’t come back on radio and TV soon…I see great havoc on earth
items.paragraph: Emerging Popular Styles (Rock/Fusion): Williams was equally outspoken about the influence of rock and commercial music on jazz. She largely disliked rock’s effect on both musicians and audiences. In the 1970s, jazz-rock fusion was in vogue and many jazz players were incorporating rock/funk beats. Williams, however, saw rock music as an anathema to jazz’s subtlety and spirit. She believed the dominance of rock on radio had harmed public taste and even people’s well-being. In a 1977 interview, she vented that “the commercial music that’s being played on radio and TV…makes people frantic” and overly nervous[[70]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=It%E2%80%99s%20music%20that%20should%20be,is%20making%20people%20too%20nervous). Jazz, in her view, was the antidote to this frenzy: “you need something to quell them…if jazz doesn’t come back on radio and TV soon…I see great havoc on earth”[[71]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=playing,is%20making%20people%20too%20nervous). This almost apocalyptic warning shows how strongly she felt that rock’s prevalence was culturally unhealthy, whereas jazz’s swing could “calm” and heal listeners. Williams singled out the heavy use of electronic amplification and loud volumes in modern music as a literal evil – she noted that her own hearing suffered and even young people were losing hearing from it, calling that “an evil to me”[[72]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=on%20radio%20and%20TV%20soon,is%20making%20people%20too%20nervous).

items.quote: accepted both musicians’ work because they could still, if they wanted to, play ‘within the tradition.’
items.paragraph: Interestingly though, Williams conceded that “something in Taylor’s music appealed to her, as did John Coltrane’s late playing.”[[67]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) She “accepted both musicians’ work because they could still, if they wanted to, play ‘within the tradition.’”[[58]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) This is a crucial insight: Mary Lou could tolerate avant-garde explorations if they came from an artist who had proven their command of jazz fundamentals (like chord changes, blues, swing). Cecil Taylor had classical training and huge technique; Coltrane had come up playing bebop and blues. She knew these men understood the language even when they chose to speak in tongues, so to speak. In contrast, she had no use for lesser players who dove into experimental music without that foundation. To her, those were “people without background…trying to be Coltrane” but failing[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them). In her words, “See the guys that they’re patterned after like Coltrane…they would never be a Coltrane because they don’t know anything about the Basie [style]. It’s just like…school – you can’t start at the top.”[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them) This quote reveals her nuanced esteem for John Coltrane: she regarded him as an advanced artist who earned his innovations through grounding in tradition. Indeed, she included Coltrane’s name on a thriving branch of her Jazz Tree (among the “vital” geniuses)[[35]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=produced%20the%20first%20spirituals,branch%20all%20to%20itself), indicating she absolutely acknowledged his importance to jazz history. She reportedly was moved by Coltrane’s spirituality – his quest in music likely resonated with her own faith. While she critiqued “free music” in general, she praised Coltrane’s integrity. She told one interviewer that Coltrane “knows what he’s doing” unlike many imitators[[69]](https://downbeat.com/archives/detail/marian-mcpartland-in-conversation-with-mary-lou-williams/P1#:~:text=Mary%20Lou%20Williams%3A%20Into%20The,But%20these%20people%20without).

items.quote: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger
items.paragraph: God's response to Rebekah's distress reveals the theological meaning of this difficult pregnancy: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). The physical struggle within the womb becomes a microcosmic representation of national struggle and divine election. The pain of pregnancy thus transmits theological significance—it demonstrates that national formation involves conflict, suffering, and divine reversal of human expectations (the younger serving the elder violates cultural primogeniture norms).[^14]

items.quote: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant
items.paragraph: The concept of covenant is fundamentally linked to maternal imagery through the promise made to Abraham: "I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant" (Gen. 17:7) [(27)](https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BB27630124). This promise establishes that the covenant relationship is transmitted through generations, creating a family-like structure where God is both father and mother to Israel.

items.quote: Give me children, or I shall die
items.paragraph: These depictions are vividly illustrated in the experiences of Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel, three of the four matriarchs whose barrenness heightens narrative drama and theological depth. Sarah's long infertility (Genesis 11:30) leads her to surrogacy with Hagar (Genesis 16:2), but God intervenes at her advanced age: "The Lord took note of Sarah" (paqad, Genesis 21:1), opening her womb for Isaac without any merit-based trigger—she shows no piety or repentance. Rebekah, barren for twenty years (Genesis 25:21), conceives twins after Isaac's prayer, with God shaping her womb (midrashically, as she lacked one initially), linking her fertility to divine mercy and national promise. Rachel, "barren" amid Leah's fertility (Genesis 29:31), despairs—"Give me children, or I shall die" (Genesis 30:1)—and uses surrogacy (Bilhah) and mandrakes, but God "remembered Rachel" (Genesis 30:22), opening her womb for Joseph without her direct appeal. These stories construct theological identity by portraying God as the life-giver, ensuring covenantal heirs like Isaac (over Ishmael) and Jacob (over Esau), while nationally, they found Israel's tribes, transforming personal anguish into communal origins.[jwa.org](https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/barren-women-in-the-bible)+更多 2

items.quote: freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development
items.paragraph: - Right to Self-Determination: It declares that “all peoples have the right to self-determination.” This means every people can “freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development”[[35]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=,which%20have%20not%20yet%20attained). The universality of this right was a bold affirmation that no colony could be excluded or indefinitely controlled under pretexts of readiness or civilization.

items.quote: for each new show, a completely new team
items.paragraph: 2. Production Model: The production structures behind TV anime and Nordic Noir dramas differ significantly due to their industry contexts. Japanese TV anime is typically produced in a high-volume, industrial mode. Dozens of anime series are made each season, often by specialized animation studios working with tight budgets and schedules. A common model is the production committee system, where a consortium of companies (studio, publisher, toy manufacturer, TV network, etc.) co-fund a series to spread risk and capitalize on various revenue streams (broadcast rights, merchandise, home video, etc.). Anime episodes are usually aired weekly on Japanese television late-night slots (for teen/adult anime) or daytime (for children’s anime), and many series run for one “cour” (season of 12–13 episodes) or longer if successful. The emphasis is on creating content that can succeed in Japan’s domestic market first – indeed, much TV anime is “domestic and mass-produced” entertainment tailored to local fan demographics[[9]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=studies%2C%20anime%20has%20been%20dislocated,produced%20anime%20TV). Series are frequently adaptations of popular manga or games, ensuring a pre-existing fan base. Production quality can vary; TV anime often uses cost-saving animation techniques (limited frame counts, repeated shots) to meet deadlines, relying on viewer imagination to fill gaps. In contrast, Nordic Noir TV dramas (e.g. Danish, Swedish series) follow a “quality over quantity” production model typical of small-market prestige television. These series are usually produced by public service broadcasters or collaborations (DR in Denmark, SVT in Sweden, etc.), sometimes with co-production funding from neighboring countries or distributors like the BBC. Instead of year-round continuous output, a Nordic noir drama is developed more like a contained project: for example, The Killing was created with one season of 20 episodes initially, and The Bridge with 10-episode seasons. Scandinavian drama production values prioritize strong writing, location cinematography, and high production quality relative to budget. Interestingly, Danish broadcaster DR adopted a policy of rotating creative teams: “for each new show, a completely new team” of writers, directors, and crew is assembled, rather than reusing the same staff, to cultivate fresh talent[[27]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=In%20fact%2C%20DR%20developed%20its,them%20for%20a%20Danish%20context). They aim for perhaps one or two successful seasons of a series, then conclude it and move talent to new projects[[28]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=They%20also%20focused%20on%20fostering,crew%20for%20each%20new%20show). This is nearly the opposite of anime’s model, where if a show is popular (e.g. Naruto), it can run for years with hundreds of episodes. Nordic Noir production also tends to be auteur-driven to an extent: specific head writers or directors often imprint a distinct style. Additionally, being publicly funded or subsidized, these dramas don’t rely on merchandising in the way anime does; success is measured in viewership and format sales abroad. In summary, anime production is highly prolific, iterative, and merchandise-linked, whereas Nordic Noir production is limited-series, filmmaker-driven, and focused on narrative coherence and export viability. One consequence is that anime studios may work on multiple series simultaneously in assembly-line fashion, while a Nordic Noir team pours resources into one story at a time.

items.quote: globally consumed niche media almost concurrently
items.paragraph: 1. Global Popularity Timeline: Both Japanese TV anime and Scandinavian “Nordic Noir” crime dramas rose from niche to global prominence in roughly the same era, albeit with different trajectories. Anime’s international boom began earlier: Japanese animation started making inroads abroad by the 1980s and 1990s – for example, with films like Akira (1988) and series like Dragon Ball Z and Sailor Moon reaching overseas audiences[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_anime#:~:text=Over%20the%20following%20decades%2C%20anime,pop%20culture%2C%20known%20for%20its). By the late 1990s and 2000s, anime had become a global phenomenon, bolstered by fan conventions, home video, and later internet streaming. The “anime wave” in North America and Europe accelerated in the late 2000s as online platforms (Crunchyroll, etc.) made series widely accessible, and anime moved from a cult following to mainstream youth culture. In contrast, Nordic Noir’s breakthrough on the world stage came in the early 2010s. While Scandinavian crime novels (e.g. Stieg Larsson’s Millennium trilogy in 2005–2007) had garnered international readers, it was the subtitled TV series that truly popularized Nordic Noir globally. The pivotal moment was the Danish series The Killing (Forbrydelsen), which originally aired in 2007 in Denmark and was later broadcast in the UK on BBC Four in 2011 – “The Killing was the breakthrough” that introduced international audiences to the style[[24]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=,of%20Communication%20and%20Media%2C%20says)[[25]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=But%20it%20didn%27t%20break%20through,at%20Aarhus%20University%20in%20Denmark). This was swiftly followed by Sweden/Denmark’s The Bridge (2011) and others; by the mid-2010s, Nordic Noir dramas had gained a dedicated global viewership. In the UK, for example, “viewers embraced a steady stream of foreign-language dramas” after the success of these Nordic series, with The Bridge drawing nearly 2 million viewers on BBC4[[26]](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2016/jan/02/foreign-tv-drama-bbc-channel4-netflix#:~:text=I%20t%E2%80%99s%20not%20only%20Faroese,only%20by%20BBC1%20and%20ITV). To summarize, anime’s global rise was more gradual (spanning late 20th century into 2000s) and initially fan-driven, whereas Nordic Noir’s export success was more sudden around 2010–2012, catalyzed by strategic broadcasting (notably BBC4) and the post-2000 appetite for high-quality international TV drama[[25]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=But%20it%20didn%27t%20break%20through,at%20Aarhus%20University%20in%20Denmark)[[26]](https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2016/jan/02/foreign-tv-drama-bbc-channel4-netflix#:~:text=I%20t%E2%80%99s%20not%20only%20Faroese,only%20by%20BBC1%20and%20ITV). Both forms became internationally prominent within a few years of each other, essentially “globally consumed niche media almost concurrently” by the late 2000s and early 2010s (to borrow an observation from academic commentary).

items.quote: has been shown to minimize anxiety
items.paragraph: - Provide a Sensory-Friendly Environment: Small classroom adjustments can buffer a student from overwhelming stimuli. For example, controlling noise levels (or offering noise-cancelling headphones) and using softer, natural lighting instead of harsh fluorescents can prevent sensory bombardment[[15]](https://learningarts.com/autism-support-strategies/#:~:text=Many%20individuals%20with%20autism%20have,greatly%20enhance%20comfort%20and%20functionality)[[16]](https://learningarts.com/autism-support-strategies/#:~:text=For%20example%2C%20some%20individuals%20with,overwhelmed%20can%20also%20be%20beneficial). A quieter, calmly lit setting means the student isn’t constantly startled by sudden loud sounds or painful bright lights, thereby lowering the frequency of unexpected sensory events that could trigger anxiety. In other words, reducing sensory input “has been shown to minimize anxiety” in autistic individuals[[17]](https://autism.org/autism-and-anxiety/#:~:text=,been%20shown%20to%20minimize%20anxiety) by decreasing the number of aversive surprises in their day.

items.quote: One of the ways she would have me learn was to sit literally right next to her while she played. You're connecting with the physicality of what she's doing; it's not intellectual, it's a physical, dynamic experience. That was how she was taught—sitting on her mother's lap and listening, watching her, being that close. It was powerful because you're not only observing close at hand, you're also feeling the intensity.
items.paragraph: One of her most distinctive teaching practices involved **intimate physical proximity**. Pianist Sumito Tonooka, one of her Duke students, recalled: "One of the ways she would have me learn was to sit literally right next to her while she played. You're connecting with the physicality of what she's doing; it's not intellectual, it's a physical, dynamic experience. That was how she was taught—sitting on her mother's lap and listening, watching her, being that close. It was powerful because you're not only observing close at hand, you're also feeling the intensity."[^1]

items.quote: AI is transforming the auditor’s role from manual data checking to strategic risk analysis.
items.paragraph: - Evolution of the Auditor’s Role and Skills: The integration of AI into auditing is changing the nature of auditors’ work and the skills they need to succeed. With AI handling a lot of data analysis, the auditor’s role is shifting from manually verifying transactions to interpreting AI results and exercising higher-level judgment. Auditors are increasingly becoming analysts and strategists, focusing on risk assessment, investigating exceptions, and communicating insights. As one commentary put it, “AI is transforming the auditor’s role from manual data checking to strategic risk analysis.”[[54]](https://skywork.ai/skypage/en/MindBridge-AI:-An-Auditor's-Deep-Dive-into-Financial-Risk-Intelligence/1975266275889311744#:~:text=Today%2C%20that%20reality%20is%20being,In%20this) Auditors must understand how to work with AI outputs – for example, understanding what a risk score implies, or validating the findings using their professional skepticism. Far from making auditors obsolete, these AI tools augment human auditors, allowing them to be more effective. Human expertise is still crucial: auditors must evaluate whether an anomaly is truly an issue or a false positive, design appropriate responses, and make judgments that AI cannot (especially around qualitative factors and context). In fact, many in the industry emphasize that human oversight becomes more essential – not less – in the age of AI auditing[[55]](https://emerj.com/paving-the-way-for-continuous-auditing-workflows-in-financial-services-with-ai-mindbridge-wells-fargo-gulfport-bank-of-china-citi/#:~:text=explaining%20it%20through%20simple%2C%20relatable,more%20essential%E2%80%94not%20less%E2%80%94in%20financial%20services). Auditors now need to blend traditional accounting knowledge with data analytics literacy. This has led to changes in training and education: firms are upskilling their staff on data analysis and AI interpretation, and some are even hiring professionals with dual backgrounds in accounting and data science. We also see new roles emerging (e.g. “AI Audit Specialist” or “Analytics Champion” within firms) who serve as liaisons between the audit team and the technology. Over time, proficiency with AI tools like MindBridge is likely to become a standard expectation for auditors, much like spreadsheet skills became essential in the past. The net impact is that the audit profession is evolving – arguably becoming more attractive to new talent – as mundane tasks are minimized and auditors can focus on deeper investigative and consultative aspects of their work[[56]](https://www.mindbridge.ai/solutions/audit-assurance/#:~:text=Attract%20and%20retain%20top%20audit,talent).
