items.quote: God remembered Rachel… and opened her womb
items.paragraph: The stories of Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel illustrate this dynamic vividly. Sarah’s conception of Isaac is a miraculous reversal of nature. Long barren and post-menopausal, Sarah conceives “at the set time of which God had spoken” – a fulfillment of covenant promise rather than ordinary biology. Abraham is the physical father, but the narrative stresses God’s power: “The LORD did for Sarah as He had promised” (Gen. 21:1). Rebekah’s pregnancy likewise occurs only after divine intervention: “Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD answered him, and Rebekah his wife conceived” (Gen. 25:21). Isaac’s role is to seek God, underscoring that conception comes by divine blessing, not automatic fertility. Rachel’s story is the most drawn-out struggle. Defined by her barrenness, Rachel at first resorts to folk remedies and having her maid bear surrogate children. Yet only when “God remembered Rachel… and opened her womb” did she finally conceive Joseph[[2]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20assignment%20of%20divine%20activity,moment%2C%20the%20womb%20was%E2%80%94by%20default%E2%80%94closed). Upon Joseph’s birth, Rachel exclaims that God has “taken away my disgrace” (Gen. 30:23), highlighting that motherhood – and the honor of founding a family – was viewed as a divine gift lifting the “shame” of childlessness[[4]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=%E2%80%9CRachel%20was%20barren%E2%80%9D%20%28Gen%2029%3A31%29,words%2C%20addressed%20to%20Jacob%2C%20are)[[5]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=Rachel%2C%20in%20naming%20Joseph%2C%20makes,clear%20what%20infertility%20feels%20like). In all these cases, the metaphors of planting and opening convey that while fathers contribute seed, it is God who causes life to sprout. The patriarchs themselves acknowledge this: human procreation is ultimately an act of God, integral to His covenant plan for Israel’s ancestors.

items.quote: immediate steps shall be taken...to transfer all powers to the people of these territories...in order to enable them to enjoy complete independence and freedom.
items.paragraph: The Declaration's first article asserted an unqualified principle: "All peoples have an inalienable right to complete freedom, the exercise of their sovereignty and the integrity of their national territory." The Declaration proceeded to declare that "immediate steps shall be taken...to transfer all powers to the people of these territories...in order to enable them to enjoy complete independence and freedom." Importantly, the Declaration stipulated that colonialism should end "unconditionally," rejecting colonial powers' arguments that dependent peoples required further tutelage.[^24][^25][^26]

items.quote: All my life I have felt that ‘the Blues’ was a special kind of music, expressing everyday experience…It’s music above racism and bitterness, and it shows heroism,
items.paragraph: Central to Williams’s view was the primacy of the blues. She did not regard blues as merely one genre or era, but rather as the lifeblood running through all of jazz history. In her words, “the blues was the spiritual feeling in jazz.”[[47]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=Langston%20Hughes%20called%20the%20blues,life%E2%80%94or%20about%20black%20American%20music) It was the element that kept the music honest, emotional, and connected to its source. Williams often pointed out that the blues transcended bitterness and conveyed a universal humanity. “All my life I have felt that ‘the Blues’ was a special kind of music, expressing everyday experience…It’s music above racism and bitterness, and it shows heroism,” she wrote in one album’s notes[[48]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=My%20Mama%20Pinned%20a%20Rose,98). Thus she felt blues expression had to permeate every stage of jazz for it to retain meaning. In her Jazz Tree diagram, as noted, she drew “BLUES” alongside each era from spirituals onward, emphasizing that blues techniques and feeling are integral to ragtime, swing, bebop and beyond[[30]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=tree%20grows%2C%E2%80%94thick%20and%20straight,the%20vital%20musicians%20in%20whose). Indeed, Williams admired figures like Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and Charlie Parker precisely because “in [their] music the blues flourish” even as the styles changed[[34]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=stopped%20on%20the%20left%2C%20where,whose%20music%20the%20blues%20flourish). Conversely, she was skeptical of any approach that removed the blues or gospel element. For Williams, to lose the blues was to lose the soul of jazz. This conviction underpinned her criticism of certain post-1950s trends (as we’ll see). It also explains why she had her students continually sing spirituals and blues – she wanted them to internalize that feeling as the foundation for any jazz they would play[[9]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=have%20to%20hear%20great%20music,semester%2C%20I%20gave%20the%20kids)[[12]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=they%20sing%2C%20%60shoo,Pushing%20back%20her).

items.quote: if load is high then scale out
items.paragraph: - Fuzzy Logic Rules: A variant of rule-based scaling that uses fuzzy logic to allow descriptive threshold rules (like “if load is high then scale out”) instead of crisp numeric cutoffs. A fuzzy auto-scaler maintains a set of human-defined If-Then rules using linguistic terms (e.g. low, medium, high CPU)[[5]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07909v1#:~:text=inter,40%2C%2016). The fuzzy inference engine interpolates these to decide how much to scale. This approach can be more flexible than fixed thresholds by handling uncertainty and providing smoother decisions. The core principle is still reactive (responding to current metrics), but with a range of response levels rather than a binary trigger. Advantages: Fuzzy rules incorporate expert knowledge and can avoid the brittleness of static thresholds (e.g. scaling gradually as “high” utilization increases). Limitations: They require deep understanding of the application to craft good rules[[6]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07909v1#:~:text=Fuzzy%20inference%2C%20in%20contrast%20to,40%2C%2016), and like threshold policies, they don’t learn or adapt on their own. Maintaining the rule base for complex systems is labor-intensive.

items.quote: In group work, even though we normally stay quiet during class, it’s actually expected that you talk to your group
items.paragraph: For example, teachers and support staff can make it a practice to directly explain important implicit rules (“When the bell rings at the end of class, that’s the signal that you can leave – even if the teacher doesn’t say ‘class dismissed’”) and context-specific expectations (“In group work, even though we normally stay quiet during class, it’s actually expected that you talk to your group”). By turning these hidden rules into visible, spoken ones, we greatly reduce the ambiguity in social and school situations. The student no longer has to predict others’ behavior or read between the lines to figure out what to do; they have a clearer map. This not only prevents misunderstandings and the negative social feedback that can follow, but also directly lowers anxiety – the student can be more at ease when they know the “code” of their environment. Researcher and educator Brenda Smith Myles emphasizes that hidden curriculum skills are essential for individuals with ASD precisely because these students often don’t detect social subtleties on their own[[29]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=The%20hidden%20curriculum%20is%20assumed,bound%2C%20literal%2C%20and%20rule%20enforcers). Without instruction, a child might inadvertently violate an unwritten rule and face ridicule or isolation, which then skyrockets anxiety in future interactions[[31]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=Impact%20of%20the%20Hidden%20Curriculum).

items.quote: people without background…trying to be Coltrane
items.paragraph: Interestingly though, Williams conceded that “something in Taylor’s music appealed to her, as did John Coltrane’s late playing.”[[67]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) She “accepted both musicians’ work because they could still, if they wanted to, play ‘within the tradition.’”[[58]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) This is a crucial insight: Mary Lou could tolerate avant-garde explorations if they came from an artist who had proven their command of jazz fundamentals (like chord changes, blues, swing). Cecil Taylor had classical training and huge technique; Coltrane had come up playing bebop and blues. She knew these men understood the language even when they chose to speak in tongues, so to speak. In contrast, she had no use for lesser players who dove into experimental music without that foundation. To her, those were “people without background…trying to be Coltrane” but failing[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them). In her words, “See the guys that they’re patterned after like Coltrane…they would never be a Coltrane because they don’t know anything about the Basie [style]. It’s just like…school – you can’t start at the top.”[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them) This quote reveals her nuanced esteem for John Coltrane: she regarded him as an advanced artist who earned his innovations through grounding in tradition. Indeed, she included Coltrane’s name on a thriving branch of her Jazz Tree (among the “vital” geniuses)[[35]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=produced%20the%20first%20spirituals,branch%20all%20to%20itself), indicating she absolutely acknowledged his importance to jazz history. She reportedly was moved by Coltrane’s spirituality – his quest in music likely resonated with her own faith. While she critiqued “free music” in general, she praised Coltrane’s integrity. She told one interviewer that Coltrane “knows what he’s doing” unlike many imitators[[69]](https://downbeat.com/archives/detail/marian-mcpartland-in-conversation-with-mary-lou-williams/P1#:~:text=Mary%20Lou%20Williams%3A%20Into%20The,But%20these%20people%20without).

items.quote: have the right to donate organs
items.paragraph: In his March 2014 Beijing Times interview, Huang stated that death-row prisoners "have the right to donate organs" and that prisoner donations would continue as part of the "voluntary" system once integrated into COTRS. items.quote: Which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?
items.paragraph: Linguistically, the Qur'an's assonance, alliteration, and vivid imagery arouse sensory responses by stimulating cognitive and emotional processing. For instance, Surah Ar-Rahman (55:1-4) repeats "Which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?" in a rhythmic pattern that builds arousal through novelty and repetition, evoking wonder and gratitude. Psychological analyses frame the Qur'an as a "cure" for emotional imbalances, arousing reflection on anger, sorrow, and fear to foster healing. In Surah Al-Imran (3:134), "Those who curb their anger and pardon people," arousal from evocative language stimulates forbearance, transforming reactive emotions into virtuous states. Emotional typologies in the Qur'an, drawing on models like Plutchik's, categorize responses such as joy or fear aroused by divine narratives, emphasizing sensory immersion through sound and imagery. This application highlights the Qur'an's role in modulating arousal for spiritual growth, though scholars note cultural adaptations are needed to avoid reductive psychologizing.[yaqeeninstitute.org](https://yaqeeninstitute.org/read/paper/perspectives-on-islamic-psychology-healing-of-emotions-in-the-quran)[iqs.sbu.ac.ir](https://iqs.sbu.ac.ir/article_105074.html)

items.quote: the blues was the spiritual feeling in jazz.
items.paragraph: Central to Williams’s view was the primacy of the blues. She did not regard blues as merely one genre or era, but rather as the lifeblood running through all of jazz history. In her words, “the blues was the spiritual feeling in jazz.”[[47]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=Langston%20Hughes%20called%20the%20blues,life%E2%80%94or%20about%20black%20American%20music) It was the element that kept the music honest, emotional, and connected to its source. Williams often pointed out that the blues transcended bitterness and conveyed a universal humanity. “All my life I have felt that ‘the Blues’ was a special kind of music, expressing everyday experience…It’s music above racism and bitterness, and it shows heroism,” she wrote in one album’s notes[[48]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=My%20Mama%20Pinned%20a%20Rose,98). Thus she felt blues expression had to permeate every stage of jazz for it to retain meaning. In her Jazz Tree diagram, as noted, she drew “BLUES” alongside each era from spirituals onward, emphasizing that blues techniques and feeling are integral to ragtime, swing, bebop and beyond[[30]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=tree%20grows%2C%E2%80%94thick%20and%20straight,the%20vital%20musicians%20in%20whose). Indeed, Williams admired figures like Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and Charlie Parker precisely because “in [their] music the blues flourish” even as the styles changed[[34]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=stopped%20on%20the%20left%2C%20where,whose%20music%20the%20blues%20flourish). Conversely, she was skeptical of any approach that removed the blues or gospel element. For Williams, to lose the blues was to lose the soul of jazz. This conviction underpinned her criticism of certain post-1950s trends (as we’ll see). It also explains why she had her students continually sing spirituals and blues – she wanted them to internalize that feeling as the foundation for any jazz they would play[[9]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=have%20to%20hear%20great%20music,semester%2C%20I%20gave%20the%20kids)[[12]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=they%20sing%2C%20%60shoo,Pushing%20back%20her).

items.quote: cutting flesh to return to father, slicing bone to return to mother
items.paragraph: - Nezha (Demon Orb vs. Spirit Pearl): In the traditional tale and older adaptations, Nezha is the reincarnation of a Lingzhu (Spirit Pearl) and is depicted as a heroic but impetuous child who rebels against authority (famously even against his father). The 1979 film showed Nezha as a righteous youth who slays the Dragon King’s son and ultimately sacrifices himself (“cutting flesh to return to father, slicing bone to return to mother”) as an act of defiance and atonement. In contrast, Ne Zha 2 (following the 2019 prequel) radically redefines Nezha’s origin: he is born with a cursed Demon Orb soul rather than the pure Spirit Pearl[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_Zha_2#:~:text=In%20the%20original%20work%2C%20there,with%20the%20help%20of%20his). This twist gives Nezha a darker, more conflicted nature – he is fated to be a demon in this storyline, which modernizes his character arc. Instead of a naïvely righteous boy, the film’s Nezha struggles with an inner demonic power versus a heroic destiny. Notably, the “Lingzhu version” of Nezha’s design in Ne Zha 2 (seen when Nezha attains an evolved immortal form) deliberately pays homage to the 1979 film’s iconic image of Nezha[[23]](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%93%AA%E5%90%92%E4%B9%8B%E9%AD%94%E7%AB%A5%E9%97%B9%E6%B5%B7#:~:text=%5D%E3%80%82%E5%AF%B9%E4%BA%8E%E4%B8%9C%E6%B5%B7%E9%BE%99%E7%8E%8B%E6%95%96%E5%85%89%EF%BC%8C%E5%88%B6%E4%BD%9C%E7%BB%84%E6%9B%BE%E6%89%93%E7%AE%97%E5%8F%82%E8%80%831992%E5%B9%B4%E9%A6%99%E6%B8%AF%E7%94%B5%E5%BD%B1%E3%80%8A%E9%B9%BF%E9%BC%8E%E8%AE%B0%E3%80%8B%E4%B8%AD%E2%80%9C%E5%87%B6%E7%A5%9E%E6%81%B6%E7%85%9E%E3%80%81%E4%BA%94%E5%A4%A7%E4%B8%89%E7%B2%97%E2%80%9D%E7%9A%84%E9%B3%8C%E6%8B%9C%E5%BD%A2%E8%B1%A1%EF%BC%8C%E4%BD%86%E5%90%8E%E6%9D%A5%E5%90%AC%E5%8F%96%E8%A7%82%E4%BC%97%E7%9A%84%E5%BB%BA%E8%AE%AE%EF%BC%8C%E6%94%B9%E4%B8%BA%E5%B8%85%E6%B0%94%E7%9A%84%E5%A3%AE%E5%B9%B4%E5%BD%A2%E8%B1%A1,%E3%80%82). Thus, the filmmakers acknowledge the classic portrayal (the traditional youthful look with the red bellyband, gold bracelets, and lotus feet) even as they update it. Additionally, Ne Zha 2 shifts Nezha’s relationship with his parents: instead of rebelling against a tyrannical father (as in myth, where Li Jing and Nezha have deep conflict[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_Zha_2#:~:text=Zha%27s%20main%20deeds%20included%20randomly,resurrection%2C%20which%20caused%20Nezha%20to)), Nezha here is motivated by family love and protection. His parents (Li Jing and Lady Yin) are supportive figures rather than antagonists, a significant departure from the anti-patriarchal angle of the original story. Overall, the film’s Nezha retains his rebellious, fiery spirit but is more complex – a teen burdened by demonic powers yet choosing righteousness, and finding strength through cooperation and parental support rather than in opposition to them.

items.quote: you could feel the prayer in the music.
items.paragraph: John Coltrane: Although Coltrane’s style (especially in the ’60s) was seen by some as part of the avant-garde or at least extremely experimental, Williams had a deep respect for John Coltrane. As noted earlier, she accepted his late, free-form ventures because she knew his grounding in tradition was strong[[58]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29). Williams had known Coltrane since his earlier years (they likely crossed paths in the 1940s–50s scene), and she recognized his immense talent and spiritual approach. In fact, Williams shared Coltrane’s spiritual orientation; both created religiously inspired music (Coltrane’s A Love Supreme, Williams’s Black Christ of the Andes and Mary Lou’s Mass). Williams reportedly said that when Coltrane played, “you could feel the prayer in the music.” She appreciated that “he knows what he’s doing” even in complex improvisations[[69]](https://downbeat.com/archives/detail/marian-mcpartland-in-conversation-with-mary-lou-williams/P1#:~:text=Mary%20Lou%20Williams%3A%20Into%20The,But%20these%20people%20without).

items.quote: kids [started] coming from all over…telling their parents they’d discovered a new kind of music
items.paragraph: Mary Lou Williams (right) sharing the piano with a student at Duke University in the late 1970s. During the 1970s, Mary Lou Williams dedicated herself to educating a new generation about jazz. In 1977 she became the first artist-in-residence at Duke University, a position she held until her death in 1981[[1]](https://www.amsmusicology.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2017-rochester.pdf#:~:text=By%20the%201970s%2C%20Mary%20Lou,In%20this%20paper%20I%20examine)[[2]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=,to%20allow%20as%20many). At Duke she taught a credited History of Jazz course (assisted by her manager, Jesuit Father Peter O’Brien) and led the Duke Jazz Ensemble[[3]](https://www.amsmusicology.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2017-rochester.pdf#:~:text=her%20death%20in%201981%2C%20she,oriented%20lecture%20style). Beyond campus, she frequently gave lecture-demonstrations, workshops, and even choral clinics at other colleges and churches during semester breaks[[2]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=,to%20allow%20as%20many). Williams saw these activities as part of a “mission – to bring jazz back to the young”, believing jazz needed to “create an educated audience” and inspire future jazz talents[[4]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=,my%20hands%20beat%20hers%20to)[[5]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%2C%20and%20a%20new%20pianist%2C,They%27re%20looking). She was excited to see students discover jazz – for example, after a 1970 club engagement, she proudly noted “kids [started] coming from all over…telling their parents they’d discovered a new kind of music”[[6]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=believes%20she%20has%20had%20an,lining%20up%20to%20get%20in).

items.quote: the woman took the baby and nursed him
items.paragraph: The **story of Moses and his biological mother Jochebed** illustrates this principle paradigmatically. After Moses's birth during the persecution of Hebrew male infants, his mother places him in a basket on the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter discovers the child and desires to keep him. Crucially, Moses's sister Miriam appears before Pharaoh's daughter and asks: "Shall I go and call a woman for you who is nursing from the Hebrew women, so that she may nurse the child for you?" (Exodus 2:7). Pharaoh's daughter agrees, and "the woman took the baby and nursed him" (Exodus 2:9)—unknowingly, this woman is Moses's biological mother, Jochebed.[^22]

items.quote: unless they are already powerful in other digital markets
items.paragraph: - Massive Economies of Scale: Operating a global cloud requires enormous capital investment in data centers, networking, and R&D. The hyperscalers benefit from scale economies that new entrants cannot easily match. For instance, building a single large-scale cloud region can cost hundreds of millions of euros and 5–6 years of lead time[[16]](https://competition-forum.com/cloud-computing-the-french-competition-authoritys-extensive-analysis-of-competition-and-future-perspectives/#:~:text=To%20get%20to%20the%20heart,taking%20five%20to%20six%20years)[[17]](https://competition-forum.com/cloud-computing-the-french-competition-authoritys-extensive-analysis-of-competition-and-future-perspectives/#:~:text=While%20these%20high%20costs%20and,a%20position%20to%20hinder%20competition). These high fixed costs and long development timelines raise entry barriers. Market leaders also realize lower unit costs by spreading investments over millions of customers, letting them price services very competitively. This scale advantage makes rapid entry by any new provider very unlikely “unless they are already powerful in other digital markets”[[18]](https://www.autoritedelaconcurrence.fr/en/press-release/cloud-computing-autorite-de-la-concurrence-issues-its-market-study-competition-cloud#:~:text=applications%20in%202021) – indeed only giant tech firms (Amazon, Microsoft, Google, etc.) have been able to compete at this top tier.

items.quote: What does this anime tell us about society, culture, or the human condition?
items.paragraph: - Textual and Thematic Analysis: A dominant approach treats anime as a text to be interpreted for meaning[[1]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/#:~:text=When%20we%20think%20about%20how,Entering%20the%20Multiverse%3A%20Perspectives%20on). Scholars in this vein analyze narratives, characters, and themes in anime much as one would literature or film. They often connect specific anime works to broader critical theories or cultural themes[[2]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/#:~:text=Hayao%20Miyazaki%E2%80%99s%20Ponyo%20on%20the,particular%20critical%20theories%20%E2%80%93%20this). For example, researchers have published readings of anime through lenses like climate fiction (cli-fi), feminism, or philosophy[[1]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/#:~:text=When%20we%20think%20about%20how,Entering%20the%20Multiverse%3A%20Perspectives%20on)[[3]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/#:~:text=imply%20connecting%20particular%20anime%20texts,terms%20%E2%80%9Cthe%20materiality%20of%20animation%E2%80%9D). Susan Napier’s early work is emblematic, examining how anime like Akira or Princess Mononoke reflect Japanese cultural imaginations (e.g. disaster, mythology, identity). This approach commonly asks “What does this anime tell us about society, culture, or the human condition?” and positions anime as a mirror of Japanese society or global issues. However, critics note that such analyses sometimes become mere summaries of plots or allegorical “book reports,” without engaging the medium’s unique properties[[3]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/#:~:text=imply%20connecting%20particular%20anime%20texts,terms%20%E2%80%9Cthe%20materiality%20of%20animation%E2%80%9D). Thomas Lamarre famously cautioned that much anime commentary treats animation as “but another text”, re-presenting story content while ignoring that anime consists of moving images and a distinct visual medium[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in). In short, the textual approach centers on content and message – often relating anime’s themes to Japanese culture, history, or universal questions – but it risks overlooking anime’s formal and technical dimensions[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in).

items.quote: organizations that provide verification services are closely linked to credit rating agencies… which already have close working relationships with [green bond] issuers
items.paragraph: Causes: As mentioned, the “issuer-pays” model means a GBER has a financial incentive to please the client. If an external reviewer is too strict or provides an unfavorable opinion (e.g. questioning the greenness of certain projects), they might fear losing repeat business. This dynamic could especially be a problem in an oligopolistic scenario – if issuers feel they have few alternatives, they may pressure the existing reviewers to be accommodating, and reviewers may oblige to retain market share. Another cause of conflicts is the multi-role nature of some institutions. For example, several Chinese credit rating agencies (CCX, Lianhe, etc.) or their affiliates perform green bond verification[[14]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=In%20China%E2%80%99s%20green%20bond%20market%2C,in%20the%20green%20bond%20market). These agencies already work for issuers to provide credit ratings, so their green review arm might be less likely to jeopardize a client relationship by issuing a negative assessment. The CPI observed that in China, “organizations that provide verification services are closely linked to credit rating agencies… which already have close working relationships with [green bond] issuers”[[14]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=In%20China%E2%80%99s%20green%20bond%20market%2C,in%20the%20green%20bond%20market). This close linkage can blur independence – a rater/verifier might be inclined to favor a key customer.

items.quote: hurl the spectator into the center of the action
items.paragraph: Definition and Origin: The Theater of Cruelty is a theatrical theory devised by French dramatist Antonin Artaud in the 1930s. Despite the ominous name, Artaud’s concept of “cruelty” did not mean mere sadism or gratuitous violence. Rather, he used it to describe a relentless, shattering force in theatre that would attack the senses of the audience and lay bare deeper truths. Artaud envisioned theater as “a primitive ceremonial experience intended to liberate the human subconscious and reveal man to himself”, using gestures, sounds, and shocking imagery as a kind of language superior to mere words[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=Encyclop%C3%A6dia%20Britannica%20describes%20the%20Theatre,theatre%20and%20strove%20to%20create). In his manifesto The Theatre and Its Double (1938), Artaud argued that Western theatre had become too genteel and text-bound; he wanted to remove the safe distance between actor and audience and immerse spectators in intense, visceral performances that “hurl the spectator into the center of the action”, hitting them with “immediate violent action” that could not be easily forgotten[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=In%20his%20writings%20on%20the,9). This was the “cruelty” – a ruthless attack on the audience’s complacency, a willingness to show disturbing, taboo, or primal images in order to wake up the audience’s emotions and consciousness. For example, Artaud imagined using eerie lighting, cacophonous sound, and grotesque stage images to bombard the audience’s senses, believing that such shock therapy had a spiritual or purgative function. The Theatre of Cruelty thus seeks to create a powerful catharsis by confronting spectators with the raw intensity of life’s pain, terror, and beauty all at once[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=Similarly%2C%20cruelty%20does%20not%20refer,According%20to%20scholar%20Nathan%20Gorelick)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency). Artaud wrote, “The theater, which is in no thing, but makes use of everything – gestures, sounds, words, screams, light, darkness – rediscovering the idea of a kind of unique language halfway between gesture and thought.” The result is a theatre that leaves the audience trembling, provoked, and transformed – a cruelty that is, in Artaud’s view, ultimately compassionate, because it forces people to face truths they habitually evade[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=For%20Artaud%2C%20cruelty%20%20is,is%20physical%20expression%20in%20space)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=Artaud%2C%20this%20was%20a%20cruel%2C,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency).

items.quote: revoke the green bond label of issuers that fail to correct non-compliance… highlighted in verification reports
items.paragraph: Mitigation Measures: Chinese regulators have recognized this risk and taken steps to address it. In late 2017, PBoC and CSRC jointly issued the Guidelines for Green Bond Assessment and Certification (Interim), which established an accreditation and supervision scheme for external reviewers[[9]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=review%20and%20an%20accreditation%20scheme,professional%20credentials%20after%20approval%2C%20establish). The newly formed Green Bonds Standard Committee (GBSC) under PBoC/CSRC requires external review firms to register and demonstrate qualifications, including having “no record of misconduct” and systems to ensure independence[[9]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=review%20and%20an%20accreditation%20scheme,professional%20credentials%20after%20approval%2C%20establish)[[47]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=CSRC%20requires%20external%20reviewers%20to,20). Importantly, the GBSC has a mandate to supervise verifiers on an ongoing basis, ensuring they maintain professional standards and “establish independence from issuers, and engage in fair pricing”[[48]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=clean%20legal%20record%2C%20professional%20liability,for%20green%20bond%20verifiers%20%E2%80%93)[[49]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=The%20Green%20Bonds%20Standard%20Committee,20). The Committee can conduct spot-checks on verification reports and even punish verifiers or issuers in cases of misbehavior – it has the power to “revoke the green bond label of issuers that fail to correct non-compliance… highlighted in verification reports” and to sanction verifiers for improper conduct[[50]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=green,While%20the%20practice)[[51]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=The%20Committee%20is%20granted%20the,widespread%2C%20regulators%20should%20ensure%20that). According to CPI’s analysis, the Committee’s authority is designed “to ensure verifiers… establish independence… The Committee… guarantee[s] independence of verification activities… [and] publishing a list of accredited verifiers should minimize any potential for conflicts of interest”[[44]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=issuers%20that%20fail%20to%20correct,publishing%20a%20list%20of%20accredited)[[10]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=authority%20has%20great%20to%20minimize,the%20Committee%20has%20already%20made). In other words, by vetting and monitoring the reviewers, and by holding the ultimate stick of withdrawing an issuer’s green label if things are misrepresented, regulators aim to realign incentives. Reviewers are aware that overly lax opinions could not only harm their reputation but also risk regulatory penalties or loss of accreditation.

items.quote: The author of AI artwork is the end user who sets the AI art’s existence into motion, like a Pollock with a paintbrush or a photographer behind the camera,
items.paragraph: - Option 3: Assign Copyright to the User who deploys the AI or provides prompts. This view treats the AI akin to a tool (like a camera or a paintbrush) and the person who directs the AI’s creation as the author. For instance, if you use Midjourney (an AI art generator) and enter a specific prompt, yielding a unique image, this approach would say you are the author of that image. Advocates compare the user to a photographer who frames a shot and clicks the shutter – the camera (or AI) is just an instrument executing the human’s vision[[33]](https://houstonlawreview.org/article/92132-what-is-an-author-copyright-authorship-of-ai-art-through-a-philosophical-lens#:~:text=the%20copyright,of%20years%20than%20traditional%20copyrights). One law review article argued: “The author of AI artwork is the end user who sets the AI art’s existence into motion, like a Pollock with a paintbrush or a photographer behind the camera,” imbued with the user’s personality and intent[[33]](https://houstonlawreview.org/article/92132-what-is-an-author-copyright-authorship-of-ai-art-through-a-philosophical-lens#:~:text=the%20copyright,of%20years%20than%20traditional%20copyrights). Pros: This approach gives individual creators control over what they generate with AI, potentially encouraging creative uses of AI. It aligns with our intuition when a person heavily guides an AI’s output (through prompt engineering, iterative feedback, or selection of outputs) that they had a form of creative input. It also avoids over-rewarding the AI maker; the user is likely closer to the final creative product. Some have suggested that even if we grant users copyright, it could be with some adjustments – e.g., maybe a shorter term of protection recognizing the work is partly machine-made[[33]](https://houstonlawreview.org/article/92132-what-is-an-author-copyright-authorship-of-ai-art-through-a-philosophical-lens#:~:text=the%20copyright,of%20years%20than%20traditional%20copyrights). Cons: On the flip side, not all AI uses involve much creative skill by the user. If a user just presses a button and the AI does everything, is that user truly an “author” or just a consumer of the AI service? It might stretch the concept of authorship to reward someone who may only have contributed a trivial prompt or no artistic judgment. There’s also a risk of inconsistent claims – if two different users get very similar outputs from the same AI (not uncommon with code assistants or some art models), each would claim copyright in their output even though the works are substantially alike, leading to potential disputes or a dilution of the originality threshold. Moreover, from the perspective of the AI developer, giving all rights to users might make it harder to commercialize the service (they couldn’t, for example, easily curate and publish a set of the best AI-generated images themselves without user agreements, since the users would own those copyrights).

items.quote: Who Stole the Lock off the Henhouse Door
items.paragraph: Williams’s lecture-recitals were a hallmark of her educational work. She developed a program called “The History of Jazz” – a lecture-performance that traced jazz’s evolution through live demonstrations. In these presentations (often given at colleges or community venues), Williams served as both narrator and pianist, guiding audiences through each major style. For example, in a 1978 Folkways record based on her lecture, she begins with spirituals, then progresses through ragtime, Kansas City swing, boogie-woogie, blues, and bebop, even addressing the avant-garde – all illustrated with representative piano pieces and her commentary[[13]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-mother-of-us-all/#:~:text=History%20was%20always%20important%20to,the%20music%20was%20then%20taking)[[14]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=The%20History%20of%20Jazz,98). She chose tunes that exemplified each era: “Who Stole the Lock off the Henhouse Door” for ragtime, “My Mama Pinned a Rose on Me” for early blues, and her own acerbic composition “A Fungus Amungus” to parody the chaotic sound of free jazz[[14]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=The%20History%20of%20Jazz,98). Through such lecture-recitals Williams literally “played through” the history, using her firsthand knowledge to bring the canon alive. Few musicians were so well suited to this task – by the late 1970s Williams had “played through each of the eras of jazz (1920s–late 1970s)”, one of the only artists who spanned from early blues and swing to modern styles[[15]](https://www.rai.ox.ac.uk/event/ive-got-a-story-to-tell#:~:text=At%20the%20time%20of%20her,of%20intellectuals%20and%20creatives%20that). This gave her a unique authority as a jazz historian-performer. Students and observers recall that she would not even let a pupil touch the piano until they understood the lineage of who came before them[[16]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-mother-of-us-all/#:~:text=Pianist%20Sumi%20Tonooka%20was%20just,that%20lingered%20in%20that%20space).

items.quote: Auto Scaling of Data Plane VNFs in 5G Networks
items.paragraph: "Auto Scaling of Data Plane VNFs in 5G Networks" proposes a Bit Rate Aware Auto Scaling (BAAS) algorithm specifically designed for data plane VNFs (Serving Gateway and Packet Gateway) in NFV-based 5G architectures. The algorithm maintains specifically configured bit rates for network slices while dynamically provisioning resources according to traffic loads. Through implementation on an NFV platform, BAAS demonstrates effective scaling of data plane VNFs while maintaining targeted bit rates across different traffic scenarios. The approach evaluates performance in terms of network throughput and number of active data plane instances needed for handling varying loads, providing a foundation for scalable, QoS-compliant network slicing in 5G environments.[^22]

items.quote: It might be okay to gently joke with a friend, but not with the principal
items.paragraph: Many of the uncertainties autistic students face are social or implicit in nature – things that neurotypical peers just “pick up” without being taught. The hidden curriculum refers to all the unwritten social rules and norms that people are expected to know but are never explicitly taught (e.g. “Don’t interrupt a teacher when they look busy” or “It might be okay to gently joke with a friend, but not with the principal”)[[29]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=The%20hidden%20curriculum%20is%20assumed,bound%2C%20literal%2C%20and%20rule%20enforcers). Autistic individuals, who tend to be more literal and routine-bound, often miss these subtle cues and unwritten rules[[30]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=The%20hidden%20curriculum%20is%20assumed,bound%2C%20literal%2C%20and%20rule%20enforcers). This can lead to confusion, social mistakes, and anxiety – the student is essentially navigating a minefield of invisible rules, never sure when they might break one. Explicitly teaching the hidden curriculum is a powerful support strategy to remove that uncertainty.

items.quote: Allah has sent down the best message, a Scripture consistent within itself… which causes the skins of those who fear their Lord to shiver, then their skins and hearts soften at the mention of Allah
items.paragraph: Application in Qur’anic Studies: Applied to the Qur’an, arousalism shifts attention to how the scripture’s sound, language, and imagery stimulate emotional and sensory responses in reciters and listeners. The Qur’an is famously melodious when recited, and its oral performance can induce feelings of awe, fear, serenity, or tears, even before one considers the semantic content. Scholars adopting an “affective” approach note that the Qur’an’s textural and sonic expressivity creates a kind of “aesthetic emotional arousal” in the audience[[1]](https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/artistic-expression/v-1/sections/arousal-theory#:~:text=Arousalism%20refers%20to%20this%20second,variety%20of%20suitably%20qualified%20perceivers). For instance, the Qur’an itself describes the powerful impact of its recitation on believers: “Allah has sent down the best message, a Scripture consistent within itself… which causes the skins of those who fear their Lord to shiver, then their skins and hearts soften at the mention of Allah”[[6]](https://quran.com/en/az-zumar/23#:~:text=%CB%B9It%20is%CB%BA%20Allah%20%CB%B9Who%CB%BA%20has,be%20left%20with%20no%20guide). In this verse (Q.39:23), the listeners’ bodily reaction – goosebumps and a softened heart – testifies to the affective arousal caused by the divine words. The Qur’an’s language is deliberately emotive: it often uses vivid imagery of Paradise and Hell, the rhythm of repeated refrains, and powerful rhetorical addresses to provoke feelings of hope, fear, humility, and reverence. For example, descriptions of the Day of Judgment portray chaos and terror (clouds rent asunder, earth quaking, etc.) in such a way that the audience experiences a visceral sense of dread and urgency. According to the arousalism concept, these aesthetic elements are not secondary; rather, they are central to the Qur’an’s purpose. The scripture’s beauty and terror work on the nerves and senses of the audience to instill spiritual attitudes (awe, repentance, devotion) through feeling. Muslim piety has long recognized this effect – it is common to see listeners moved to tears or trembling during Quranic recitation[[7]](https://myislam.org/surah-zumar/ayat-23/#:~:text=The%20skins%20of%20those%20who,That)[[8]](https://qurangallery.app/topics/softening-hearts-lin-al-qulub-islam-quran#:~:text=Softening%20of%20Hearts%20%28L%C4%ABn%20al,The). By analyzing such responses through arousalism, scholars underscore that the Qur’an communicates not only through meaning but through mood, engaging the believer’s heart and body as instruments of understanding. This approach complements traditional exegesis by highlighting how the Qur’an’s form (sound and style) is inseparable from its spiritual impact.

items.quote: The Lord took note of Sarah
items.paragraph: These depictions are vividly illustrated in the experiences of Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel, three of the four matriarchs whose barrenness heightens narrative drama and theological depth. Sarah's long infertility (Genesis 11:30) leads her to surrogacy with Hagar (Genesis 16:2), but God intervenes at her advanced age: "The Lord took note of Sarah" (paqad, Genesis 21:1), opening her womb for Isaac without any merit-based trigger—she shows no piety or repentance. Rebekah, barren for twenty years (Genesis 25:21), conceives twins after Isaac's prayer, with God shaping her womb (midrashically, as she lacked one initially), linking her fertility to divine mercy and national promise. Rachel, "barren" amid Leah's fertility (Genesis 29:31), despairs—"Give me children, or I shall die" (Genesis 30:1)—and uses surrogacy (Bilhah) and mandrakes, but God "remembered Rachel" (Genesis 30:22), opening her womb for Joseph without her direct appeal. These stories construct theological identity by portraying God as the life-giver, ensuring covenantal heirs like Isaac (over Ishmael) and Jacob (over Esau), while nationally, they found Israel's tribes, transforming personal anguish into communal origins.[jwa.org](https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/barren-women-in-the-bible)+更多 2

items.quote: Given your medical profile, Treatment A is predicted to improve 5-year survival (about 70% vs 50% with B). Guidelines also favor A in cases like yours. Therefore, A could offer better odds, though it does have these side effects to consider…
items.paragraph: By combining these functionalities, AI-SDM leverages predictive modeling, evidence-based reasoning, and generative communication together. For example, the predictive model might output that Treatment A has a 20% higher 5-year survival than Treatment B for this patient; the evidence-synthesis AI adds that Treatment A is recommended by latest guidelines for patients of this genotype; and the generative AI then formulates a conversational explanation: “Given your medical profile, Treatment A is predicted to improve 5-year survival (about 70% vs 50% with B). Guidelines also favor A in cases like yours. Therefore, A could offer better odds, though it does have these side effects to consider…” All of this would be shared and discussed with the patient, usually with the clinician mediating. The structured framework ensures the AI’s contributions are context-aware and human-interpretable, fitting naturally into the dialogue of an SDM session rather than being an isolated algorithmic output[[11]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2022.1016366/full#:~:text=importance%20of%20broadening%20the%20view,interaction%20with%20the%20systems%20available).

items.quote: If it is thus, why do I exist?
items.paragraph: While some biblical pregnancies proceed without complication, the text gives disproportionate narrative attention to **difficult and conflicted births**, transforming them into symbolic representations of theological truths about covenant, election, and national struggle. Rebecca's pregnancy with Jacob and Esau exemplifies this pattern most strikingly. The text records that "the children struggled together within her" (Genesis 25:22), causing Rebekah such anguish that she cries out: "If it is thus, why do I exist?" (Genesis 25:22). This is not merely medical observation; the struggling within the womb foreshadows the lifelong conflict between the twins and—more theologically significant—represents the struggle between two future nations within a single body.[^12][^13]

items.quote: Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD answered him, and Rebekah his wife conceived
items.paragraph: The stories of Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel illustrate this dynamic vividly. Sarah’s conception of Isaac is a miraculous reversal of nature. Long barren and post-menopausal, Sarah conceives “at the set time of which God had spoken” – a fulfillment of covenant promise rather than ordinary biology. Abraham is the physical father, but the narrative stresses God’s power: “The LORD did for Sarah as He had promised” (Gen. 21:1). Rebekah’s pregnancy likewise occurs only after divine intervention: “Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD answered him, and Rebekah his wife conceived” (Gen. 25:21). Isaac’s role is to seek God, underscoring that conception comes by divine blessing, not automatic fertility. Rachel’s story is the most drawn-out struggle. Defined by her barrenness, Rachel at first resorts to folk remedies and having her maid bear surrogate children. Yet only when “God remembered Rachel… and opened her womb” did she finally conceive Joseph[[2]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20assignment%20of%20divine%20activity,moment%2C%20the%20womb%20was%E2%80%94by%20default%E2%80%94closed). Upon Joseph’s birth, Rachel exclaims that God has “taken away my disgrace” (Gen. 30:23), highlighting that motherhood – and the honor of founding a family – was viewed as a divine gift lifting the “shame” of childlessness[[4]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=%E2%80%9CRachel%20was%20barren%E2%80%9D%20%28Gen%2029%3A31%29,words%2C%20addressed%20to%20Jacob%2C%20are)[[5]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=Rachel%2C%20in%20naming%20Joseph%2C%20makes,clear%20what%20infertility%20feels%20like). In all these cases, the metaphors of planting and opening convey that while fathers contribute seed, it is God who causes life to sprout. The patriarchs themselves acknowledge this: human procreation is ultimately an act of God, integral to His covenant plan for Israel’s ancestors.

items.quote: largely managed to overcome Dutch disease
items.paragraph: Outcomes and Lessons: Norway’s model has been remarkably successful in avoiding the resource curse. By strictly limiting budgetary use of oil money to a modest, sustainable level, Norway prevented the excessive government spending and debt accumulation that plagued other petro-states[[2]](https://resourcegovernance.org/sites/default/files/nrgi_Resource-Curse.pdf#:~:text=governments%20often%20over,manufacturing%2C%20by%20causing%20inflation%20or). The volatility of oil prices has little direct impact on Norway’s fiscal health – when oil prices soared, Norwegians didn’t suddenly get large tax cuts or a government spending binge; when prices crashed, there was no fiscal crisis. This stability has contributed to steady economic growth and low inflation/unemployment, in stark contrast to the boom-bust cycles seen in many oil exporters. Furthermore, investing abroad and keeping a tight rein on spending helped Norway avoid Dutch disease: manufacturing and other industries did not suffer undue contraction from an overheated currency, because oil export earnings were largely saved offshore[[53]](https://resourcegovernance.org/sites/default/files/nrgi_Resource-Curse.pdf#:~:text=in%20the%20economy%20that%20generate,managed%20to%20overcome%20Dutch%20disease). Indeed, Norway, along with countries like Chile and Indonesia, is cited as having “largely managed to overcome Dutch disease” in the past few decades through prudent policies[[53]](https://resourcegovernance.org/sites/default/files/nrgi_Resource-Curse.pdf#:~:text=in%20the%20economy%20that%20generate,managed%20to%20overcome%20Dutch%20disease).

items.quote: See the guys that they’re patterned after like Coltrane…they would never be a Coltrane because they don’t know anything about Basie.
items.paragraph: However, Williams did worry about musicians trying to imitate Coltrane without his background. In her Saturday mentoring sessions in New York, she encountered many young players who idolized Coltrane. She famously said: “See the guys that they’re patterned after like Coltrane…they would never be a Coltrane because they don’t know anything about Basie.”[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them) By this she meant Coltrane himself did know Basie, blues and swing – he paid his dues in bands and understood simplicity – which is why he could reach such heights. But his imitators were often starting with the cacophonous final chapter without reading the earlier ones, leading to poor results. So Williams’s evaluation of Coltrane was that he was a genius firmly in the jazz canon, but one whose influence could mislead others if they missed the context. She placed Coltrane in the lineage of greats (her Jazz Tree leaves), highlighting him as a continuation of bebop into modal and spiritual jazz[[35]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=produced%20the%20first%20spirituals,branch%20all%20to%20itself). In private conversations, she praised Coltrane’s devotion – how he practiced incessantly and sought higher truth in music. She also defended him against detractors who called his late work noise, emphasizing that he could play beautifully in older styles when he wanted. For example, Williams noted Coltrane’s ballad playing was gorgeous and bluesy, which proved he hadn’t abandoned the core values. In summary, Mary Lou Williams admired John Coltrane for his mastery and soul, even if she personally did not emulate his avant-garde extremes. She saw him as one of the last major innovators who still upheld jazz’s spirit.

items.quote: when you sit at home and when you travel on the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
items.paragraph: The **Hebrew term *meneket* (wet nurse) appears exclusively for women and refers specifically to breastfeeding**, signaling that the act of nursing itself carries distinctive theological weight in the biblical conceptual framework. The practice of breastfeeding in the ancient Near East was understood to transmit not merely nutrition but identity itself. Rabbinic commentary on Hannah's prayer and Samuel's dedication emphasizes that **mothers were primary transmitters of Torah and covenant law**, with the Shema passage (Deuteronomy 6:7) explicitly commanding parents to teach their children covenant obligations "when you sit at home and when you travel on the road, when you lie down and when you get up."[^30][^31]

items.quote: authors must be human, not machines
items.paragraph: The Copyright Office denied Thaler's application, and in 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit affirmed this decision. The court held that human authorship is a constitutional and statutory requirement for copyright protection, stating that "the present submission lacks traditional human authorship—it was autonomously generated by an AI". The court emphasized that many provisions of the Copyright Act "only make sense" if an author is a human being, and thus the statutory requirement includes that "authors must be human, not machines".[^28]

items.quote: When the bell rings at the end of class, that’s the signal that you can leave – even if the teacher doesn’t say ‘class dismissed’
items.paragraph: For example, teachers and support staff can make it a practice to directly explain important implicit rules (“When the bell rings at the end of class, that’s the signal that you can leave – even if the teacher doesn’t say ‘class dismissed’”) and context-specific expectations (“In group work, even though we normally stay quiet during class, it’s actually expected that you talk to your group”). By turning these hidden rules into visible, spoken ones, we greatly reduce the ambiguity in social and school situations. The student no longer has to predict others’ behavior or read between the lines to figure out what to do; they have a clearer map. This not only prevents misunderstandings and the negative social feedback that can follow, but also directly lowers anxiety – the student can be more at ease when they know the “code” of their environment. Researcher and educator Brenda Smith Myles emphasizes that hidden curriculum skills are essential for individuals with ASD precisely because these students often don’t detect social subtleties on their own[[29]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=The%20hidden%20curriculum%20is%20assumed,bound%2C%20literal%2C%20and%20rule%20enforcers). Without instruction, a child might inadvertently violate an unwritten rule and face ridicule or isolation, which then skyrockets anxiety in future interactions[[31]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=Impact%20of%20the%20Hidden%20Curriculum).

items.quote: fully supports China’s complete prohibition on the use of organs from death penalty prisoners for transplantation, implemented on January 1, 2015,
items.paragraph: Official stance vs. international medical community reactions: By the end of 2015, the official Chinese stance was that the country had established a transplant system in line with global standards and had “completely prohibited” the use of organs from executed prisoners for transplantation[[59]](https://www.wma.net/policy-tags/execution/#:~:text=Prisoners%20at%20the%20223,meeting%20in%20Nairobi%202023%2C%20stating). Chinese authorities (and medical leaders like Huang) stressed the rapid growth of voluntary donations and celebrated the fact that China’s donation rates were climbing dramatically[[45]](http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2014-12/04/content_19025683.htm#:~:text=At%20the%20same%20time%2C%20the,more%20fair%2C%20efficient%20and%20transparent). In statements to international audiences, the Chinese Medical Association insisted it “fully supports China’s complete prohibition on the use of organs from death penalty prisoners for transplantation, implemented on January 1, 2015,” crediting this policy for the successful expansion of voluntary donation[[60]](https://www.wma.net/policy-tags/execution/#:~:text=Whereas%20the%20Chinese%20Medical%20Association,meeting%20in%20Nairobi%202023%2C%20stating). In other words, the official narrative was that China had turned the page on the prisoner organ era and should be welcomed back into the fold of ethical transplant medicine.

items.quote: There’s nothing heroic about war… It’s just sickening, repulsive and insane.
items.paragraph: Aleksievich’s aim was to reveal a side of war that official history and propaganda had glossed over. In the Soviet Union, World War II (the defeat of Nazi Germany) was sacralized as a glorious victory, remembered in grand narratives of heroism, male camaraderie, and patriotic sacrifice. Aleksievich sought out the “unwomanly” truths that didn’t fit that mold. The title itself implies that war, as traditionally recounted, has no woman’s face – i.e., women’s experiences have been made invisible or are considered unfeminine and thus not spoken of. Her interviews show that women remembered the war in ways that often conflicted with the sanitized, valorous legend. Rather than battles and medals, they spoke of dirt, blood, fear, loss, and also the specific pains of being a woman in war (from coping with menstruation at the front to being shamed for unfeminine toughness after the war)[[33]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=decorations,as%20sickening%2C%20repulsive%20and%20insane)[[34]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=the%20immediate%20postwar%20years%2C%20when,20s%2C%20never%20felt%20young%20again). Aleksievich was not interested in what she calls “tales of heroism, but of ‘small great human beings.’”[[35]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=A%20million%20women%20fought%20in,as%20sickening%2C%20repulsive%20and%20insane) She wanted the intimate, raw, everyday reality of war – the crying of wounded men at night, the smell of a burning tank, the tenderness of a moment of love amid ruins, or the trauma of a sniper who cannot forget the faces of those she killed. By focusing on these human-scale memories, Aleksievich deconstructs the patriotic war narrative. As one of her conclusions, she famously noted: “There’s nothing heroic about war… It’s just sickening, repulsive and insane.”[[36]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=accountant%20who%2C%20as%20a%20sniper,as%20sickening%2C%20repulsive%20and%20insane) Through women’s eyes, war appears not as the grand adventure often depicted by male veterans or state propaganda, but as a kind of collective tragedy and trauma.

items.quote: secures considerably less freedom to text and data mine than [it] initially appear[s]
items.paragraph: One important difference from the U.S. approach is that the EU’s exceptions are clear-cut rules rather than a case-by-case fairness test. If you fall under Article 3 or 4 and meet its conditions, you’re safe from infringement claims; if not, you must get permission. For instance, a commercial AI project in the EU does not have the broad flexible shield of “fair use” – it must either ensure the content wasn’t opted-out or else negotiate licenses. Critics have pointed out that Article 4’s opt-out clause significantly weakens its freedom. In fact, commentators note that the opt-out in Article 4 leaves commercial data miners “at the mercy of the content owners.” In practice, a rights holder can shut down unpermissioned mining simply by saying so in their terms or metadata[[15]](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/the-new-copyright-directive-text-and-data-mining-articles-3-and-4/#:~:text=reproductions%20and%20extractions%20may%20be,other%20cases%2C%20it%20can%20be)[[18]](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/the-new-copyright-directive-text-and-data-mining-articles-3-and-4/#:~:text=In%20conclusion%2C%20the%20TDM%20provisions,without%20any%20of%20the%20TDM). This stands in contrast to the U.S., where (as mentioned) companies have scraped data under an assumption of fair use even for profit, without an opt-out mechanism for owners. As a Kluwer Copyright Blog analysis concluded, the EU’s TDM framework “secures considerably less freedom to text and data mine than [it] initially appear[s]” – innovation in Europe could be hindered if many content owners choose to forbid mining, whereas in the U.S. such mining might be allowed under fair use regardless of the rights holder’s wishes[[18]](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/the-new-copyright-directive-text-and-data-mining-articles-3-and-4/#:~:text=In%20conclusion%2C%20the%20TDM%20provisions,without%20any%20of%20the%20TDM).

items.quote: played through each of the eras of jazz (1920s–late 1970s)
items.paragraph: Williams’s lecture-recitals were a hallmark of her educational work. She developed a program called “The History of Jazz” – a lecture-performance that traced jazz’s evolution through live demonstrations. In these presentations (often given at colleges or community venues), Williams served as both narrator and pianist, guiding audiences through each major style. For example, in a 1978 Folkways record based on her lecture, she begins with spirituals, then progresses through ragtime, Kansas City swing, boogie-woogie, blues, and bebop, even addressing the avant-garde – all illustrated with representative piano pieces and her commentary[[13]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-mother-of-us-all/#:~:text=History%20was%20always%20important%20to,the%20music%20was%20then%20taking)[[14]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=The%20History%20of%20Jazz,98). She chose tunes that exemplified each era: “Who Stole the Lock off the Henhouse Door” for ragtime, “My Mama Pinned a Rose on Me” for early blues, and her own acerbic composition “A Fungus Amungus” to parody the chaotic sound of free jazz[[14]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=The%20History%20of%20Jazz,98). Through such lecture-recitals Williams literally “played through” the history, using her firsthand knowledge to bring the canon alive. Few musicians were so well suited to this task – by the late 1970s Williams had “played through each of the eras of jazz (1920s–late 1970s)”, one of the only artists who spanned from early blues and swing to modern styles[[15]](https://www.rai.ox.ac.uk/event/ive-got-a-story-to-tell#:~:text=At%20the%20time%20of%20her,of%20intellectuals%20and%20creatives%20that). This gave her a unique authority as a jazz historian-performer. Students and observers recall that she would not even let a pupil touch the piano until they understood the lineage of who came before them[[16]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-mother-of-us-all/#:~:text=Pianist%20Sumi%20Tonooka%20was%20just,that%20lingered%20in%20that%20space).

items.quote: mission – to bring jazz back to the young
items.paragraph: Mary Lou Williams (right) sharing the piano with a student at Duke University in the late 1970s. During the 1970s, Mary Lou Williams dedicated herself to educating a new generation about jazz. In 1977 she became the first artist-in-residence at Duke University, a position she held until her death in 1981[[1]](https://www.amsmusicology.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2017-rochester.pdf#:~:text=By%20the%201970s%2C%20Mary%20Lou,In%20this%20paper%20I%20examine)[[2]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=,to%20allow%20as%20many). At Duke she taught a credited History of Jazz course (assisted by her manager, Jesuit Father Peter O’Brien) and led the Duke Jazz Ensemble[[3]](https://www.amsmusicology.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2017-rochester.pdf#:~:text=her%20death%20in%201981%2C%20she,oriented%20lecture%20style). Beyond campus, she frequently gave lecture-demonstrations, workshops, and even choral clinics at other colleges and churches during semester breaks[[2]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=,to%20allow%20as%20many). Williams saw these activities as part of a “mission – to bring jazz back to the young”, believing jazz needed to “create an educated audience” and inspire future jazz talents[[4]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=,my%20hands%20beat%20hers%20to)[[5]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%2C%20and%20a%20new%20pianist%2C,They%27re%20looking). She was excited to see students discover jazz – for example, after a 1970 club engagement, she proudly noted “kids [started] coming from all over…telling their parents they’d discovered a new kind of music”[[6]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=believes%20she%20has%20had%20an,lining%20up%20to%20get%20in).
