items.quote: Some parts might be different than I imagine, but I have some idea of the kinds of differences and I’m prepared
items.paragraph: - Use “Pre-Play” and Scenario Planning: To further cultivate flexible prediction skills, teachers can encourage a form of mental simulation of possible outcomes for upcoming events. This has been likened to the ancient practice of imagining multiple battle outcomes to “reduce prediction error” if any one occurs[[26]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Regulatory%20flexibility%20is%20the%20ability,brain%E2%80%99s%20way%20of%20rehearsing%20uncertainty)[[27]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=possibilities%20and%20stay%20open%20to,we%20stay%20grounded%20and%20adaptive). In a modern school context, this might mean before a field trip or a big change, sitting down with the student to brainstorm several possible scenarios. For instance: “Let’s think of what might happen at the school assembly. Maybe we will sit in the front, or maybe in the middle. Perhaps the microphone might squeak loudly once, or maybe it won’t. If it does, what could we do? Maybe cover our ears for a moment.” By “pre-playing” various possibilities, the student practices coping with uncertainty in advance[[26]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Regulatory%20flexibility%20is%20the%20ability,brain%E2%80%99s%20way%20of%20rehearsing%20uncertainty). They learn to expect variability – that there is not just one rigid expected outcome, but a range of things that could happen, and they can handle that range[[27]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=possibilities%20and%20stay%20open%20to,we%20stay%20grounded%20and%20adaptive). This technique is powerful because it shifts the student from a black-and-white prediction (“It must go exactly this way or I’ll panic”) to a more resilient stance (“Some parts might be different than I imagine, but I have some idea of the kinds of differences and I’m prepared”). When the actual event unfolds, the student is less likely to be thrown off-balance because one of their mental scenarios coming true feels familiar. Essentially, they have seen the movie trailer for several versions of the event, so the real “movie” doesn’t shock them as much.

items.quote: a product of the interest of the majority in colonial problems
items.paragraph: The UN General Assembly as an Anti-Colonial Arena: From its earliest years, the General Assembly (UNGA) provided a stage for debates over colonialism, often driven by non-Western countries and later by newly independent states. In the late 1940s, a small but vocal group of member states – including Latin American republics, Arab-Asian countries like India (which, though not independent until 1947, was an original UN member), the Philippines, and the Soviet Union – began pressing the Assembly to address issues such as the treatment of Indians in South Africa, the Indonesian struggle for independence, and the status of North African colonies. The United States and United Kingdom initially hoped to keep the UN’s focus away from contentious colonial questions, but pressure mounted as more Asian, Middle Eastern, and eventually African nations joined the UN. A key mechanism was the “Committee on Information from Non-Self-Governing Territories,” a special committee of the General Assembly that first met in 1947 to review the reports submitted under Article 73(e). As a U.S. official noted in 1954, “the large majority of Members of the United Nations believe that there is no field in which the UN can do more important work than in the colonial field”. These countries “constantly urge increased UN activity in the colonial field and an extension of UN supervision over colonial territories.” The General Assembly’s Information Committee was “a product of the interest of the majority in colonial problems”, and through it (and other forums) they applied “constant pressure” on colonial powers “to account for their stewardship and accelerate the rate of development” of their territories[[34]](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v03/d881#:~:text=,rate%20of%20development%20of%20their). In other words, the UN became a grand tribunal of world opinion on colonialism, where imperial powers had to defend their record and policies. This scrutiny sometimes provoked defensive reactions – colonial states tried to present themselves as responsible guardians preparing colonies for autonomy, while critics exposed abuses and demanded timelines for independence. The Committee’s work, albeit limited to reviewing information, kept colonial issues on the agenda and built a normative case against endless colonial rule. By the 1950s, as decolonization wars and movements intensified (in Algeria, Kenya, Indochina, etc.), the General Assembly’s tone grew bolder. Newly independent countries such as India, Pakistan, Burma (Myanmar), Indonesia, and a wave of decolonized states in 1957–1960 brought first-hand experience to UN debates. They helped move the conversation from polite appeals to assertive resolutions asserting the right of colonies to independence. In 1952, the General Assembly for the first time explicitly affirmed that “all peoples have the right to self-determination,” setting the stage for more robust action later[[35]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=,which%20have%20not%20yet%20attained).

items.quote: Personally, I have always believed that bebop was here to stay,
items.paragraph: In Williams’s eyes, bebop was the last great unifying era of jazz, and she regarded it with particular reverence. She herself had been a mentor to bop players (like Monk, Parker, Gillespie) and embraced their advances. “Personally, I have always believed that bebop was here to stay,” she wrote in 1954, insisting that new styles like Dave Brubeck’s cool jazz, while interesting, “are not bop.”[[52]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-MyLifewKoJ-1954.html#:~:text=the%20phrasing%20been%20like%20it,to%20continue%20writing%20and%20experimenting) She saw bop’s complex phrasing and harmonies as a natural evolution of jazz’s language without discarding its roots. Indeed, she encouraged the original modernists “to continue writing and experimenting” back then[[52]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-MyLifewKoJ-1954.html#:~:text=the%20phrasing%20been%20like%20it,to%20continue%20writing%20and%20experimenting). By the 1970s, however, Williams felt jazz history had hit a crisis after the bebop era. In her words, “after the bop era it just all went to pot.”[[41]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,have%20her%20students%20sing%20the) She believed that the late 1950s and 1960s brought a fragmentation where some musicians lost touch with the core lineage. Two main culprits she cited were the rise of commercial popular music (rock & roll) and certain forms of avant-garde jazz. Williams saw many jazz players in the ’60s chasing commercial success by playing rock or funk, or going to the opposite extreme of playing an “free” avant-garde that eschewed melody and blues. “Musicians started playing commercial rock and what they call ‘free music,’ and all the feeling went out of it,” she lamented of that period[[41]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,have%20her%20students%20sing%20the). To her, these trends broke the once-continuous evolution of the music. She would tell students that if a creative musician listens only to such music lacking the great traditions, “he can’t ever get off the ground. You have to hear great music in order to…create something new.”[[39]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,sing%20the%20music%20they%27re%20hearing) In other words, without the grounding of Armstrong, Ellington, Basie, Parker, etc., there can be no meaningful innovation – only chaos or commercial dilution.

items.quote: How does anime as animation work? What are its stylistic and industrial characteristics?
items.paragraph: - Media/Formal Analysis (Anime as a Medium): Another major approach treats anime as a distinctive media form and scrutinizes its formal properties, production, and technology. Here the guiding questions are “How does anime as animation work? What are its stylistic and industrial characteristics?” Scholars like Thomas Lamarre spearheaded this by insisting on the “materiality of animation” – examining anime’s visual techniques, image composition, and technologies, rather than only its narrative[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in). This approach might analyze animation methods (e.g. limited animation, stylized motion, use of layers and effects) or the visual iconography (such as the famous “big eyes” style or techniques for conveying speed/emotion). Researchers in this vein argue that anime studies must engage with anime as animation, not just as illustrated storybooks[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in)[[8]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=reviews.%20,of%20the%20materiality%20of%20animation). They point out that anime is largely a TV-based medium with specific production constraints and viewing habits, which shape its storytelling. Mitsuyo Wada-Marciano, for instance, highlights that academic discourse tended to privilege a canon of visually complex anime films (like Akira or Ghost in the Shell) while neglecting the mass-produced TV anime series that form anime’s core in Japan[[9]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=studies%2C%20anime%20has%20been%20dislocated,produced%20anime%20TV)[[10]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=around%20canons%2C%20which%20serve%20to,%E2%80%9D). She notes that focusing only on a few artful films (often for their grand themes like cyberpunk or environmentalism) ignores the local, temporal, and technological specificities of most anime – such as how series are made for specific audiences and time-slots, or how they fit into popular culture trends[[9]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=studies%2C%20anime%20has%20been%20dislocated,produced%20anime%20TV)[[10]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=around%20canons%2C%20which%20serve%20to,%E2%80%9D). The media-form approach, therefore, looks at anime’s industry, form, and reception context: production committees, TV broadcasting models, genre conventions, visual and sonic style, etc. It often involves comparing anime to other animation traditions or media forms. By viewing anime “not for what it shows, but how it shows it,” this approach shifts emphasis to anime’s unique language of images and its place in media history[[11]](https://animetudes.com/2020/03/05/defining-anime-part-2/#:~:text=scholars%20chosen%20to%20discard%20an,are%20forever%20blurry%20and%20expanding). In practice, this means scholars might study things like the narrative structures of long-running series, the interplay of manga and anime (adaptation studies), or the transmedia techniques (how anime narratives extend into games, toys, etc.). In summary, the media/formal approach treats anime as an audiovisual medium with its own grammar and production ecosystem, focusing on form, style, and medium-specific context rather than primarily on content message[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in)[[8]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=reviews.%20,of%20the%20materiality%20of%20animation).

items.quote: As soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children
items.paragraph: Childbirth, with all its drama, becomes a stage for God’s providence and the foreshadowing of Israel’s destiny. Difficult or extraordinary births (twins wrestling, breech presentations, last-minute reversals) are more than family anecdotes; they operate as prophecies in miniature. The struggle of Jacob and Esau in Rebekah’s womb prefigures centuries of struggle between their descendant nations[[6]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=,Peretz%29%20will%20be%20dominant). The breach made by Perez in Tamar’s womb anticipates the “breach” by which his line will produce Israel’s kings[[24]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=The%20story%20is%20meant%20as,5)[[25]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=hand%2C%20then%20withdrawing%20it%20in,favor%20of%20his%20brother). In this way, the authors use birth stories to construct a national theology of election and survival. Israel is repeatedly characterized as the younger, weaker twin who prevails by God’s choice – the nation is “born” to surpass expectations and older rivals (whether Esau/Edom, or other firstborn nations). Moreover, the very idea of national birth is woven into Israel’s sacred history: the Exodus is portrayed as the birth moment of Israel as a people, complete with the pain (slavery, plagues) and triumph (deliverance through waters) that accompany a birth. Biblical poets and prophets explicitly connect a woman’s labor to Zion’s emergence: “As soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children” – a nation born in a day by God’s decree. By linking the Exodus and other redemptive events to birth imagery[[10]](https://www.lookstein.org/professional-dev/bible/implications-feminine-imagery-bible/#:~:text=Egypt%20and%20the%20birth%20of,over%20you%2C%20and%20I%20covered), the Bible frames Israel’s identity as that of a child lovingly delivered by God. Even the convulsions of later history (exile and restoration) are described as birth pangs of a new Israel. This grand metaphor reassures the nation that their God is a faithful midwife: He will not bring them to the brink of birth and then abandon them (cf. Isa. 66:9). The frequent recurrence of birth pangs and newborns in Israel’s origin stories cements the idea that the nation was born amid divine struggle and care – it did not simply appear; it was labored into existence by God.

items.quote: PCB assembly sequencing and grouping problem
items.paragraph: - Setup Optimization Models: A significant body of work deals with the “PCB assembly sequencing and grouping problem”. One approach defines a hybrid setup optimization: group jobs into families to share a setup, and sequence them to minimize total changeovers. Salonen (2009) introduced an Integer Programming model to minimize a weighted sum of setup occasions and feeder changes[[44]](https://www.utupub.fi/bitstream/10024/42449/3/dissKariSalonen091008d.2.bgt.pdf#:~:text=industry,practical%20size%20which%20can%20be)[[45]](https://www.utupub.fi/bitstream/10024/42449/3/dissKariSalonen091008d.2.bgt.pdf#:~:text=feeder%20changes%20depending%20on%20the,and%20sometimes%20even%20optimal%20solutions). The objective can be tuned (via weights) to balance between fewer big changeovers versus smaller continuous tweaks. Because solving the IP for many boards is hard (combinatorial explosion), they developed heuristic algorithms that achieve near-optimal sequences in reasonable time[[47]](https://www.utupub.fi/bitstream/10024/42449/3/dissKariSalonen091008d.2.bgt.pdf#:~:text=model,other%20methods%20found%20in%20literature). This kind of model-driven approach is widely used: essentially, schedule boards in an order that minimizes the number of component feeder changes, thereby cutting downtime. In practice, modern SMT scheduling software uses heuristics like “ranked positional weight” or “minimal changeover” rules to decide the next job, which implement these principles.

items.quote: Recommended Practice for Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Migration.
items.paragraph: - IEEE P3172 – “Recommended Practice for Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Migration.” Provides a multi-step methodology for organizations to integrate post-quantum cryptography into their systems[[40]](https://qunet-initiative.de/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/List-of-norms-and-standards_v.2.0.pdf#:~:text=P3172%20Recommended%20Practice%20for%20Post,key). It covers using hybrid cryptographic schemes (combining conventional and PQC algorithms) and emphasizes crypto-agility and planning to transition to quantum-safe security. (PAR approved May 2022.)

items.quote: shocks [them] out of their complacency
items.paragraph: Application in Qur’anic Studies: The Qur’an’s own use of intense, even frightening imagery – especially in its eschatological and apocalyptic passages – has been likened to a “theater of cruelty” that God stages within the text to jolt the audience’s moral and spiritual awareness[[16]](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/14/7/827#:~:text=In%20effect%2C%20the%20holy%20book,The%20Quranic%20%E2%80%9CTheater%20of%20Cruelty%E2%80%9D). The Qur’an does not shy away from graphic descriptions of divine punishment and the horrors of Hell. These descriptions serve a clear pedagogical purpose: much as Artaud’s shocking theatre was meant to purge and awaken the audience, the Qur’an’s terrifying imagery is meant to shake the reader out of spiritual heedlessness. For example, in Surah Al-Hajj the punishment of unbelievers in Hell is described in visceral detail: “Garments of Fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads, melting whatever is in their bellies and skins. For them are maces of iron. Every time they try to escape from anguish, they will be driven back in and [told], ‘Taste the torment of burning!’.”[[23]](https://quran.com/en/al-hajj/19-22#:~:text=,22%3A20)[[24]](https://quran.com/en/ad-dukhan/43/tafsirs#:~:text=Tafsir%20Surah%20Ad,It%20will%20go). Such depictions are undeniably cruel-sounding, and they are meant to be harrowing. The reader or listener can almost feel the heat and terror in these verses – an experience not unlike an audience member feeling overwhelmed by a harrowing scene in an Artaud play. From a theatrical standpoint, the Qur’an creates a kind of immersive horror scene within the imagination: the Day of Resurrection is painted with quaking earth, darkened sun, and people appearing drunken with fear (Q.22:1–2); Hell is rendered with blazing flames, black smoke, the wails of its inhabitants, and grotesque torments. These elements work together to produce a “convulsive shock” in the believer’s heart, ideally steering them to repentance and righteousness. Modern scholars drawing this parallel argue that the Qur’an’s apocalyptic aesthetics function similarly to Artaud’s Theatre of Cruelty: they eliminate any comfortable distance between the message and the audience. One is not simply reading about punishment intellectually; one is almost made to feel its horror. In Artaud’s terms, the Qur’an’s imagery “exposes [the audience] to the dangers of life” and “shocks [them] out of their complacency”[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency). Importantly, this “cruelty” is in service of moral purification – much as Artaud aimed to purify art and audiences, the Qur’an’s fierce warnings aim to purify souls. The experience of fear and awe is intended to lead to humility, obedience, and a sincere awareness of divine reality. By reading these verses as a form of divinely-orchestrated theater, we appreciate how the Qur’an deliberately stages emotional experiences for its audience. The believer becomes both spectator and participant in a cosmic drama of salvation and damnation. This aesthetic perspective emphasizes the experiential impact of the Qur’an: just as a night at an Artaudian theater might leave one deeply rattled but enlightened, pondering life’s truths, so too the Qur’an’s most dramatic passages leave an indelible emotional impression that reinforces its spiritual teachings.

items.quote: treat these animated movies as mirrors of Japanese culture, assuming a homogeneous audience
items.paragraph: - Japanese Identity and “Japaneseness”: A notable focus is how anime represents Japanese culture or identity. Especially among non-Japanese academics, there has been a tendency to single out iconic works (often auteur films by Miyazaki, Oshii, etc.) and discuss how they exemplify “Japanese” aesthetics or values[[19]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=%3E%20Non,arises%20from%20different%20ways%20of). For example, foreign scholars have looked at Miyazaki’s films for their depiction of traditional folklore, familial structures, or harmony with nature as distinctly Japanese traits. In this mode, anime is often taken as a cultural emblem – a representative object that can be used to explain Japan to outsiders. Jaqueline Berndt critiques this trend, noting that analysts frequently “treat these animated movies as mirrors of Japanese culture, assuming a homogeneous audience”[[5]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=%3E%20Non,it%20also%20involves%20a%20widespread). Such studies assume that what is seen on screen directly maps to the beliefs or conditions of Japanese people, thereby using anime as an ethnographic proxy for Japan itself.

items.quote: It must go exactly this way or I’ll panic
items.paragraph: - Use “Pre-Play” and Scenario Planning: To further cultivate flexible prediction skills, teachers can encourage a form of mental simulation of possible outcomes for upcoming events. This has been likened to the ancient practice of imagining multiple battle outcomes to “reduce prediction error” if any one occurs[[26]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Regulatory%20flexibility%20is%20the%20ability,brain%E2%80%99s%20way%20of%20rehearsing%20uncertainty)[[27]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=possibilities%20and%20stay%20open%20to,we%20stay%20grounded%20and%20adaptive). In a modern school context, this might mean before a field trip or a big change, sitting down with the student to brainstorm several possible scenarios. For instance: “Let’s think of what might happen at the school assembly. Maybe we will sit in the front, or maybe in the middle. Perhaps the microphone might squeak loudly once, or maybe it won’t. If it does, what could we do? Maybe cover our ears for a moment.” By “pre-playing” various possibilities, the student practices coping with uncertainty in advance[[26]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Regulatory%20flexibility%20is%20the%20ability,brain%E2%80%99s%20way%20of%20rehearsing%20uncertainty). They learn to expect variability – that there is not just one rigid expected outcome, but a range of things that could happen, and they can handle that range[[27]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=possibilities%20and%20stay%20open%20to,we%20stay%20grounded%20and%20adaptive). This technique is powerful because it shifts the student from a black-and-white prediction (“It must go exactly this way or I’ll panic”) to a more resilient stance (“Some parts might be different than I imagine, but I have some idea of the kinds of differences and I’m prepared”). When the actual event unfolds, the student is less likely to be thrown off-balance because one of their mental scenarios coming true feels familiar. Essentially, they have seen the movie trailer for several versions of the event, so the real “movie” doesn’t shock them as much.

items.quote: join hands to resist fate’s wheel together
items.paragraph: - Ao Bing (Dragon Prince Reimagined): Ao Bing, the third son of the Dragon King of the East Sea, is traditionally an adversary to Nezha. In the 1979 movie (and the original myth), Nezha kills Ao Bing outright – a rash act that triggers the Dragon King’s wrath[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_Zha_2#:~:text=as%20a%20demon%20reincarnation%20in,resurrection%2C%20which%20caused%20Nezha%20to). The 2003 Legend of Nezha series likewise cast Ao Bing as an enemy (and his death by Nezha’s hand was depicted, continuing the classic “slaying the dragon” narrative). Ne Zha 2 completely overturns this dynamic. Here, Ao Bing survives and becomes Nezha’s ally and close friend. In fact, their fates are intertwined: after the catastrophic finale of the first film, Nezha and Ao Bing’s bodies were destroyed, and Ne Zha 2 opens with Ao Bing’s spirit preserved by Nezha’s master. Ao Bing is revived to share Nezha’s body for a time, allowing the two to literally cooperate as one. This is a bold subversion of the familiar rivalry – instead of mortal enemies, the “Demon Child” Nezha and the Spirit Pearl Ao Bing learn to coexist and fight side by side. Ao Bing’s characterization in the new film is sympathetic and noble, in contrast to his earlier villainous portrayals. He struggles with guilt and duty but ultimately stands for justice, even defying his own father Ao Guang when necessary. Visually, Ao Bing’s design emphasizes an icy blue color palette (complementing Nezha’s fiery red), symbolizing the yin-yang balance between them[[26]](https://www.chinawriter.com.cn/n1/2025/0206/c404076-40413506.html#:~:text=%E5%BD%93%E4%BB%A3%E5%AE%A1%E7%BE%8E%E5%8A%A9%E6%8E%A8%E4%BC%A0%E7%BB%9F%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E5%88%9B%E6%96%B0%EF%BC%8C%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%92%E4%B9%8B%E9%AD%94%E7%AB%A5%E9%97%B9%E6%B5%B7%E3%80%8B%EF%BC%88%E4%BB%A5%E4%B8%8B%E7%AE%80%E7%A7%B0%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%922%E3%80%8B%EF%BC%89%E9%A2%87%E5%85%B7%E5%B7%A7%E6%80%9D%E7%9A%84%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E5%85%83%E7%B4%A0%E6%97%A0%E7%96%91%E4%BB%A4%E4%BA%BA%E7%9C%BC%E5%89%8D%E4%B8%80%E4%BA%AE%E3%80%82%E5%8A%A8%E7%94%BB%E5%88%B6%E4%BD%9C%E7%BB%84%E4%BB%A5%E8%B4%B4%E5%90%88%E5%BD%93%E4%BB%A3%E8%A7%82%E4%BC%97%E7%9A%84%E5%AE%A1%E7%BE%8E%E8%A6%81%E6%B1%82%E5%AF%B9%E4%BC%A0%E7%BB%9F%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E5%B1%95%E5%BC%80%E4%BA%8C%E6%AC%A1%E5%88%9B%E4%BD%9C%EF%BC%8C%20%E5%8A%9B%E6%B1%82%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96%E5%85%83%E7%B4%A0%E4%B8%8E%E6%83%85%E8%8A%82%E9%80%BB%E8%BE%91%E7%9B%B8%E7%BB%9F%E4%B8%80%EF%BC%8C%E5%9C%A8%E5%92%8C%E8%B0%90%E4%B8%AD%E5%90%84%E8%87%AA%E5%87%BA%E5%BD%A9%E3%80%82%E8%AF%A5%E7%89%87%E4%B8%AD%E5%A4%9A%E4%B8%AA%E5%9C%BA%E6%99%AF%E3%80%81%E4%BA%BA%E7%89%A9%E3%80%81%E7%89%A9%E5%93%81%E8%AE%BE%E8%AE%A1%E7%9A%86%E6%B3%A8%E9%87%8D%E8%89%B2%E5%BD%A9%E7%BE%8E%E5%AD%A6%E7%9A%84%E8%BF%90%E7%94%A8%EF%BC%8C%E6%95%96%E4%B8%99%E4%B8%8E%E5%93%AA%E5%90%92%E4%B8%80%E8%93%9D%E4%B8%80%E7%BA%A2%EF%BC%8C%E6%98%AF%E2%80%9C%E5%B8%9D%E9%87%8A%E9%9D%92%E2%80%9D%E4%B8%8E%E2%80%9C%E6%9C%B1%E7%A0%82%E7%BA%A2%E2%80%9D%E7%9A%84%E7%A2%B0%E6%92%9E%E4%BA%A4%E8%9E%8D%EF%BC%9B%E9%87%8D%E5%A1%91%20%E8%82%89%E8%BA%AB%E7%9A%84%E6%B3%95%E5%99%A8%E5%AE%9D%E8%8E%B2%E8%9E%8D%E5%90%88%E2%80%9C%E6%A1%83%E5%A4%AD%E2%80%9D%E4%B8%8E%E2%80%9C%E7%90%A5%E7%8F%80%E9%BB%84%E2%80%9D%E5%90%8E%E7%BC%93%E7%BC%93%E7%BB%BD%E5%BC%80%EF%BC%9B%E4%BB%99%E9%97%A8%E9%87%8D%E5%9C%B0%E7%8E%89%E8%99%9A%E5%AE%AB%E7%9A%84%E8%89%B2%E5%BD%A9%E4%B8%8E%E5%B8%83%E5%B1%80%EF%BC%8C%E6%98%AF%E5%AF%B9%E5%AE%8B%E5%BE%BD%E5%AE%97%E8%B5%B5%E4%BD%B6%E3%80%8A%E7%91%9E%E9%B9%A4%E5%9B%BE%E3%80%8B%E7%9A%84%E8%87%B4%E6%95%AC%E2%80%A6%E2%80%A6%E4%B8%AD%E5%BC%8F%E4%BC%A0%E7%BB%9F%E8%89%B2%E5%BD%A9%E7%9A%84%E7%A2%B0%E6%92%9E%E5%B8%A6%E7%BB%99%E8%A7%82%E4%BC%97%E6%9C%80%E7%BA%AF%E7%B2%B9%E7%9A%84%E8%89%B2%E5%BD%A9%E4%BA%AB%E5%8F%97%E3%80%82). The alliance of Ao Bing and Nezha – once “irreconcilable foes” in the old story – is one of the film’s most significant innovations, conveying a message of overcoming prejudices. As one Chinese commentator noted, the stereotype of Nezha and Ao Bing being “destined enemies” is gradually dismantled in Ne Zha 2, as the two “join hands to resist fate’s wheel together”[[27]](https://www.chinawriter.com.cn/n1/2025/0206/c404076-40413506.html#:~:text=%E6%AD%A3%E9%82%AA%E7%A2%B0%E6%92%9E%EF%BC%8C%E9%A2%A0%E8%A6%86%E5%88%BB%E6%9D%BF%E5%8D%B0%E8%B1%A1%E7%9A%84%E4%BA%BA%E7%89%A9%E5%A1%91%E9%80%A0%E5%85%B1%E5%90%8C%E8%B0%B1%E5%86%99%E7%9D%80%E6%96%B0%E7%9A%84%E7%A5%9E%E9%AD%94%E6%95%85%E4%BA%8B%E3%80%82%E9%99%AA%E4%BC%B4%E8%AE%B8%E5%A4%9A%E2%80%9C90%E5%90%8E%E2%80%9D%E5%B9%B4%E8%BD%BB%E4%BA%BA%E6%88%90%E9%95%BF%E7%9A%84%E5%8A%A8%E7%94%BB%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%92%E4%BC%A0%E5%A5%87%E3%80%8B%E4%B8%AD%EF%BC%8C%E7%9F%B3%E5%A4%B4%E4%BF%AE%E7%82%BC%E8%80%8C%E6%88%90%E7%9A%84%E9%AD%94%E5%A4%B4%E7%9F%B3%E7%9F%B6%E5%A8%98%E5%A8%98%E4%B8%8E%E9%87%8E%E5%BF%83%E5%8B%83%E5%8B%83%E7%9A%84%E7%94%B3%E5%85%AC%E8%B1%B9%E6%98%AF%E2%80%9C%E5%8F%8D%E6%B4%BE%E2%80%9D%20%E7%9A%84%E4%BB%A3%E8%A1%A8%EF%BC%9B%E8%BF%91%E5%B9%B4%E4%B8%8A%E6%98%A0%E7%9A%84%E3%80%8A%E6%96%B0%E7%A5%9E%E6%A6%9C%EF%BC%9A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%92%E9%87%8D%E7%94%9F%E3%80%8B%E4%B8%AD%EF%BC%8C%E4%B8%8D%E8%A7%81%E7%9F%B3%E7%9F%B6%E4%B8%8E%E7%94%B3%E5%85%AC%E8%B1%B9%E7%9A%84%E8%BA%AB%E5%BD%B1%EF%BC%8C%E6%AD%A3%E9%82%AA%E6%95%85%E4%BA%8B%E7%9A%84%E8%B0%B1%E5%86%99%E5%8F%AA%E5%9C%A8%E5%93%AA%E5%90%92%E4%B8%8E%E6%95%96%E4%B8%99%E8%BA%AB%E4%B8%8A%E5%B1%95%E5%BC%80%EF%BC%8C%E2%80%9C%E6%8A%BD%E9%BE%99%E7%AD%8B%E2%80%9D%E7%9A%84%E6%83%85%E8%8A%82%E8%AE%BE%E8%AE%A1%E4%BE%9D%E6%97%A7%E5%BB%B6%E7%BB%AD%E4%BA%86%E4%B9%8B%E5%89%8D%E7%9A%84%E5%8A%A8%E7%94%BB%EF%BC%8C%E5%B0%86%E6%95%96%E4%B8%99%E5%A1%91%E9%80%A0%E6%88%90%E2%80%9C%20%E9%82%AA%E2%80%9D%EF%BC%8C%E6%AD%A3%E9%82%AA%E7%9B%B8%E4%BA%89%EF%BC%8C%E5%AD%B0%E8%83%9C%E5%AD%B0%E8%B4%A5%E6%97%A9%E6%9C%89%E5%AE%9A%E8%AE%BA%E3%80%82%E8%BF%99%E4%BA%9B%E4%BD%9C%E5%93%81%E5%9B%BA%E7%84%B6%E6%98%AF%E4%BD%B3%E4%BD%9C%EF%BC%8C%E5%8D%B4%E4%B9%9F%E7%9B%B8%E5%BA%94%E5%B8%A6%E6%9C%89%E5%90%84%E8%87%AA%E6%97%B6%E4%BB%A3%E7%9A%84%E7%83%99%E5%8D%B0%EF%BC%8C%E7%B2%BE%E5%BD%A9%E6%9C%89%E4%BD%99%EF%BC%8C%E7%8B%AC%E7%89%B9%E7%95%A5%E6%9C%89%E4%B8%8D%E8%B6%B3%E3%80%82). This humanization of Ao Bing transforms the original tragedy (Nezha slaying a dragon prince) into a tale of brotherhood and redemption.

items.quote: My life is determined by me, not by Heaven
items.paragraph: In summary, Ne Zha 2 retains the rebellious spirit of the Nezha legend – Nezha is still defying “heaven’s rules” – but it modernizes the themes to be more nuanced and socially resonant. The individual rebellion against a father or a dragon king has transformed into a collective uprising against injustice, fueled by friendship, trust, and love. The film upholds the core message of “fate can be changed” (as in the famous line “My life is determined by me, not by Heaven” from the first film) and extends it: if the “established order won’t allow it, we will together change the world”[[49]](https://www.chinawriter.com.cn/n1/2025/0206/c404076-40413506.html#:~:text=%E5%85%89%EF%BC%8C%E3%80%8A%E5%93%AA%E5%90%922%E3%80%8B%E4%B8%AD%E7%9A%84%E4%BB%96%E5%A7%8B%E7%BB%88%E4%B8%80%E8%BA%AB%E6%AD%A3%E6%B0%94%E3%80%81%E5%BF%83%E6%80%9D%E7%BB%86%E8%85%BB%E3%80%81%E6%9E%81%E5%85%B7%E9%A2%86%E8%A2%96%E6%B0%94%E8%B4%A8%EF%BC%8C%E5%9C%A8%E9%BE%99%E6%97%8F%E9%9D%A2%E4%B8%B4%E5%8D%B1%E9%99%A9%E6%97%B6%E6%AF%AB%E4%B8%8D%E9%80%80%E8%AE%A9%EF%BC%8C%E9%9D%A2%E5%AF%B9%E5%AD%A9%E5%AD%90%E6%97%B6%E5%8F%88%E8%83%BD%E5%B1%95%E9%9C%B2%E6%9F%94%E6%83%85%EF%BC%8C%E4%BB%8E%E4%B8%8D%E4%BB%A5%E8%80%81%E4%B8%80%E8%BE%88%E7%9A%84%E7%BB%8F%E9%AA%8C%E6%8D%86%E7%BB%91%E4%BB%96%E4%BA%BA%E3%80%82). This collaborative, compassionate, and balance-seeking thematic stance distinguishes Ne Zha 2 as a truly contemporary retelling of the Nezha myth.

items.quote: move backward and do all the spirituals again
items.paragraph: In her teaching, Williams placed paramount importance on feeling and the oral tradition of jazz. She believed jazz should be learned by ear and through direct experience rather than solely from books. “Jazz doesn’t come out of school,” she argued – many greats like Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane “were playing before they ever studied” formally[[7]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=learned%20them%20in%20about%2015,Then%2C%20in%201942%2C%20she%20moved). Williams felt a purely academic, technical approach produces sterile results: “Sure, you can play like a typewriter [by studying in school], but it’ll make your audience nervous…It’s nothing that’s written down in a book”, she said bluntly[[8]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,in%20a%20hook%2C%20you%20know). Instead, she tried to “teach the feeling” of the music[[9]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=have%20to%20hear%20great%20music,semester%2C%20I%20gave%20the%20kids). Her methods were hands-on and immersive: she would “go back to the beginnings of jazz, to spirituals and gospel and the blues,” having students listen and sing along to internalize the sound[[9]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=have%20to%20hear%20great%20music,semester%2C%20I%20gave%20the%20kids). “I have them sing all the eras of jazz,” she explained – for instance, when covering bebop she had the class scat “shoo-be-doo-be-doo” lines[[10]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=going%20back%20to%20the%20beginnings,backward%20and%20did%20all%20the). Only once students “saturate the entire mind” with the sound and feeling of one era would she move on to the next[[11]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%20they%27re%20hearing.%20,Pushing%20back%20her). If they lacked the proper feel – as when one class’s blues singing “sounded cold” – Williams would “move backward and do all the spirituals again” until they gained the needed warmth[[12]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=they%20sing%2C%20%60shoo,Pushing%20back%20her). This approach stemmed from her conviction that jazz’s essence is best transmitted “in the ears” and spirit, not just the intellect[[11]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%20they%27re%20hearing.%20,Pushing%20back%20her).

items.quote: live the situations, one after the other, trying to visualize the climate of the historical occurrences through the activity of the heroes of the story as though he were living then.
items.paragraph: From a situationist perspective, the Qur'an's narrative structure creates a kind of immersive, participatory experience where meaning is not pre-given but emerges through the reader's active navigation of the text's recursive patterns. The Qur'anic narrative style employs dialogue extensively—exchanges between God and the Prophet, between the Prophet and his interlocutors, between characters within stories—creating dynamic scenes where readers "live the situations, one after the other, trying to visualize the climate of the historical occurrences through the activity of the heroes of the story as though he were living then." Rather than merely receiving information about historical events, the reader becomes temporally and imaginatively situated within the event itself, transforming passive reception into active phenomenological engagement.[^13]

items.quote: modest, compassionate, and dedicated leader who rescued the Jews from slavery.
items.paragraph: This narrative structure—where Jochebed is hired as a wet nurse to her own biological child—appears to encode a crucial theological message about maternal spiritual transmission. The text specifies that **Jochebed nurses Moses through the critical early years before his weaning and adoption into Pharaoh's household**. Jewish tradition recognizes that during these nursing years, Jochebed could transmit Hebrew faith, language, and identity to the child who would later become Israel's liberator. Rabbinic commentary emphasizes that Jochebed's faith and instruction during the nursing period shaped Moses into the "modest, compassionate, and dedicated leader who rescued the Jews from slavery." Her breastfeeding thus becomes an act of resistance against Pharaonic oppression—through nursing, she inserts Hebrew identity into the consciousness of the future deliverer, even as he grows up in Pharaoh's household.[^23][^24]

items.quote: Can a mother forget her nursing child? … I will not forget you
items.paragraph: Breastfeeding and nurturing, finally, extend the metaphor into the post-birth realm, highlighting how Israel is reared into its identity. The nurturing figures – mothers, nurses, midwives – who appear at critical moments act almost as surrogate figures for God’s own nurturing of Israel. When infant Moses suckles from his Hebrew mother, or Joash is hidden and nursed in the Temple, it is as if God is ensuring that His “child” Israel receives pure milk, untainted by paganism or tyranny[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite)[[26]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=mouth%20which%20will%20speak%20with,Sotah%2012b). In the grand story, God often works through these faithful women to preserve the covenant line and instill covenant values in the next generation. The very intimacy of nursing becomes a political act: Pharaoh’s daughter unwittingly undermines Pharaoh’s genocidal policy by paying Moses’s mother to nurse him, thus financing the survival of Israel’s future deliverer. In narrative after narrative, the self-sacrificial care of a woman secures Israel’s future leader – be it a prophet, judge, or king. This pattern elevates the maternal realm to a place of honor in the national saga. It conveys that identity in Israel is not only inherited biologically but also transmitted through nurturing within the faith community[[13]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Chapman%20concludes%20that%20breastfeeding%20confers,Israelite%20identity%20of%20these%20figures)[[14]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Conclusion). The Bible thus presents the breast and the womb as sanctified instruments of God’s plan: just as God “fathers” Israel by covenant, He also “mothers” Israel through compassionate sustainment. Indeed, God is compared to a nursing mother in Scripture (e.g. Isa. 49:15, “Can a mother forget her nursing child? … I will not forget you”), and Moses in the wilderness feels the weight of being asked to nurse Israel like a mother (Num. 11:12)[[27]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=And%20Moses%20said%20to%20the,Numbers%2011%3A11%E2%80%9315)[[28]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Moses%20likens%20himself%20to%20a,meat%20for%20the%20complaining%20people). These images reinforce the theological point that God’s relationship with Israel encompasses motherly qualities of nourishment, protection, and mercy.

items.quote: no longer have heroes – like Babe Ruth
items.paragraph: Underlying Mary Lou Williams’s pedagogy was a kind of tough love and deep faith in jazz’s value. She believed young musicians needed heroes and role models from the past: “How can anyone advance without listening to someone older?” she asked, lamenting that modern kids “no longer have heroes – like Babe Ruth” in music[[5]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%2C%20and%20a%20new%20pianist%2C,They%27re%20looking)[[17]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,Jazz%20has%20healing%20in%20it). Rather than scold or dictate, she felt a master’s inspiring example was key: “Not someone who’s always telling them, ‘Do this, do that,’... but somebody they want to pay attention to”[[17]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,Jazz%20has%20healing%20in%20it). Williams happily filled that mentor role. Her students, she said, were “great kids. They’re looking for love, and that’s what’s in the music I’m teaching. Jazz has healing in it, and a lot of love.”[[18]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,Arts%2C%20is%20a%20freelance) This almost spiritual view of teaching jazz – as passing on “healing” and “love” – flowed from her own mid-life religious conversion (to Catholicism in 1957) and charity work[[19]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=The%20importance%20of%20the%20blues,technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling)[[20]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling). She truly saw jazz as a positive force for the soul. Indeed, Williams often referred to jazz as “music with healing in it and spiritual feeling,” and she worked “in defiance of those who would call jazz ‘the devil’s music’”[[19]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=The%20importance%20of%20the%20blues,technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling)[[21]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=According%20to%20Father%20Peter%20O%E2%80%99Brien%2C,%E2%80%9D). Whether leading a jazz Mass in a cathedral or a bebop choir in a classroom, her goal was the same: to “open ears” and let people “hear and feel jazz” in its authentic form[[22]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=Mary%20Lou%20and%20the%20bassist,out%20the%20parts%20I%20had). By all accounts, Mary Lou Williams in her final decade became a fervent jazz evangelist, intent on “saving” the music by educating new listeners and players in its rich heritage[[23]](https://music.unc.edu/event/kernodle-pruettlecture24/#:~:text=decades%20that%20followed%20World%20War,movement%20and%20jazz%2C%20her%20work)[[24]](https://music.unc.edu/event/kernodle-pruettlecture24/#:~:text=pianist%2Fcomposer%2Farranger%20Mary%20Lou%20Williams%20during,and%20provide%20another%20means%20for).

items.quote: automate mundane tasks and enable focus on meaningful work
items.paragraph: - Augmentation of Human Skills (Complementarity): Rather than simply replacing workers, generative AI often complements human labor by taking over low-level tasks and freeing up workers to focus on higher-value activities. Analysts note that AI systems excel at handling routine content generation and data processing, which can “automate mundane tasks and enable focus on meaningful work”[[10]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=AI%20may%20be%20used%20to,augment%20and%20improve%20work). For instance, AI chatbots can handle basic customer inquiries so that human agents focus on complex cases[[11]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=Further%2C%20AI%20may%20be%20able,rather%20than%20reactive%20maintenance%20tasks). In medicine and law, large language models can draft reports or summarize information, acting as assistive tools for doctors or lawyers while the professionals make final decisions[[12]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=AI%20may%20increase%20job%20satisfaction,rather%20than%20replace%20human%20expertise). An IMF analysis by Pizzinelli et al. (2023) identified many high-skill occupations (e.g. surgeons, lawyers, judges) as highly likely to be complemented – not replaced – by AI, underscoring how generative AI can support human expertise rather than substitute for it[[12]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=AI%20may%20increase%20job%20satisfaction,rather%20than%20replace%20human%20expertise). This augmentation dynamic can also improve job satisfaction, as workers spend more time on creative or interpersonal aspects of their jobs instead of rote tasks[[10]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=AI%20may%20be%20used%20to,augment%20and%20improve%20work). In sum, optimistic views suggest generative AI will act as a collaborator – a “co-pilot” that handles repetitive work and amplifies human creativity and decision-making.

items.quote: It came about at the time she was giving birth, that behold, there were twins in her womb. Moreover, it happened that one put out his hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, 'This one came out first.' But afterward his brother came out, and the scarlet thread was on his hand
items.paragraph: Similarly, Tamar's childbirth with Perez and Zerah presents another paradigmatic difficult birth whose very strangeness carries theological weight. The narrative records an unusual reversal: "It came about at the time she was giving birth, that behold, there were twins in her womb. Moreover, it happened that one put out his hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, 'This one came out first.' But afterward his brother came out, and the scarlet thread was on his hand" (Genesis 38:27-30). The reversal itself—the hand withdrawn, then the brother emerging first—dramatizes divine sovereignty over human expectation and birthright succession.[^15]

items.quote: I will greatly multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children
items.paragraph: The Hebrew word for "birth pain" or "travail" is 'etsab, which appears in Genesis 3:16 in God's judgment on Eve: "I will greatly multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children" . This term carries broader connotations of labor, sorrow, and suffering beyond physical childbirth. The related noun 'ese b refers to sorrow, labor, and toil, establishing a semantic field that connects childbirth pain with broader human experiences of suffering and struggle [(61)](https://skipmoen.com/2022/02/birth-rite/).

items.quote: ensure that companies keep investing in the technology, safe in the knowledge they will get a return
items.paragraph: - Option 2: Assign Copyright to the AI’s Developer/Programmer. Another perspective is that the creator of the AI algorithm (or the company behind it) should be deemed the author/owner of works generated by that AI. This is somewhat analogous to how UK law’s default might be interpreted (the person making the necessary arrangements – often the developer)[[22]](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/wipo-magazine/articles/artificial-intelligence-and-copyright-40141#:~:text=%E2%80%9CIn%20the%20case%20of%20a,%E2%80%9D). Pros: This would ensure a clear owner exists, typically the party that invested in creating the generative technology. It would reward the investment and skill that went into building the AI, under the logic that without the developer’s efforts the work wouldn’t exist[[32]](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/wipo-magazine/articles/artificial-intelligence-and-copyright-40141#:~:text=Granting%20copyright%20to%20the%20person,a%20return%20on%20their%20investment). Proponents say this approach would “ensure that companies keep investing in the technology, safe in the knowledge they will get a return” on AI-generated works[[32]](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/wipo-magazine/articles/artificial-intelligence-and-copyright-40141#:~:text=Granting%20copyright%20to%20the%20person,a%20return%20on%20their%20investment). It might also be administratively simpler in cases where one company’s AI produces millions of works – ownership would vest in that company by default. Cons: This approach arguably ignores the actual creative contribution to the specific work. The developer wrote the software but often has no hand in the particular output (they might not even know of its existence). It’s akin to giving the manufacturer of a paintbrush the copyright to paintings made with it – which feels counterintuitive[[23]](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/wipo-magazine/articles/artificial-intelligence-and-copyright-40141#:~:text=This%20leaves%20open%20the%20question,generating%20a%20work%2C%20the%20user%E2%80%99s). There’s also a concern that it could concentrate a huge volume of copyrights in the hands of a few AI firms, potentially giving them monopoly control over vast swaths of AI-generated content. Meanwhile, the end-users or artists who use the AI tool get nothing, which could seem unfair if those users did play a role in guiding the output. Another downside is it doesn’t solve the “multiple authors” issue: modern AI often builds on open-source code or pre-trained models from many contributors – attributing sole authorship to one company might disregard others’ contributions (and potentially the training data creators’ rights, though that’s a separate input issue).

items.quote: Joash remained hidden with his nurse at the temple of the LORD for six years while Athaliah ruled the land
items.paragraph: Most tellingly, **the story of King Joash and his nurse Jehosheba** reveals the theological significance of nursing relationships for preserving the Davidic line. When the usurper queen Athaliah murders the royal family, Jehosheba (the sister of King Ahaziah) "took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the sons of the king who were being murdered, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom" (2 Chronicles 22:11). The text emphasizes the role of his nurse in preserving Joash through six years of concealment in the temple: "Joash remained hidden with his nurse at the temple of the LORD for six years while Athaliah ruled the land" (2 Kings 11:3).[^28][^29]

items.quote: designed an illustration of a tree
items.paragraph: Thus, Mary Lou Williams’s Jazz Tree presents a clear narrative: Jazz grew from the suffering of Black Americans (the roots) into spirituals, then through ragtime, swing, and bebop (the sturdy trunk), nourished all along by the blues (the sap of the tree). The great jazz innovators adorn the flourishing branches at the top, while the misdirections (avant-garde extremism, soulless technique, commercial rock, etc.) are depicted as withered limbs cut off from the nourishing roots[[42]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=Down%20into%20the%20earth%20of,the%20vital%20musicians%20in%20whose)[[36]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=the%20evolution%20of%20the%20music%2C,whose%20music%20the%20blues%20flourish). This visual aid reinforced to her students and audiences that the true lineage of jazz is continuous and rooted in Black musical traditions and emotional expression, whereas paths that stray from that lineage tend to wither. Williams boldly used the diagram to argue for her credo about jazz history. As one Catholic newspaper described, she “designed an illustration of a tree” for her lectures to show that jazz “comes from suffering” and “can never be separated from it”[[25]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=As%20Williams%E2%80%99%20popularity%20grew%2C%20she,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it)[[43]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=jazz%2C%20for%20use%20at%20her,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it). The blues and spirituals are the ever-present life force in the music, giving it the “spiritual dimension” born of hardship[[44]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=Jazz%2C%20she%20believed%2C%20was%20something,souls%2C%E2%80%9D%20those%20who%20were%20suffering). Meanwhile, pursuits like purely commercial pop or abstract experimentation are portrayed as unnatural offshoots that lack roots and thus bear no fruit. Williams’s Jazz Tree, often printed as a poster by Jazzmobile for educational use, distilled decades of jazz evolution into a single powerful image – one that championed the primacy of the Black spiritual/blues tradition in jazz while pointedly critiquing the trends she saw as betraying that tradition[[45]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=held%20conviction%20about%20the%20origin,of%20the%20music)[[46]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=appear%20such%20words%20as%20%E2%80%9Ccults,whose%20music%20the%20blues%20flourish).

items.quote: to maintain peace amid the turbulences of decolonisation and civil wars within the emerging nations of the Third World,
items.paragraph: New Functions of the United Nations – Peacekeeping and Beyond: Decolonization also compelled the United Nations to develop new operational roles, most notably peacekeeping, to address conflicts that arose from the end of empire. Many early UN peacekeeping missions in the 1950s–60s were directly connected to decolonization crises. For example, the first large-scale UN peacekeeping force, the UN Emergency Force (UNEF) in 1956, was deployed after the Suez Crisis – a conflict triggered when Egypt (recently independent and nationalist under Nasser) was invaded by Britain, France, and Israel over the Suez Canal. UNEF helped supervise the withdrawal of invading forces, essentially mediating a post-colonial power dispute. Even more telling was the UN Operation in the Congo (ONUC) from 1960 to 1964. When the Congo became independent from Belgium in 1960, it plunged into chaos – Belgian settlers and troops rebelled, and the mineral-rich Katanga province seceded with European backing. The UN, at the request of the Congolese government, sent a massive peacekeeping mission to prevent civil war and thwart foreign intervention. ONUC became a precedent for robust UN action (including use of force) to preserve the territorial integrity and stability of a newly decolonized state. Similarly, in the early 1960s the UN sent missions to assist in the transition of West New Guinea from Dutch rule to Indonesian control (UNTEA in 1962-63) and to mediate in Cyprus following its independence and outbreak of inter-communal conflict (UNFICYP from 1964)[[59]](https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/un-peacekeeping-or-the-reinvention-of-colonialism-an-interview-with-margot-tudor/#:~:text=Blue%20Helmet%20Bureaucrats%3A%20United%20Nations,bureaucrats%27%20extended%20colonial%20structures%20and). These missions reflected how the UN had to step into the security vacuum sometimes left by departing colonial powers. Traditional historiography has often presented UN peacekeeping as a benevolent effort “to maintain peace amid the turbulences of decolonisation and civil wars within the emerging nations of the Third World,” preventing local conflicts from escalating into superpower confrontations[[60]](https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/un-peacekeeping-or-the-reinvention-of-colonialism-an-interview-with-margot-tudor/#:~:text=Traditional%20historiography%20has%20regarded%20the,Cambridge%20University%20Press%2C%202023). Indeed, peacekeepers (the iconic “blue helmets”) became symbols of the UN’s commitment to global stability in newly independent states. They also took on tasks like helping organize elections (as in West New Guinea 1962 or later in Namibia 1989) and training local security forces, thus smoothing the path of state-building.

items.quote: The theater, which is in no thing, but makes use of everything – gestures, sounds, words, screams, light, darkness – rediscovering the idea of a kind of unique language halfway between gesture and thought.
items.paragraph: Definition and Origin: The Theater of Cruelty is a theatrical theory devised by French dramatist Antonin Artaud in the 1930s. Despite the ominous name, Artaud’s concept of “cruelty” did not mean mere sadism or gratuitous violence. Rather, he used it to describe a relentless, shattering force in theatre that would attack the senses of the audience and lay bare deeper truths. Artaud envisioned theater as “a primitive ceremonial experience intended to liberate the human subconscious and reveal man to himself”, using gestures, sounds, and shocking imagery as a kind of language superior to mere words[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=Encyclop%C3%A6dia%20Britannica%20describes%20the%20Theatre,theatre%20and%20strove%20to%20create). In his manifesto The Theatre and Its Double (1938), Artaud argued that Western theatre had become too genteel and text-bound; he wanted to remove the safe distance between actor and audience and immerse spectators in intense, visceral performances that “hurl the spectator into the center of the action”, hitting them with “immediate violent action” that could not be easily forgotten[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=In%20his%20writings%20on%20the,9). This was the “cruelty” – a ruthless attack on the audience’s complacency, a willingness to show disturbing, taboo, or primal images in order to wake up the audience’s emotions and consciousness. For example, Artaud imagined using eerie lighting, cacophonous sound, and grotesque stage images to bombard the audience’s senses, believing that such shock therapy had a spiritual or purgative function. The Theatre of Cruelty thus seeks to create a powerful catharsis by confronting spectators with the raw intensity of life’s pain, terror, and beauty all at once[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=Similarly%2C%20cruelty%20does%20not%20refer,According%20to%20scholar%20Nathan%20Gorelick)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency). Artaud wrote, “The theater, which is in no thing, but makes use of everything – gestures, sounds, words, screams, light, darkness – rediscovering the idea of a kind of unique language halfway between gesture and thought.” The result is a theatre that leaves the audience trembling, provoked, and transformed – a cruelty that is, in Artaud’s view, ultimately compassionate, because it forces people to face truths they habitually evade[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=For%20Artaud%2C%20cruelty%20%20is,is%20physical%20expression%20in%20space)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=Artaud%2C%20this%20was%20a%20cruel%2C,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency).

items.quote: the present submission lacks traditional human authorship—it was autonomously generated by an AI
items.paragraph: The Copyright Office denied Thaler's application, and in 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit affirmed this decision. The court held that human authorship is a constitutional and statutory requirement for copyright protection, stating that "the present submission lacks traditional human authorship—it was autonomously generated by an AI". The court emphasized that many provisions of the Copyright Act "only make sense" if an author is a human being, and thus the statutory requirement includes that "authors must be human, not machines".[^28]

items.quote: extend the reach and value of human expertise
items.paragraph: - Skill Democratization and Inclusivity: Some scholars highlight generative AI’s potential to “democratize” skills and expertise across a broader workforce[[19]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=significant%20benefits%20in%20productivity%20were,to%20improve%20performance%20for%20all). Because modern AI tools have user-friendly interfaces (one can prompt an AI in natural language), workers without advanced technical training can harness capabilities that previously required specialist skills. Research shows that AI assistance disproportionately helps less-experienced workers improve their performance, thus narrowing skill gaps within teams[[9]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=Several%20studies%20have%20suggested%20AI,to%20improve%20performance%20for%20all). For example, generative code assistants enabled junior programmers to produce code at a speed approaching that of senior developers[[20]](https://www.bis.org/publ/work1208.htm#:~:text=Our%20findings%20indicate%20that%20LLMs,than%20the%20tool%20being%20less)[[21]](https://www.bis.org/publ/work1208.htm#:~:text=increased%20by%2055,the%20lower%20impact%20on%20senior). In writing tasks, access to ChatGPT helped weaker writers generate outputs closer in quality to those of stronger writers[[3]](https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/productivity-effects-generative-artificial-intelligence#:~:text=the%20results%20of%20an%20experiment,between%20writers%20of%20varying%20abilities)[[4]](https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/productivity-effects-generative-artificial-intelligence#:~:text=The%20treatment%20group%20overwhelmingly%20chose,before%20heavily%20editing%20its%20output). This suggests AI tools can raise the floor of productivity and capability. By lowering barriers to knowledge (since “programming skills are not needed” to use an LLM[[19]](https://www.commerce.nc.gov/news/the-lead-feed/generative-ai-and-future-work#:~:text=significant%20benefits%20in%20productivity%20were,to%20improve%20performance%20for%20all)), generative AI could empower a wider group of people to perform complex tasks, from drafting business plans to analyzing data. Some experts even argue this technology could help reverse job polarization. Autor (2023) contends that AI offers a “unique opportunity” to “extend the reach and value of human expertise” beyond elite professionals[[22]](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w32140/w32140.pdf#:~:text=which%20is%20the%20province%20of,are%20currently%20arrogated%20to%20elite). By equipping mid-skill workers with AI decision-support, a larger pool of employees could take on higher-level duties (e.g. nurses using AI to diagnose, paralegals using AI to write contracts, etc.), potentially rebuilding middle-class jobs that were eroded by earlier automation[[23]](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w32140/w32140.pdf#:~:text=to%20extend%20the%20relevance%2C%20reach%2C,lawyers%2C%20software%20coding%20to%20computer)[[24]](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w32140/w32140.pdf#:~:text=undergraduate%20education%20to%20professors,out%20by%20automation%20and%20globalization). In essence, generative AI could spread advanced capabilities more evenly, making the economy more inclusive if training and access are widely provided.

items.quote: If we drop two objects, which will hit the ground first?
items.paragraph: - Explicitly Teach Cause-and-Effect and Inference Skills: Some autistic students may benefit from direct instruction in how to use clues and past information to make predictions. This can be done through academic exercises that double as life skills. For example, in reading comprehension lessons, teachers often ask students to predict what will happen next in a story. For an autistic student, this is not just a literacy skill but also a practice in real-world prediction. Teachers can scaffold this by pointing out obvious cues (“The sky turned dark and cloudy in the story – what do you think might happen?”) and guiding the student to form a prediction (“Maybe it will rain”). Connecting these dots explicitly can translate to the student’s daily life (dark clouds mean rain is likely, so they can predict indoor recess). Likewise, science experiments offer a chance to hypothesize (“If we drop two objects, which will hit the ground first?”) and then observe outcomes – a concrete way to see that making guesses and seeing them corrected is a normal process. By training the brain’s prediction muscles in low-stakes contexts, we help the student build confidence and skill in anticipating and updating expectations. This reduces anxiety because the student gradually learns that uncertainty can be approached systematically rather than avoided – they start engaging in the same “automatic process we go through when decision making” but in a more deliberate, practiced manner[[28]](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/13/6/575#:~:text=,making%2C%20and%20modelling%20this).

items.quote: go back to the beginnings of jazz, to spirituals and gospel and the blues,
items.paragraph: In her teaching, Williams placed paramount importance on feeling and the oral tradition of jazz. She believed jazz should be learned by ear and through direct experience rather than solely from books. “Jazz doesn’t come out of school,” she argued – many greats like Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane “were playing before they ever studied” formally[[7]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=learned%20them%20in%20about%2015,Then%2C%20in%201942%2C%20she%20moved). Williams felt a purely academic, technical approach produces sterile results: “Sure, you can play like a typewriter [by studying in school], but it’ll make your audience nervous…It’s nothing that’s written down in a book”, she said bluntly[[8]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,in%20a%20hook%2C%20you%20know). Instead, she tried to “teach the feeling” of the music[[9]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=have%20to%20hear%20great%20music,semester%2C%20I%20gave%20the%20kids). Her methods were hands-on and immersive: she would “go back to the beginnings of jazz, to spirituals and gospel and the blues,” having students listen and sing along to internalize the sound[[9]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=have%20to%20hear%20great%20music,semester%2C%20I%20gave%20the%20kids). “I have them sing all the eras of jazz,” she explained – for instance, when covering bebop she had the class scat “shoo-be-doo-be-doo” lines[[10]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=going%20back%20to%20the%20beginnings,backward%20and%20did%20all%20the). Only once students “saturate the entire mind” with the sound and feeling of one era would she move on to the next[[11]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%20they%27re%20hearing.%20,Pushing%20back%20her). If they lacked the proper feel – as when one class’s blues singing “sounded cold” – Williams would “move backward and do all the spirituals again” until they gained the needed warmth[[12]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=they%20sing%2C%20%60shoo,Pushing%20back%20her). This approach stemmed from her conviction that jazz’s essence is best transmitted “in the ears” and spirit, not just the intellect[[11]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%20they%27re%20hearing.%20,Pushing%20back%20her).

items.quote: What are the implications of anime’s form?
items.paragraph: - Points of Focus Summary: In contrast to the representational approach, which asks “What does this anime mean?”, the media-form approach asks “How does anime work?” and “What are the implications of anime’s form?”. Key points of focus are: visual style and animation technique, narrative form shaped by medium (seriality, genre conventions), production processes and industry context, cross-media integration, and the experiential impact of anime’s audio-visual features. For instance, a media-form scholar might investigate why anime characters have such a broad range of facial stylization and what effect that has on audience empathy – a question rooted in form, not just representation. Lamarre’s critique encapsulates this orientation: he notes that too many analyses “ignore that [anime’s] object consists of moving images” and urges engagement with the specific material qualities of anime as animation[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in). In practice, this means exploring areas like the use of camera movement in anime, the role of voice acting (seiyū performances) in conveying character, or the impact of digital animation tools on the look of contemporary anime. By focusing on these elements, the media-form approach provides a detailed understanding of anime’s unique language and its place within media arts, complementing the cultural/textual interpretations with insight into how anime creates meaning through form[[8]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=reviews.%20,of%20the%20materiality%20of%20animation)[[7]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,intertextual%20references%2C%20or%20cute%20characters).

items.quote: O you who believe... / “O you who disbelieve…
items.paragraph: Application in Qur’anic Studies: When applied to the Qur’an, the concept of situationist constructs offers a way to understand the scripture’s unique narrative style as experientially immersive. Unlike a conventional historical or storybook narrative, the Qur’anic text does not follow a straightforward linear chronology. Instead, it presents a collage of revelations, shifting rapidly between scenes, times, and voices. This can be seen as the Qur’an “constructing situations” for the reader or listener. Rather than telling one continuous story, it drops the audience into a series of vivid vignettes, moral admonitions, and spiritual dialogs that must be actively navigated. Scholars have noted that the Qur’an’s revelation is arranged by divine wisdom to speak directly to the context of the Prophet Muhammad’s mission, often “arranging the story fragments without chronological order” to maximize their moral and emotional resonance[[12]](https://ejournal.uin-suka.ac.id/ushuluddin/esensia/article/view/5372#:~:text=The%20narration%20of%20Qur%27anic%20stories%2C,reveals%20that%20the%20parts%20of)[[13]](https://ejournal.uin-suka.ac.id/ushuluddin/esensia/article/view/5372#:~:text=language,story%20fragments%20without%20chronological%20order). The effect is that the listener is immersed in a living conversation: at times the Qur’an addresses the Prophet, then shifts to humanity at large (“O mankind…”), then to the believers or disbelievers (“O you who believe... / “O you who disbelieve…”), and even directly questions the reader (“So where are you going?” – Q.81:26). This constant change of address and scene creates an interactive experience. The audience cannot remain passive; the Qur’an engages them with rhetorical questions and appeals to their reason and conscience[[14]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/1251/61e1d0de751b11c165aa97b429b8e1560bc1.pdf#:~:text=,second%20person%20in%20the)[[15]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397557486_Remittances_Review_Interpreting_Quranic_Rhetorical_Questions_as_Indirect_Speech_Acts_Part-II#:~:text=,its%20content%2C%20context%2C%20and). For example, in Surah al-Rahman (Q.55), the refrain “Which of your Lord’s favors will you deny?” repeats 31 times, practically pulling the listener into responding and reflecting. Such techniques break the “fourth wall” of narrative, much as Situationist happenings broke the barrier between performer and spectator. The Qur’an thus “exits” the normal flow of sacred history and creates a timeless, participatory space where past prophets, future judgment, and present guidance collide in a single tapestry[[16]](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/14/7/827#:~:text=In%20effect%2C%20the%20holy%20book,The%20Quranic%20%E2%80%9CTheater%20of%20Cruelty%E2%80%9D). We might say the Qur’anic discourse constructs a spiritual situation: the listener is simultaneously in 7th-century Arabia hearing the Prophet, and in the eschatological future witnessing scenes of Judgment, and in an intimate dialogue with the Almighty in the here-and-now. This non-linear, multi-layered storytelling compels the reader to actively piece together meaning – very much like the Situationist aim of prompting individuals to actively construct the significance of their experience. By interpreting the Qur’an’s narrative style through Debord’s notion of constructed situations, scholars highlight the immersive quality of the text. The Qur’an is not a distant story to observe; it is an environment one enters, a guided experience that transforms the receptive participant.

items.quote: can never be separated from it
items.paragraph: Thus, Mary Lou Williams’s Jazz Tree presents a clear narrative: Jazz grew from the suffering of Black Americans (the roots) into spirituals, then through ragtime, swing, and bebop (the sturdy trunk), nourished all along by the blues (the sap of the tree). The great jazz innovators adorn the flourishing branches at the top, while the misdirections (avant-garde extremism, soulless technique, commercial rock, etc.) are depicted as withered limbs cut off from the nourishing roots[[42]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=Down%20into%20the%20earth%20of,the%20vital%20musicians%20in%20whose)[[36]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=the%20evolution%20of%20the%20music%2C,whose%20music%20the%20blues%20flourish). This visual aid reinforced to her students and audiences that the true lineage of jazz is continuous and rooted in Black musical traditions and emotional expression, whereas paths that stray from that lineage tend to wither. Williams boldly used the diagram to argue for her credo about jazz history. As one Catholic newspaper described, she “designed an illustration of a tree” for her lectures to show that jazz “comes from suffering” and “can never be separated from it”[[25]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=As%20Williams%E2%80%99%20popularity%20grew%2C%20she,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it)[[43]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=jazz%2C%20for%20use%20at%20her,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it). The blues and spirituals are the ever-present life force in the music, giving it the “spiritual dimension” born of hardship[[44]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=Jazz%2C%20she%20believed%2C%20was%20something,souls%2C%E2%80%9D%20those%20who%20were%20suffering). Meanwhile, pursuits like purely commercial pop or abstract experimentation are portrayed as unnatural offshoots that lack roots and thus bear no fruit. Williams’s Jazz Tree, often printed as a poster by Jazzmobile for educational use, distilled decades of jazz evolution into a single powerful image – one that championed the primacy of the Black spiritual/blues tradition in jazz while pointedly critiquing the trends she saw as betraying that tradition[[45]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=held%20conviction%20about%20the%20origin,of%20the%20music)[[46]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=appear%20such%20words%20as%20%E2%80%9Ccults,whose%20music%20the%20blues%20flourish).

items.quote: returning life history to the individual.
items.paragraph: Following Estonia's regained independence in 1991, Takk positioned himself as what scholars term a "memory entrepreneur"—an individual actively responsible for creating and promoting particular interpretations of the past through commemorative and narrative practices. This role was characteristic of individuals who served as cultural producers and intermediaries in the broader field of commemoration and memory work that emerged in post-Soviet Estonia. Takk's activities exemplified the broader Estonian phenomenon of the 1990s, where citizens engaged in intensive memory work, writing life stories and participating in what Kõresaar describes as a process of "returning history to the nation" and "returning life history to the individual." This memory work was not merely personal reflection but constituted a form of grassroots recognition politics, where individuals sought to have their experiences acknowledged and integrated into the newly forming official historical narratives of independent Estonia.[^3][^4][^5]

items.quote: respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples
items.paragraph: Colonial Issues at the United Nations’ Founding: The United Nations, established in 1945, inherited the question of colonialism at a pivotal moment. On one hand, the UN was founded by states that included the world’s major colonial powers (Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, etc.), which sought to preserve their overseas territories. On the other hand, the devastation of World War II and ideals of the UN Charter generated new momentum for self-determination. The UN Charter pointedly acknowledges “respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples” (Article 1(2)), signaling that independence for colonial peoples was now an international concern. However, at the founding San Francisco Conference in 1945, colonial powers pushed back against any outright condemnation of imperialism. The compromise reached was to include general obligations for colonial administrators without immediately dismantling empire. Thus, Chapter XI of the Charter, titled “Declaration Regarding Non-Self-Governing Territories,” declared that the interests of colonial peoples were “paramount” and bound member states to promote the well-being and progressive development of those territories[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_list_of_non-self-governing_territories#:~:text=Chapter%20XI%20of%20the%20United,self%20governing%20territories%20under%20member). Specifically, Article 73 of the Charter obliged administering powers to “develop self-government, to take due account of the political aspirations of the peoples,” and to assist them in progressive development[[27]](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1951v02/d455#:~:text=Historical%20Documents%20,assist%20them%20in%20the). Importantly, Article 73(e) required colonial powers to transmit yearly information to the UN on the economic, social, and educational conditions in each non-self-governing territory[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_list_of_non-self-governing_territories#:~:text=). This reporting clause meant that colonial affairs, once the private domain of empires, would be subject to international scrutiny at the United Nations.
