items.quote: Don’t interrupt a teacher when they look busy
items.paragraph: Many of the uncertainties autistic students face are social or implicit in nature – things that neurotypical peers just “pick up” without being taught. The hidden curriculum refers to all the unwritten social rules and norms that people are expected to know but are never explicitly taught (e.g. “Don’t interrupt a teacher when they look busy” or “It might be okay to gently joke with a friend, but not with the principal”)[[29]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=The%20hidden%20curriculum%20is%20assumed,bound%2C%20literal%2C%20and%20rule%20enforcers). Autistic individuals, who tend to be more literal and routine-bound, often miss these subtle cues and unwritten rules[[30]](https://autismspectrumnews.org/a-look-inside-the-hidden-curriculum/#:~:text=The%20hidden%20curriculum%20is%20assumed,bound%2C%20literal%2C%20and%20rule%20enforcers). This can lead to confusion, social mistakes, and anxiety – the student is essentially navigating a minefield of invisible rules, never sure when they might break one. Explicitly teaching the hidden curriculum is a powerful support strategy to remove that uncertainty.

items.quote: My husband is a salaryman. He goes to the office every day. I am a housewife and take care of the children.
items.paragraph: Specific examples from Genki illustrate these problems. In family-related dialogues and role-play exercises, characters are portrayed in traditional heterosexual structures, such as "My husband is a salaryman. He goes to the office every day. I am a housewife and take care of the children." This assumes a nuclear family with opposite-sex parents, excluding same-sex couples or single-parent households, which can distress LGBTQ+ students by making them feel their experiences are invalid or invisible. In vocabulary and picture card activities, Genki includes images like a man in makeup, heels, and a skirt to teach "jirojiro miru" (to stare), eliciting classroom laughter and reinforcing stereotypes of gender nonconformity as odd or worthy of scrutiny. Another example from Genki II shows two men touching in a scenario for "chikan" (pervert), implying negative associations with same-sex contact and potentially stigmatizing gay or bisexual identities. These elements convey a hidden curriculum of heteronormativity, where learners internalize binary gender roles and heterosexual defaults, leading to discomfort for students questioning their identity or from diverse backgrounds.[sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0898589814000485)[asset.library.wisc.edu](https://asset.library.wisc.edu/1711.dl/QXNZN2B3JOQSC82/R/file-ed6b9.pdf)

items.quote: should only be assigned to natural or legal persons that created the work
items.paragraph: However, outside those examples, most countries have not created special rules for AI outputs. Instead, they rely on traditional principles – which, as discussed, usually mean no human author = no copyright. The European Parliament has debated this issue and given some non-binding guidance. In its Resolution of 20 October 2020 on intellectual property and AI, the European Parliament refused the idea of granting AI systems legal personhood or authorship, and it stressed “the principle of originality, which is linked to a natural person.” The Parliament noted that AI-generated creations currently likely fail the originality test since there’s no human creative act, and thus they might not qualify for protection[[20]](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2020-0277_EN.html#:~:text=robots%20might%20not%20be%20eligible,based%20and%20technologically). The resolution went on to recommend that if any copyright or rights were to be considered for AI-generated works, the ownership “should only be assigned to natural or legal persons that created the work” (i.e. to a human creator or a corporate entity behind the AI) and not to the AI or machine itself[[26]](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2020-0277_EN.html#:~:text=concept%20of%20%E2%80%98intellectual%20creation%E2%80%99%20addresses,based%20and%20technologically). Furthermore, the Parliament emphasized that if AI works incorporate copyrighted material (from the training data or otherwise), then the rights should only vest in a human if that use of material was authorized or covered by an exception[[26]](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2020-0277_EN.html#:~:text=concept%20of%20%E2%80%98intellectual%20creation%E2%80%99%20addresses,based%20and%20technologically). In essence, the EU perspective (as of 2020–2021) was: stick to human authorship, perhaps clarify rules uniformly across member states, and do not create a new category of “AI as author.” Indeed, the Parliament suggested the Commission study it more and consider a “horizontal” solution, but any such solution should keep humans in the loop of ownership[[27]](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2020-0277_EN.html#:~:text=robots%20might%20not%20be%20eligible,based%20and%20technologically).

items.quote: at the set time of which God had spoken
items.paragraph: The stories of Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel illustrate this dynamic vividly. Sarah’s conception of Isaac is a miraculous reversal of nature. Long barren and post-menopausal, Sarah conceives “at the set time of which God had spoken” – a fulfillment of covenant promise rather than ordinary biology. Abraham is the physical father, but the narrative stresses God’s power: “The LORD did for Sarah as He had promised” (Gen. 21:1). Rebekah’s pregnancy likewise occurs only after divine intervention: “Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD answered him, and Rebekah his wife conceived” (Gen. 25:21). Isaac’s role is to seek God, underscoring that conception comes by divine blessing, not automatic fertility. Rachel’s story is the most drawn-out struggle. Defined by her barrenness, Rachel at first resorts to folk remedies and having her maid bear surrogate children. Yet only when “God remembered Rachel… and opened her womb” did she finally conceive Joseph[[2]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20assignment%20of%20divine%20activity,moment%2C%20the%20womb%20was%E2%80%94by%20default%E2%80%94closed). Upon Joseph’s birth, Rachel exclaims that God has “taken away my disgrace” (Gen. 30:23), highlighting that motherhood – and the honor of founding a family – was viewed as a divine gift lifting the “shame” of childlessness[[4]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=%E2%80%9CRachel%20was%20barren%E2%80%9D%20%28Gen%2029%3A31%29,words%2C%20addressed%20to%20Jacob%2C%20are)[[5]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=Rachel%2C%20in%20naming%20Joseph%2C%20makes,clear%20what%20infertility%20feels%20like). In all these cases, the metaphors of planting and opening convey that while fathers contribute seed, it is God who causes life to sprout. The patriarchs themselves acknowledge this: human procreation is ultimately an act of God, integral to His covenant plan for Israel’s ancestors.

items.quote: Let’s think of what might happen at the school assembly. Maybe we will sit in the front, or maybe in the middle. Perhaps the microphone might squeak loudly once, or maybe it won’t. If it does, what could we do? Maybe cover our ears for a moment.
items.paragraph: - Use “Pre-Play” and Scenario Planning: To further cultivate flexible prediction skills, teachers can encourage a form of mental simulation of possible outcomes for upcoming events. This has been likened to the ancient practice of imagining multiple battle outcomes to “reduce prediction error” if any one occurs[[26]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Regulatory%20flexibility%20is%20the%20ability,brain%E2%80%99s%20way%20of%20rehearsing%20uncertainty)[[27]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=possibilities%20and%20stay%20open%20to,we%20stay%20grounded%20and%20adaptive). In a modern school context, this might mean before a field trip or a big change, sitting down with the student to brainstorm several possible scenarios. For instance: “Let’s think of what might happen at the school assembly. Maybe we will sit in the front, or maybe in the middle. Perhaps the microphone might squeak loudly once, or maybe it won’t. If it does, what could we do? Maybe cover our ears for a moment.” By “pre-playing” various possibilities, the student practices coping with uncertainty in advance[[26]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Regulatory%20flexibility%20is%20the%20ability,brain%E2%80%99s%20way%20of%20rehearsing%20uncertainty). They learn to expect variability – that there is not just one rigid expected outcome, but a range of things that could happen, and they can handle that range[[27]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=possibilities%20and%20stay%20open%20to,we%20stay%20grounded%20and%20adaptive). This technique is powerful because it shifts the student from a black-and-white prediction (“It must go exactly this way or I’ll panic”) to a more resilient stance (“Some parts might be different than I imagine, but I have some idea of the kinds of differences and I’m prepared”). When the actual event unfolds, the student is less likely to be thrown off-balance because one of their mental scenarios coming true feels familiar. Essentially, they have seen the movie trailer for several versions of the event, so the real “movie” doesn’t shock them as much.

items.quote: See the guys that they’re patterned after like Coltrane…they would never be a Coltrane because they don’t know anything about the Basie [style]. It’s just like…school – you can’t start at the top.
items.paragraph: Interestingly though, Williams conceded that “something in Taylor’s music appealed to her, as did John Coltrane’s late playing.”[[67]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) She “accepted both musicians’ work because they could still, if they wanted to, play ‘within the tradition.’”[[58]](https://jazztimes.com/features/profiles/mary-lou-williams-cecil-taylor-embraceable-you/#:~:text=African%20styles%20in%20dress%E2%80%9D%29) This is a crucial insight: Mary Lou could tolerate avant-garde explorations if they came from an artist who had proven their command of jazz fundamentals (like chord changes, blues, swing). Cecil Taylor had classical training and huge technique; Coltrane had come up playing bebop and blues. She knew these men understood the language even when they chose to speak in tongues, so to speak. In contrast, she had no use for lesser players who dove into experimental music without that foundation. To her, those were “people without background…trying to be Coltrane” but failing[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them). In her words, “See the guys that they’re patterned after like Coltrane…they would never be a Coltrane because they don’t know anything about the Basie [style]. It’s just like…school – you can’t start at the top.”[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them) This quote reveals her nuanced esteem for John Coltrane: she regarded him as an advanced artist who earned his innovations through grounding in tradition. Indeed, she included Coltrane’s name on a thriving branch of her Jazz Tree (among the “vital” geniuses)[[35]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=produced%20the%20first%20spirituals,branch%20all%20to%20itself), indicating she absolutely acknowledged his importance to jazz history. She reportedly was moved by Coltrane’s spirituality – his quest in music likely resonated with her own faith. While she critiqued “free music” in general, she praised Coltrane’s integrity. She told one interviewer that Coltrane “knows what he’s doing” unlike many imitators[[69]](https://downbeat.com/archives/detail/marian-mcpartland-in-conversation-with-mary-lou-williams/P1#:~:text=Mary%20Lou%20Williams%3A%20Into%20The,But%20these%20people%20without).

items.quote: tales of heroism, but of ‘small great human beings.’
items.paragraph: Aleksievich’s aim was to reveal a side of war that official history and propaganda had glossed over. In the Soviet Union, World War II (the defeat of Nazi Germany) was sacralized as a glorious victory, remembered in grand narratives of heroism, male camaraderie, and patriotic sacrifice. Aleksievich sought out the “unwomanly” truths that didn’t fit that mold. The title itself implies that war, as traditionally recounted, has no woman’s face – i.e., women’s experiences have been made invisible or are considered unfeminine and thus not spoken of. Her interviews show that women remembered the war in ways that often conflicted with the sanitized, valorous legend. Rather than battles and medals, they spoke of dirt, blood, fear, loss, and also the specific pains of being a woman in war (from coping with menstruation at the front to being shamed for unfeminine toughness after the war)[[33]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=decorations,as%20sickening%2C%20repulsive%20and%20insane)[[34]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=the%20immediate%20postwar%20years%2C%20when,20s%2C%20never%20felt%20young%20again). Aleksievich was not interested in what she calls “tales of heroism, but of ‘small great human beings.’”[[35]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=A%20million%20women%20fought%20in,as%20sickening%2C%20repulsive%20and%20insane) She wanted the intimate, raw, everyday reality of war – the crying of wounded men at night, the smell of a burning tank, the tenderness of a moment of love amid ruins, or the trauma of a sniper who cannot forget the faces of those she killed. By focusing on these human-scale memories, Aleksievich deconstructs the patriotic war narrative. As one of her conclusions, she famously noted: “There’s nothing heroic about war… It’s just sickening, repulsive and insane.”[[36]](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2017/aug/02/unwomanly-face-of-war-svetlana-alexievich-review#:~:text=accountant%20who%2C%20as%20a%20sniper,as%20sickening%2C%20repulsive%20and%20insane) Through women’s eyes, war appears not as the grand adventure often depicted by male veterans or state propaganda, but as a kind of collective tragedy and trauma.

items.quote: Those who curb their anger and pardon people,
items.paragraph: Linguistically, the Qur'an's assonance, alliteration, and vivid imagery arouse sensory responses by stimulating cognitive and emotional processing. For instance, Surah Ar-Rahman (55:1-4) repeats "Which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?" in a rhythmic pattern that builds arousal through novelty and repetition, evoking wonder and gratitude. Psychological analyses frame the Qur'an as a "cure" for emotional imbalances, arousing reflection on anger, sorrow, and fear to foster healing. In Surah Al-Imran (3:134), "Those who curb their anger and pardon people," arousal from evocative language stimulates forbearance, transforming reactive emotions into virtuous states. Emotional typologies in the Qur'an, drawing on models like Plutchik's, categorize responses such as joy or fear aroused by divine narratives, emphasizing sensory immersion through sound and imagery. This application highlights the Qur'an's role in modulating arousal for spiritual growth, though scholars note cultural adaptations are needed to avoid reductive psychologizing.[yaqeeninstitute.org](https://yaqeeninstitute.org/read/paper/perspectives-on-islamic-psychology-healing-of-emotions-in-the-quran)[iqs.sbu.ac.ir](https://iqs.sbu.ac.ir/article_105074.html)

items.quote: decolonized nations announced to the world that they would no longer accept a subordinate role
items.paragraph: The Bandung Conference addressed decolonization both as historical fact and as ongoing international political issue. Participants collectively condemned colonialism in all forms and adopted a ten-point declaration establishing principles of peaceful coexistence. The conference marked a pivotal moment when "decolonized nations announced to the world that they would no longer accept a subordinate role" in global politics. By enshrining principles of sovereignty and equality among nations of all sizes and development levels, the Bandung Conference established that "every country, no matter how small or recently independent, claimed the same fundamental rights as any great power."[^42][^41]

items.quote: from the founding of the NAM, its stated aim has been to give a voice to developing countries and to encourage their concerted action in world affairs.
items.paragraph: Rise of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Group of 77: A key development was the formation of new international groupings by developing countries to amplify their voice. The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was founded in 1961 in Belgrade by leaders of recently independent states – notably Josip Broz Tito of Yugoslavia, Jawaharlal Nehru of India, Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt, Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana, and Sukarno of Indonesia[[48]](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Non-Aligned-Movement#:~:text=determination%20against%20all%20forms%20of,Ghana%2C%20and%20Sukarno%20of%20Indonesia). They and other Asian-African leaders had earlier laid groundwork at the 1955 Bandung Conference, which proclaimed unity among Afro-Asian nations against colonialism, racism, and Cold War domination. NAM members committed to non-alignment – not formally aligning with either the American or Soviet military blocs – as a matter of principle. This did not mean political passivity or neutrality on issues of justice. As Britannica notes, “from the founding of the NAM, its stated aim has been to give a voice to developing countries and to encourage their concerted action in world affairs.” Non-alignment was about independent policy and solidarity among the post-colonial nations, rather than isolation[[49]](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Non-Aligned-Movement#:~:text=conflicts,concerted%20action%20in%20world%20affairs). During the 1960s and 1970s, the NAM grew to include nearly all African, Middle Eastern, Asian, and Latin American countries that were not in formal alliances. It became an influential voting bloc at the UN General Assembly. Decolonization and disarmament were early core objectives of NAM, along with opposition to apartheid and support for the Palestinian cause – issues where East and West often had proxies but the NAM took independent stances. By aligning together, these states shifted power dynamics in forums like the UN: they could sponsor resolutions, demand debates, and bring moral pressure to bear on the superpowers. For example, NAM unity was critical in isolating South Africa over apartheid and in lobbying for sanctions against Rhodesia (Zimbabwe) after its white minority regime’s unilateral declaration of independence in 1965. The complexity here is evident – while officially non-aligned, many NAM countries still leaned toward one superpower or the other in practice, and internal divisions existed. Yet, overall, the movement served as a counter-weight to superpower agendas and kept global equity issues squarely on the international agenda[[50]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=States%20had%20been%20admitted%20in,XV).

items.paragraph: - Main Law: Uruguay pioneered protections for artists with the “Estatuto del Artista y Oficios Conexos” (Law No. 18.384), passed in October 2008[[62]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=Estatuto%20del%20Artista%20y%20Oficios,Conexos)[[63]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=%3E%20%3E%20,de%20la%20acci%C3%B3n%20p%C3%BAblica3). This law creates a special labor and social security status for artists and related workers. It established a National Registry of Artists and Related Trades under the Ministry of Labor, which artists must join to access benefits[[64]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=21%20En%20la%20ley%20se,El%20mismo%20establec%C3%ADa)[[65]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=,%E2%80%9D4). The Statute was a response to the “historical injustice” that artists were not seen as workers – its goal is to grant artists full worker rights, especially retirement/pension rights, acknowledging the intermittent nature of artistic careers[[63]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=%3E%20%3E%20,de%20la%20acci%C3%B3n%20p%C3%BAblica3)[[66]](https://journals.openedition.org/artelogie/10319#:~:text=,esto%2C%20en%20todo%20caso%2C%20debe).

items.quote: It’s all spiritual music – healing to the soul
items.paragraph: Mary Lou Williams’s understanding of jazz history was deeply informed by her personal experience across eras and her spiritual outlook. At its core, her historiography held that jazz is rooted in the African-American experience – especially the pain and resilience of that experience – and in sacred musical expression. She believed the origin of jazz lay in the spirituals sung by enslaved Africans and their descendants, which carried the suffering, hope, and faith of Black people[[26]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=held%20conviction%20about%20the%20origin,of%20the%20music)[[25]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=As%20Williams%E2%80%99%20popularity%20grew%2C%20she,never%20be%20separated%20from%20it). Those spirituals, in her view, infused early jazz with a profound spirit. “The ability to play good jazz is a gift from God,” Williams said. “This music is based on the spirituals – it’s our only original American art form – and should be played everywhere, including church.”[[20]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling) She vehemently rejected the notion that jazz was “devil’s music.” On the contrary, for Williams jazz was sacred at its roots: it had the power to uplift and heal, precisely because it sprang from the trials and soul of a people. In her classes she often asserted that “It’s all spiritual music – healing to the soul”[[19]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=The%20importance%20of%20the%20blues,technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling). This spiritual conception of jazz’s essence colored her judgments of every style.

items.quote: The LORD did for Sarah as He had promised
items.paragraph: The stories of Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel illustrate this dynamic vividly. Sarah’s conception of Isaac is a miraculous reversal of nature. Long barren and post-menopausal, Sarah conceives “at the set time of which God had spoken” – a fulfillment of covenant promise rather than ordinary biology. Abraham is the physical father, but the narrative stresses God’s power: “The LORD did for Sarah as He had promised” (Gen. 21:1). Rebekah’s pregnancy likewise occurs only after divine intervention: “Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren; and the LORD answered him, and Rebekah his wife conceived” (Gen. 25:21). Isaac’s role is to seek God, underscoring that conception comes by divine blessing, not automatic fertility. Rachel’s story is the most drawn-out struggle. Defined by her barrenness, Rachel at first resorts to folk remedies and having her maid bear surrogate children. Yet only when “God remembered Rachel… and opened her womb” did she finally conceive Joseph[[2]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20assignment%20of%20divine%20activity,moment%2C%20the%20womb%20was%E2%80%94by%20default%E2%80%94closed). Upon Joseph’s birth, Rachel exclaims that God has “taken away my disgrace” (Gen. 30:23), highlighting that motherhood – and the honor of founding a family – was viewed as a divine gift lifting the “shame” of childlessness[[4]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=%E2%80%9CRachel%20was%20barren%E2%80%9D%20%28Gen%2029%3A31%29,words%2C%20addressed%20to%20Jacob%2C%20are)[[5]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=Rachel%2C%20in%20naming%20Joseph%2C%20makes,clear%20what%20infertility%20feels%20like). In all these cases, the metaphors of planting and opening convey that while fathers contribute seed, it is God who causes life to sprout. The patriarchs themselves acknowledge this: human procreation is ultimately an act of God, integral to His covenant plan for Israel’s ancestors.

items.quote: You yourself drew me from the womb, made me secure at my mother’s breast… From my mother’s womb You have been my God
items.paragraph: Beyond individual stories, biblical language often fuses birth imagery with national deliverance. The prophets, for instance, compare the Exodus from Egypt to a birthing event for Israel. Isaiah evokes the momentous escape from bondage in maternal terms: “Before she was in labor she gave birth… Shall a land be born in one day? Or shall a nation be delivered in one moment? For as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children” (Isa. 66:7–8). Here Zion (representing Israel) is pictured as a woman in labor, miraculously delivering a new nation. Likewise, God likens His rescue of Israel to the work of a midwife or mother: “You yourself drew me from the womb, made me secure at my mother’s breast… From my mother’s womb You have been my God” (Ps. 22:9–10). Such verses connect individual birth with national rebirth. Indeed, later Jewish tradition explicitly describes the Red Sea as a birth canal and the Exodus as the birth of Israel as God’s child[[10]](https://www.lookstein.org/professional-dev/bible/implications-feminine-imagery-bible/#:~:text=Egypt%20and%20the%20birth%20of,over%20you%2C%20and%20I%20covered). Even certain Hebrew terms carry dual meanings in this respect. For example, the word zeraʿ can mean both “seed/offspring” and literal grain seed; God’s promise to “make Hagar’s zeraʿ numerous” (Gen. 16:10) hints at offspring as a crop yielded by God[[11]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/biblically-how-are-babies-conceived#:~:text=Traces%20of%20a%20two,12)[[12]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/biblically-how-are-babies-conceived#:~:text=Z%20era%20%CA%BF%20can%20mean,is%20blessed%20in%20similar%20terms). And when Moses complains about leading Israel, he asks, “Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that You should say to me, ‘Carry them in your bosom as a nurse carries an infant’?” (Num. 11:12). The rhetorical questions show Moses recognizing that it was God, not any human, who “birthed” the nation. In short, the Bible’s pregnancy and birth imagery—especially in difficult birth stories repeatedly highlighted in Genesis—serves to depict Israel’s own genesis. Through pain, struggle, and surprising reversals, a people is born under God’s midwifery. Each birth narrative, from Jacob and Esau to Perez and Zerah, functions as microcosm and metaphor: Israel’s national identity is one of hard-won emergence by God’s design, like a child delivered amid travail yet destined for greatness.

items.quote: the spiritual feeling that arises out of suffering
items.paragraph: **Blues**: The blues held a similarly foundational status in Williams' historiography. She understood the blues as expressing **"the spiritual feeling that arises out of suffering"**, connecting them directly to the African-American experience while acknowledging their distinct articulation of redemptive spirituality. Unlike some jazz historians who treated blues as one style among many, Williams positioned the blues as **the affective and harmonic constant** running through all jazz development, providing the emotional vocabulary that all jazz musicians would draw from.[^16]

items.quote: any attempt aimed at the partial or total disruption of the national unity and territorial integrity
items.paragraph: - National Unity and Territorial Integrity: Anticipating problems that could arise post-independence, the Declaration warns against “any attempt aimed at the partial or total disruption of the national unity and territorial integrity” of a country after independence[[44]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=And%20there%20is%20the%20warning%2C,7). This clause was meant to prevent colonial powers from Balkanizing territories or inciting secessionist conflicts as they withdrew (a reference, for example, to Katanga’s secession in the Congo or fears of new states fragmenting).

items.quote: Garments of Fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads, melting whatever is in their bellies and skins. For them are maces of iron. Every time they try to escape from anguish, they will be driven back in and [told], ‘Taste the torment of burning!’.
items.paragraph: Application in Qur’anic Studies: The Qur’an’s own use of intense, even frightening imagery – especially in its eschatological and apocalyptic passages – has been likened to a “theater of cruelty” that God stages within the text to jolt the audience’s moral and spiritual awareness[[16]](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/14/7/827#:~:text=In%20effect%2C%20the%20holy%20book,The%20Quranic%20%E2%80%9CTheater%20of%20Cruelty%E2%80%9D). The Qur’an does not shy away from graphic descriptions of divine punishment and the horrors of Hell. These descriptions serve a clear pedagogical purpose: much as Artaud’s shocking theatre was meant to purge and awaken the audience, the Qur’an’s terrifying imagery is meant to shake the reader out of spiritual heedlessness. For example, in Surah Al-Hajj the punishment of unbelievers in Hell is described in visceral detail: “Garments of Fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads, melting whatever is in their bellies and skins. For them are maces of iron. Every time they try to escape from anguish, they will be driven back in and [told], ‘Taste the torment of burning!’.”[[23]](https://quran.com/en/al-hajj/19-22#:~:text=,22%3A20)[[24]](https://quran.com/en/ad-dukhan/43/tafsirs#:~:text=Tafsir%20Surah%20Ad,It%20will%20go). Such depictions are undeniably cruel-sounding, and they are meant to be harrowing. The reader or listener can almost feel the heat and terror in these verses – an experience not unlike an audience member feeling overwhelmed by a harrowing scene in an Artaud play. From a theatrical standpoint, the Qur’an creates a kind of immersive horror scene within the imagination: the Day of Resurrection is painted with quaking earth, darkened sun, and people appearing drunken with fear (Q.22:1–2); Hell is rendered with blazing flames, black smoke, the wails of its inhabitants, and grotesque torments. These elements work together to produce a “convulsive shock” in the believer’s heart, ideally steering them to repentance and righteousness. Modern scholars drawing this parallel argue that the Qur’an’s apocalyptic aesthetics function similarly to Artaud’s Theatre of Cruelty: they eliminate any comfortable distance between the message and the audience. One is not simply reading about punishment intellectually; one is almost made to feel its horror. In Artaud’s terms, the Qur’an’s imagery “exposes [the audience] to the dangers of life” and “shocks [them] out of their complacency”[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency). Importantly, this “cruelty” is in service of moral purification – much as Artaud aimed to purify art and audiences, the Qur’an’s fierce warnings aim to purify souls. The experience of fear and awe is intended to lead to humility, obedience, and a sincere awareness of divine reality. By reading these verses as a form of divinely-orchestrated theater, we appreciate how the Qur’an deliberately stages emotional experiences for its audience. The believer becomes both spectator and participant in a cosmic drama of salvation and damnation. This aesthetic perspective emphasizes the experiential impact of the Qur’an: just as a night at an Artaudian theater might leave one deeply rattled but enlightened, pondering life’s truths, so too the Qur’an’s most dramatic passages leave an indelible emotional impression that reinforces its spiritual teachings.

items.quote: from the famed Japanese anime studio…
items.paragraph: 5. “Cultural Uniqueness” and Transnational Branding: In their transnational dissemination, both Japanese anime and Nordic Noir have been consciously (and sometimes unconsciously) labeled with a kind of cultural uniqueness that becomes part of their global appeal. For anime, its very branding internationally often emphasizes it as “Japanese anime” – highlighting an exotic or special flavor distinct from Western animation. The Japanese government even built a soft power strategy around this: the Cool Japan initiative explicitly packages anime (along with manga, J-pop, etc.) as a showcase of Japan’s unique pop culture to entice foreign audiences[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_Japan#:~:text=Cool%20Japan%20,1%20%5D%5B%202). Thus, anime is endowed with a “Japanese cool” label – from Hello Kitty to Naruto, these cultural exports carry an association with modern Japan’s creativity. In global marketing, anime’s cultural origin is sometimes used as a mark of authenticity (e.g. “from the famed Japanese anime studio…”) and fans often appreciate that anime comes steeped in Japanese language, settings, and folklore, providing a window into a different culture. At the same time, scholars like Koichi Iwabuchi have noted anime can be “culturally odorless” – many sci-fi or fantasy anime avoid overtly Japanese settings, enabling them to travel easily. But even then, the fan discourse often celebrates Japan as the birthplace of anime, and anime’s mystique is tied to perceptions of Japanese society (whether accurate or stereotyped). This can lead to a double-edged exoticism: as Berndt observed, over-focusing on anime as a Japanese artifact can “reinforce exoticism and neo-nationalism”, treating it as something almost insularly unique[[21]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=International%20Journal%20of%20Comic%20Art,of%20variations%20within%20the%20medium)[[6]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=times%2C%20its%20genesis%20is%20the,examine%20multiple%20perspectives%20on%20them). Nonetheless, in the global arena, the label “anime” itself has come to imply a distinct style of animation rooted in Japanese culture, and that cultural tag has been a selling point – it signifies a set of expected differences (visual style, narrative approach) that many viewers find attractive. In the case of Nordic Noir, the cultural branding is literally in the name – Nordic. This label was in fact coined and popularized outside the Nordic countries (by UK critics and academics in the early 2010s) to categorize this wave of crime drama[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_noir#:~:text=Until%20the%202010s%2C%20the%20genre,that%20%2079%E2%80%99s%20Millennium%20Trilogy). The term “Nordic Noir” itself markets these shows on the basis of their regional origin, promising viewers a uniquely Scandinavian experience – typically, a blend of picturesque Nordic settings and dark, socially conscious storytelling. The international promotion of series like The Killing or The Bridge often foregrounded elements like Scandinavian scenery, or the novelty of hearing Danish/Swedish language on TV, as part of their charm. In essence, the shows are sold as coming from the lands of fjords and midnight sun, but revealing a hidden darkness – a very alluring concept for foreign audiences. This plays into a broader Nordic cultural brand that had gained traction, emphasizing things like Nordic social models, design, and now, noir storytelling[[39]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=The%20boom%20in%20crime%20literature,quality%20design)[[35]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=Nordic%20Noir%20has%20both%20contributed,into%20branding%20of%20the%20Nordic). Scholars note that Nordic Noir both contributed to and benefited from the global “Nordic” brand – it undercuts the image of Nordic countries as utopias by showing their dark side, which paradoxically reinforces the fascination with Nordic societies[[35]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=Nordic%20Noir%20has%20both%20contributed,into%20branding%20of%20the%20Nordic)[[40]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=What%20seems%20clear%20is%20that,have%20also%20been%20successfully%20explored). In practical terms, British and other international broadcasters leaned into the Nordicness (for instance, BBC Four’s advertising for these dramas would often reference their Danish/Swedish origins, sometimes even the iconic knitwear of The Killing’s heroine became a talking point symbolizing Scandinavian style). Thus, like anime, Nordic Noir is strongly associated with its culture of origin in the global imagination, giving audiences a sense of consuming something authentically “other.” Importantly, both have leveraged this cultural uniqueness to stand out: anime became synonymous with a bold, boundary-pushing Japanese creativity in animation, and Nordic Noir became synonymous with sophisticated Scandinavian storytelling in crime fiction. There is also a similarity in that both Japan and the Nordic region eventually embraced these labels in a form of cultural export pride – Japan through Cool Japan policies, and the Nordic countries through supporting their TV industry’s exports (e.g. the Danish government funding subtitling for foreign distribution, or pan-Nordic collaborations to market their content abroad)[[35]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=Nordic%20Noir%20has%20both%20contributed,into%20branding%20of%20the%20Nordic).

items.quote: Then God remembered Rachel, and God heeded her and opened her womb
items.paragraph: Rachel's story introduces additional complexity to the barrenness-to-fertility narrative pattern. Her infertility creates significant tension in Jacob's household, leading to the use of surrogate mothers Bilhah and Zilpah (Gen. 30:1-24). The narrative emphasizes divine intervention: "Then God remembered Rachel, and God heeded her and opened her womb" (Gen. 30:22) [(31)](https://www.jointhejourney.com/4920-god-is-sovereign-over-the-womb). When Rachel finally conceives and bears Joseph, she declares: "God has taken away my reproach" (Gen. 30:23), indicating that barrenness was understood as a form of divine displeasure or social stigma .

items.quote: Model-driven Auto-scaling of Green Cloud Computing Infrastructure
items.paragraph: "Model-driven Auto-scaling of Green Cloud Computing Infrastructure" addresses energy efficiency through a model-driven engineering approach to optimize auto-scaling configurations for energy consumption. The research presents a systematic methodology for deriving optimal auto-scaling configurations using constraint solvers, specifically targeting reduction of idle resource consumption. By applying model-driven optimization to determine configuration parameters, the approach significantly reduces power consumption and operating costs compared to traditional provisioning strategies, demonstrating the feasibility of achieving substantial energy savings—50% or higher—while maintaining performance objectives through intelligent auto-scaling configuration.[^19]

Global income distribution reflected this inequality: the international economic order allocated only 30% of the world's income to 70% of the global population living in developing countries, impossible foundation for balanced global development.[^48]

items.quote: Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?
items.paragraph: However, the Hebrew Bible consistently emphasizes that children are a gift from God. God’s direct role is underscored by the recurring phrase “the Lord opened her womb.” When the matriarchs Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel face infertility, their eventual conceptions are attributed to divine intervention rather than human potency. For instance, “God opened [Rachel’s] womb” and she at last conceived Joseph[[2]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20assignment%20of%20divine%20activity,moment%2C%20the%20womb%20was%E2%80%94by%20default%E2%80%94closed). In fact, the text says the same of fertile Leah before her first son[[3]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20best%20proof%20of%20this,4). This suggests that, from the biblical perspective, every conception is enabled by God’s action – as if a woman’s womb is “by nature” closed until God unseals it[[3]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20best%20proof%20of%20this,4). The human father’s role, though biologically necessary, is theologically secondary. Abraham and Jacob both father children, but their wives conceive only at God’s promise or in God’s timing. Isaac poignantly prays on behalf of barren Rebekah, and “the LORD granted his prayer” so that she conceived (Gen. 25:21). When Rachel demands children, Jacob exclaims in anger, “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?” – acknowledging that fertility lies in God’s hands (Gen. 30:2). In short, the authors depict God as the true giver of life: it is God who “visited” Sarah and enabled her to conceive Isaac in old age, and God who “remembered” Rachel and granted her a son[[2]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/god-opened-her-womb-the-biblical-conception-of-fertility#:~:text=The%20assignment%20of%20divine%20activity,moment%2C%20the%20womb%20was%E2%80%94by%20default%E2%80%94closed). Human procreation is thus folded into a divine drama – each new child of Israel is born because God wills it, fulfilling divine promises rather than mere human initiative.

items.quote: Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son
items.paragraph: The Hebrew Bible extends the symbolic significance of birth beyond individual narratives to encompass the nation's collective experience. The prophets frequently employ birth metaphors to describe Israel's restoration and the coming of the Messiah. Isaiah 66:7-9 presents a powerful image of Zion giving birth without labor pains, reversing the curse of Genesis 3:16: "Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son" [(72)](https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BA86918401?l=en).

items.quote: Before she was in labor she gave birth… Shall a land be born in one day? Or shall a nation be delivered in one moment? For as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children
items.paragraph: Beyond individual stories, biblical language often fuses birth imagery with national deliverance. The prophets, for instance, compare the Exodus from Egypt to a birthing event for Israel. Isaiah evokes the momentous escape from bondage in maternal terms: “Before she was in labor she gave birth… Shall a land be born in one day? Or shall a nation be delivered in one moment? For as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children” (Isa. 66:7–8). Here Zion (representing Israel) is pictured as a woman in labor, miraculously delivering a new nation. Likewise, God likens His rescue of Israel to the work of a midwife or mother: “You yourself drew me from the womb, made me secure at my mother’s breast… From my mother’s womb You have been my God” (Ps. 22:9–10). Such verses connect individual birth with national rebirth. Indeed, later Jewish tradition explicitly describes the Red Sea as a birth canal and the Exodus as the birth of Israel as God’s child[[10]](https://www.lookstein.org/professional-dev/bible/implications-feminine-imagery-bible/#:~:text=Egypt%20and%20the%20birth%20of,over%20you%2C%20and%20I%20covered). Even certain Hebrew terms carry dual meanings in this respect. For example, the word zeraʿ can mean both “seed/offspring” and literal grain seed; God’s promise to “make Hagar’s zeraʿ numerous” (Gen. 16:10) hints at offspring as a crop yielded by God[[11]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/biblically-how-are-babies-conceived#:~:text=Traces%20of%20a%20two,12)[[12]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/biblically-how-are-babies-conceived#:~:text=Z%20era%20%CA%BF%20can%20mean,is%20blessed%20in%20similar%20terms). And when Moses complains about leading Israel, he asks, “Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that You should say to me, ‘Carry them in your bosom as a nurse carries an infant’?” (Num. 11:12). The rhetorical questions show Moses recognizing that it was God, not any human, who “birthed” the nation. In short, the Bible’s pregnancy and birth imagery—especially in difficult birth stories repeatedly highlighted in Genesis—serves to depict Israel’s own genesis. Through pain, struggle, and surprising reversals, a people is born under God’s midwifery. Each birth narrative, from Jacob and Esau to Perez and Zerah, functions as microcosm and metaphor: Israel’s national identity is one of hard-won emergence by God’s design, like a child delivered amid travail yet destined for greatness.

items.quote: to promote the political, economic, social, and educational advancement of the inhabitants of the trust territories, and their progressive development towards self-government or independence.
items.paragraph: The Trusteeship System, established by Charter Chapters XII and XIII, represented both continuity with and advancement beyond the League's mandate system. Like mandates, trusteeships theoretically aimed at preparing territories toward independence and were subject to international oversight through the UN Trusteeship Council. However, the new system incorporated conceptual refinements reflecting decolonial pressure. Most significantly, the Trusteeship Charter explicitly stated the "primary objective" of the system was "to promote the political, economic, social, and educational advancement of the inhabitants of the trust territories, and their progressive development towards self-government or independence." Unlike the mandate system's ambiguity regarding ultimate goals, the trusteeship system established independence as an explicit objective.[^14][^15][^1]

In Nakama, particles are taught as "masculine" or "feminine" with warnings about social reactions to mismatches, e.g., "Women using zo may sound rough," reinforcing stereotypes without discussing queer or fluid uses. Research up to 2020, including a 2019 analysis of learner perspectives, showed this rigidity led to "linguistic failure" for LGBTQ+ students, who faced barriers in self-expression and risked misgendering or unwanted disclosure. For instance, non-binary students using boku might receive stares or corrections, as reported in classroom experiences, highlighting how such teaching overlooked intersections of gender and sexuality.[asset.library.wisc.edu](https://asset.library.wisc.edu/1711.dl/QXNZN2B3JOQSC82/R/file-ed6b9.pdf)+更多 2

items.quote: Which of your Lord’s favors will you deny?
items.paragraph: Application in Qur’anic Studies: When applied to the Qur’an, the concept of situationist constructs offers a way to understand the scripture’s unique narrative style as experientially immersive. Unlike a conventional historical or storybook narrative, the Qur’anic text does not follow a straightforward linear chronology. Instead, it presents a collage of revelations, shifting rapidly between scenes, times, and voices. This can be seen as the Qur’an “constructing situations” for the reader or listener. Rather than telling one continuous story, it drops the audience into a series of vivid vignettes, moral admonitions, and spiritual dialogs that must be actively navigated. Scholars have noted that the Qur’an’s revelation is arranged by divine wisdom to speak directly to the context of the Prophet Muhammad’s mission, often “arranging the story fragments without chronological order” to maximize their moral and emotional resonance[[12]](https://ejournal.uin-suka.ac.id/ushuluddin/esensia/article/view/5372#:~:text=The%20narration%20of%20Qur%27anic%20stories%2C,reveals%20that%20the%20parts%20of)[[13]](https://ejournal.uin-suka.ac.id/ushuluddin/esensia/article/view/5372#:~:text=language,story%20fragments%20without%20chronological%20order). The effect is that the listener is immersed in a living conversation: at times the Qur’an addresses the Prophet, then shifts to humanity at large (“O mankind…”), then to the believers or disbelievers (“O you who believe... / “O you who disbelieve…”), and even directly questions the reader (“So where are you going?” – Q.81:26). This constant change of address and scene creates an interactive experience. The audience cannot remain passive; the Qur’an engages them with rhetorical questions and appeals to their reason and conscience[[14]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/1251/61e1d0de751b11c165aa97b429b8e1560bc1.pdf#:~:text=,second%20person%20in%20the)[[15]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397557486_Remittances_Review_Interpreting_Quranic_Rhetorical_Questions_as_Indirect_Speech_Acts_Part-II#:~:text=,its%20content%2C%20context%2C%20and). For example, in Surah al-Rahman (Q.55), the refrain “Which of your Lord’s favors will you deny?” repeats 31 times, practically pulling the listener into responding and reflecting. Such techniques break the “fourth wall” of narrative, much as Situationist happenings broke the barrier between performer and spectator. The Qur’an thus “exits” the normal flow of sacred history and creates a timeless, participatory space where past prophets, future judgment, and present guidance collide in a single tapestry[[16]](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/14/7/827#:~:text=In%20effect%2C%20the%20holy%20book,The%20Quranic%20%E2%80%9CTheater%20of%20Cruelty%E2%80%9D). We might say the Qur’anic discourse constructs a spiritual situation: the listener is simultaneously in 7th-century Arabia hearing the Prophet, and in the eschatological future witnessing scenes of Judgment, and in an intimate dialogue with the Almighty in the here-and-now. This non-linear, multi-layered storytelling compels the reader to actively piece together meaning – very much like the Situationist aim of prompting individuals to actively construct the significance of their experience. By interpreting the Qur’an’s narrative style through Debord’s notion of constructed situations, scholars highlight the immersive quality of the text. The Qur’an is not a distant story to observe; it is an environment one enters, a guided experience that transforms the receptive participant.

items.quote: Take this child and nurse him for me,
items.paragraph: One striking example is the infancy of Moses. In Exodus 2, the baby Moses is under mortal threat due to Pharaoh’s decree to kill Hebrew male infants. Through a twist of providence and cleverness, Moses is not only spared but nursed by his own Hebrew mother. After Pharaoh’s daughter rescues Moses from the Nile, Moses’s sister offers to find a wet nurse and brings Jochebed (Moses’s birth mother) to nurse him[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite)[[16]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Then%20said%20his%20sister%20to,Sotah%2012b). The text emphasizes this arrangement: “Take this child and nurse him for me,” says Pharaoh’s daughter, unwittingly returning Moses to his true mother’s breast[[17]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Then%20his%20sister%20said%20to,%28Exodus%202%3A7%E2%80%939)[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite). This detail carries symbolic weight. Ancient readers and later Jewish tradition understood that nursing an infant could impart lasting identity. The Talmud surmises that God orchestrated Moses’s Hebrew nursing because “the mouth that will speak with the Divine Presence should not suckle what is unclean”[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite). In other words, Moses refused to nurse from an Egyptian woman, so he was given to a Hebrew nurse—ensuring his physical sustenance came from within his own people[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite). The Midrash adds that this prevented Egyptians from claiming credit for his upbringing[[18]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=mouth%20which%20will%20speak%20with,Sotah%2012b). By drinking Hebrew mother’s milk, Moses would absorb the faith and culture of Israel from his earliest days. Thus, breastfeeding becomes a conduit of covenantal identity: the greatest prophet of Israel was literally nurtured on the milk of an Israelite mother, even while growing up in Pharaoh’s palace. This nurturing not only saved Moses’s life but also constituted a quiet act of resistance against Pharaoh’s genocidal policy – a Hebrew woman nourishing the very child who would one day overthrow Egypt’s oppression.

items.quote: the large majority of Members of the United Nations believe that there is no field in which the UN can do more important work than in the colonial field
items.paragraph: The UN General Assembly as an Anti-Colonial Arena: From its earliest years, the General Assembly (UNGA) provided a stage for debates over colonialism, often driven by non-Western countries and later by newly independent states. In the late 1940s, a small but vocal group of member states – including Latin American republics, Arab-Asian countries like India (which, though not independent until 1947, was an original UN member), the Philippines, and the Soviet Union – began pressing the Assembly to address issues such as the treatment of Indians in South Africa, the Indonesian struggle for independence, and the status of North African colonies. The United States and United Kingdom initially hoped to keep the UN’s focus away from contentious colonial questions, but pressure mounted as more Asian, Middle Eastern, and eventually African nations joined the UN. A key mechanism was the “Committee on Information from Non-Self-Governing Territories,” a special committee of the General Assembly that first met in 1947 to review the reports submitted under Article 73(e). As a U.S. official noted in 1954, “the large majority of Members of the United Nations believe that there is no field in which the UN can do more important work than in the colonial field”. These countries “constantly urge increased UN activity in the colonial field and an extension of UN supervision over colonial territories.” The General Assembly’s Information Committee was “a product of the interest of the majority in colonial problems”, and through it (and other forums) they applied “constant pressure” on colonial powers “to account for their stewardship and accelerate the rate of development” of their territories[[34]](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v03/d881#:~:text=,rate%20of%20development%20of%20their). In other words, the UN became a grand tribunal of world opinion on colonialism, where imperial powers had to defend their record and policies. This scrutiny sometimes provoked defensive reactions – colonial states tried to present themselves as responsible guardians preparing colonies for autonomy, while critics exposed abuses and demanded timelines for independence. The Committee’s work, albeit limited to reviewing information, kept colonial issues on the agenda and built a normative case against endless colonial rule. By the 1950s, as decolonization wars and movements intensified (in Algeria, Kenya, Indochina, etc.), the General Assembly’s tone grew bolder. Newly independent countries such as India, Pakistan, Burma (Myanmar), Indonesia, and a wave of decolonized states in 1957–1960 brought first-hand experience to UN debates. They helped move the conversation from polite appeals to assertive resolutions asserting the right of colonies to independence. In 1952, the General Assembly for the first time explicitly affirmed that “all peoples have the right to self-determination,” setting the stage for more robust action later[[35]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=,which%20have%20not%20yet%20attained).

items.quote: Donation and Transplantation of Human Organs
items.paragraph: Meaning of the “stop using prisoner organs” announcement: When Chinese officials announced in December 2014 that “from January 1, 2015, only voluntarily donated organs from citizens would be used” for transplants[[42]](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(15%2960484-6/fulltext#:~:text=On%20Dec%203%2C%202014%2C%20Jiefu,does%20not%20reflect%20the%20reality), it was portrayed as a definitive end to harvesting organs from executed prisoners. In effect, the policy meant that organs would only be allocated through the national donation system, which requires documented voluntary consent and prohibits black-market dealings. Importantly, however, the announcement did not explicitly outlaw organ donations from prisoners – instead, it reclassified death-row prisoners as eligible “citizen donors” under the same framework. Huang Jiefu emphasized this point in media interviews: “Death-row prisoners are also citizens and have the right to donate organs… Once the organs from willing death-row prisoners are enrolled into our unified allocation system, they are then counted as voluntary donation from citizens; the so-called donation from death-row prisoners doesn’t exist any longer”[[41]](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(15%2960484-6/fulltext#:~:text=executed%20prisoners%20into%20the%20existing,the%20plan%20has%20never%20been). In other words, the practice of procuring organs from executed individuals was to be administratively folded into the civilian donation system rather than carried out through separate channels. This move built upon existing laws – notably the 1984 regulations that had technically allowed using executed criminals’ organs with consent of the prisoner or family[[52]](http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2014-12/04/content_19025683.htm#:~:text=According%20to%20relevant%20regulations%20issued,medical%20use%20of%20the%20body). Even after 2007’s transplant law reforms, no Chinese statute outright banned organ use from prisoners; it remained a legally gray area governed by internal guidelines. The 2015 policy change, accompanied by planned amendments to the regulations (to be renamed “Donation and Transplantation of Human Organs” per Huang[[44]](http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2014-12/04/content_19025683.htm#:~:text=The%20State%20Council%20passed%20the,legal%20basis%20to%20supervise%20transplants)), sought to align China’s transplant practice with international ethical standards on paper. It signaled that organs should come from consented donors only, closing the door to overt prisoner organ “harvesting.” However, by counting prisoner donations as voluntary**, China was effectively asserting that as long as a prisoner signs a consent (presumably without coercion), those organs are legally and ethically equivalent to any citizen’s donation[[41]](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(15%2960484-6/fulltext#:~:text=executed%20prisoners%20into%20the%20existing,the%20plan%20has%20never%20been)[[49]](http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2014-12/04/content_19025683.htm#:~:text=Prisoners%20are%20still%20among%20the,the%20future%2C%20Huang%20told%20reporters).

items.paragraph: When it came to younger “avant” players aside from Coltrane, she had very little praise. She openly dismissed many free jazz musicians as charlatans or lacking talent. For instance, she criticized the “guys [who] come up playing avant-garde” without learning basics, saying they were essentially frauds riding on trendiness[[68]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=I%20have%20a%20lot%20of,advice%20I%20could%20give%20them). items.quote: the only true American art form
items.paragraph: Her historiographical vision positioned jazz as **"the only true American art form"**, uniquely rooted in African-American experience and inextricable from African-American history. After her conversion to Catholicism in 1957, she integrated this spiritual framework with her understanding of jazz's origins, seeing the music as inherently **carrying spiritual content** rooted in African-American redemptive traditions. items.quote: What did you expect would occur? And what actually happened? Was it as bad as you feared, or different from what you imagined?
items.paragraph: - Teach “Prediction Awareness” and Flexible Thinking: Educators can help students build an awareness of their own predictions and learn that outcomes can diverge from expectations without disaster. One classroom technique is to openly discuss events after they happen: “What did you expect would occur? And what actually happened? Was it as bad as you feared, or different from what you imagined?” This kind of guided reflection teaches the student that not all predictions will be correct, and that’s okay[[23]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=We%20can%20support%20neurodivergent%20learners,by). By labeling surprises and outcomes, the teacher demystifies them – a surprise is no longer a terrifying unknown but an event that can be analyzed and learned from. Over time, the student can internalize that prediction errors are information, not merely threats[[24]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=pathways%20as%20you%20rise%20out,of%20the%20pit)[[25]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=Mindset%20and%20Neurodivergent%20Brains). For example, if an unexpected fire drill occurs, later the teacher might gently review: “You thought there was a real fire and were very scared. But it turned out to be just a practice – next time, we know that if the alarm rings and the teacher is calm, it’s likely just a drill.” Such debriefs help update the child’s predictive model of the world, making it more accurate and less anxiety-prone. Additionally, explicitly framing mistakes or surprises as learning opportunities (“errors provide us data to improve our predictions”[[24]](https://www.beyondbridgeseducation.com/blogs/what-mindset-really-is#:~:text=pathways%20as%20you%20rise%20out,of%20the%20pit)) can reshape a student’s mindset. They begin to see that if something unexpected happens, they can adapt rather than panic, fostering cognitive flexibility.

items.quote: the use of copyrighted works by ML systems should generally be fair
items.paragraph: Under U.S. law, these four factors are balanced – no one factor is decisive[[5]](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-training-fair-use.html#:~:text=No%20single%20factor%20alone%20determines,harm%20the%20original%20creator%27s%20commercial). In practice, courts tend to give considerable weight to the first and fourth factors, especially the question of transformativeness and market harm[[5]](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-training-fair-use.html#:~:text=No%20single%20factor%20alone%20determines,harm%20the%20original%20creator%27s%20commercial). The concept of transformative use comes from cases like Campbell v. Acuff-Rose and has been crucial in modern fair use cases. A use is transformative if it “adds new meaning or message” or employs the original in a new way that doesn’t simply substitute for the original[[7]](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-training-fair-use.html#:~:text=transformative%20nature%20of%20the%20use,interests%20or%20potential%20licensing%20markets). Training an AI has been likened to a transformative activity: the AI “reads” the originals to glean facts or patterns (much like a human researcher might) and does not expose the expressive content in its original form when it operates[[8]](https://texaslawreview.org/fair-learning/#:~:text=use%20doctrine%2C%20robots%20that%20do,18)[[4]](https://texaslawreview.org/fair-learning/#:~:text=transformative%20as%20that%20term%20has,which%20ML%20systems%20may%20be). Prominent scholars argue that “the use of copyrighted works by ML systems should generally be fair” because the purpose is to learn ideas and patterns, not to exploit the expression[[4]](https://texaslawreview.org/fair-learning/#:~:text=transformative%20as%20that%20term%20has,which%20ML%20systems%20may%20be). Indeed, it’s often said that “reading by robots doesn’t count” as infringement[[8]](https://texaslawreview.org/fair-learning/#:~:text=use%20doctrine%2C%20robots%20that%20do,18) – a notion supported by past court decisions upholding intermediate copying for functions like search indexing and data analysis.

items.quote: constantly urge increased UN activity in the colonial field and an extension of UN supervision over colonial territories.
items.paragraph: The UN General Assembly as an Anti-Colonial Arena: From its earliest years, the General Assembly (UNGA) provided a stage for debates over colonialism, often driven by non-Western countries and later by newly independent states. In the late 1940s, a small but vocal group of member states – including Latin American republics, Arab-Asian countries like India (which, though not independent until 1947, was an original UN member), the Philippines, and the Soviet Union – began pressing the Assembly to address issues such as the treatment of Indians in South Africa, the Indonesian struggle for independence, and the status of North African colonies. The United States and United Kingdom initially hoped to keep the UN’s focus away from contentious colonial questions, but pressure mounted as more Asian, Middle Eastern, and eventually African nations joined the UN. A key mechanism was the “Committee on Information from Non-Self-Governing Territories,” a special committee of the General Assembly that first met in 1947 to review the reports submitted under Article 73(e). As a U.S. official noted in 1954, “the large majority of Members of the United Nations believe that there is no field in which the UN can do more important work than in the colonial field”. These countries “constantly urge increased UN activity in the colonial field and an extension of UN supervision over colonial territories.” The General Assembly’s Information Committee was “a product of the interest of the majority in colonial problems”, and through it (and other forums) they applied “constant pressure” on colonial powers “to account for their stewardship and accelerate the rate of development” of their territories[[34]](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v03/d881#:~:text=,rate%20of%20development%20of%20their). In other words, the UN became a grand tribunal of world opinion on colonialism, where imperial powers had to defend their record and policies. This scrutiny sometimes provoked defensive reactions – colonial states tried to present themselves as responsible guardians preparing colonies for autonomy, while critics exposed abuses and demanded timelines for independence. The Committee’s work, albeit limited to reviewing information, kept colonial issues on the agenda and built a normative case against endless colonial rule. By the 1950s, as decolonization wars and movements intensified (in Algeria, Kenya, Indochina, etc.), the General Assembly’s tone grew bolder. Newly independent countries such as India, Pakistan, Burma (Myanmar), Indonesia, and a wave of decolonized states in 1957–1960 brought first-hand experience to UN debates. They helped move the conversation from polite appeals to assertive resolutions asserting the right of colonies to independence. In 1952, the General Assembly for the first time explicitly affirmed that “all peoples have the right to self-determination,” setting the stage for more robust action later[[35]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=,which%20have%20not%20yet%20attained).

items.quote: the global leader in AI-powered financial risk discovery and anomaly detection
