Designed by renowned green architect Fernando Abruña, known as “the father of green architecture in PR”[[29]](https://casaresilientepuertorico.wordpress.com/casas-resilientes-para-puerto-rico/casa-rescate/#:~:text=El%20arquitecto%20Fernando%20Abru%C3%B1a%20es,del%20Ca%C3%B1o%20Mart%C3%ADn%20Pe%C3%B1a%2C%20dise%C3%B1%C3%B3).

items.quote: exposes [the audience] to the dangers of life
items.paragraph: Application in Qur’anic Studies: The Qur’an’s own use of intense, even frightening imagery – especially in its eschatological and apocalyptic passages – has been likened to a “theater of cruelty” that God stages within the text to jolt the audience’s moral and spiritual awareness[[16]](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/14/7/827#:~:text=In%20effect%2C%20the%20holy%20book,The%20Quranic%20%E2%80%9CTheater%20of%20Cruelty%E2%80%9D). The Qur’an does not shy away from graphic descriptions of divine punishment and the horrors of Hell. These descriptions serve a clear pedagogical purpose: much as Artaud’s shocking theatre was meant to purge and awaken the audience, the Qur’an’s terrifying imagery is meant to shake the reader out of spiritual heedlessness. For example, in Surah Al-Hajj the punishment of unbelievers in Hell is described in visceral detail: “Garments of Fire will be cut out for them, and boiling water will be poured over their heads, melting whatever is in their bellies and skins. For them are maces of iron. Every time they try to escape from anguish, they will be driven back in and [told], ‘Taste the torment of burning!’.”[[23]](https://quran.com/en/al-hajj/19-22#:~:text=,22%3A20)[[24]](https://quran.com/en/ad-dukhan/43/tafsirs#:~:text=Tafsir%20Surah%20Ad,It%20will%20go). Such depictions are undeniably cruel-sounding, and they are meant to be harrowing. The reader or listener can almost feel the heat and terror in these verses – an experience not unlike an audience member feeling overwhelmed by a harrowing scene in an Artaud play. From a theatrical standpoint, the Qur’an creates a kind of immersive horror scene within the imagination: the Day of Resurrection is painted with quaking earth, darkened sun, and people appearing drunken with fear (Q.22:1–2); Hell is rendered with blazing flames, black smoke, the wails of its inhabitants, and grotesque torments. These elements work together to produce a “convulsive shock” in the believer’s heart, ideally steering them to repentance and righteousness. Modern scholars drawing this parallel argue that the Qur’an’s apocalyptic aesthetics function similarly to Artaud’s Theatre of Cruelty: they eliminate any comfortable distance between the message and the audience. One is not simply reading about punishment intellectually; one is almost made to feel its horror. In Artaud’s terms, the Qur’an’s imagery “exposes [the audience] to the dangers of life” and “shocks [them] out of their complacency”[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Cruelty#:~:text=The%20Theatre%20of%20Cruelty%20aimed,them%20out%20of%20their%20complacency). Importantly, this “cruelty” is in service of moral purification – much as Artaud aimed to purify art and audiences, the Qur’an’s fierce warnings aim to purify souls. The experience of fear and awe is intended to lead to humility, obedience, and a sincere awareness of divine reality. By reading these verses as a form of divinely-orchestrated theater, we appreciate how the Qur’an deliberately stages emotional experiences for its audience. The believer becomes both spectator and participant in a cosmic drama of salvation and damnation. This aesthetic perspective emphasizes the experiential impact of the Qur’an: just as a night at an Artaudian theater might leave one deeply rattled but enlightened, pondering life’s truths, so too the Qur’an’s most dramatic passages leave an indelible emotional impression that reinforces its spiritual teachings.

items.quote: don’t count your chickens before they hatch
items.paragraph: - 2. Bird-in-Hand Rule: The “bird-in-hand” approach is a very conservative saving rule designed for intergenerational equity. In this framework, the government only spends the income generated by already accumulated oil wealth, rather than spending anticipated future revenues[[14]](https://odi.org/documents/4071/8393.pdf#:~:text=In%20the%20extreme%20case%E2%80%94the%20so,Hand%20approach%20is%20applied). In other words, oil earnings are first saved (converted to financial assets), and then the annual budget may use only the interest or returns on those savings. This effectively back-loads expenditures to later years and prevents the government from treating unextracted oil as a cash cow[[14]](https://odi.org/documents/4071/8393.pdf#:~:text=In%20the%20extreme%20case%E2%80%94the%20so,Hand%20approach%20is%20applied). The logic is akin to the adage “don’t count your chickens before they hatch” – ensure actual wealth is in hand (“bird in hand”) and preserve the principal for future generations. The bird-in-hand rule thus delinks spending not only from price volatility but also from uncertain future production, forcing high savings upfront[[14]](https://odi.org/documents/4071/8393.pdf#:~:text=In%20the%20extreme%20case%E2%80%94the%20so,Hand%20approach%20is%20applied). Representative example: Norway is often cited as applying a bird-in-hand strategy[[14]](https://odi.org/documents/4071/8393.pdf#:~:text=In%20the%20extreme%20case%E2%80%94the%20so,Hand%20approach%20is%20applied). All of Norway’s petroleum revenue is saved in its sovereign wealth fund, and the government only withdraws a small, sustainable percentage each year (the expected investment return). This means Norway spends only the “interest” on its oil wealth, effectively treating the principal as untouchable – a classic bird-in-hand approach. Such a rule ensures wealth transfer to future generations and shields the economy from revenue shocks, though it can be criticized for limiting spending on immediate development needs in lower-income countries.

items.quote: having someone to catch me if I messed up – so I wrote a much crazier story than I normally would
items.paragraph: 4. Support for Creative Risk-Taking:Creative writing thrives on risk-taking – trying out bold ideas, unusual structures, or experimenting with voice – often with the possibility of failure. AI tools can create a safety net that emboldens students to take these creative risks. Because AI assistance reduces the cost of failure (you can always get a new suggestion or revise with AI help), students may feel freer to attempt something innovative. For instance, a student might normally shy away from using humor or irony in a second language, fearing it won’t come across. But with an AI tool, they could draft a witty sentence and then ask the AI, “Is this phrase conveying humor?” The AI’s feedback or rephrasing can confirm and sharpen the joke, encouraging the student to go ahead with this creative choice. In research settings, learners described AI as a confidence booster that gave them “permission” to be more inventive. One high school EFL student said that using an AI chatbot was like “having someone to catch me if I messed up – so I wrote a much crazier story than I normally would”. In quantitative terms, studies have found that groups using AI showed greater variety in narrative techniques and plotlines, suggesting they diverged more from formulaic writing, likely due to feeling supported in those risks[[11]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.02478#:~:text=Cluster%20analyses%20revealed%20some%20benefit,We%20suggest%20differentiated%2C%20pedagogical). The immediate feedback loop means students can try a risk (say, writing a paragraph from the antagonist’s perspective), get quick input on how it reads, and either continue or adjust course – a kind of interactive creative experimentation that would be slow or impossible in a traditional setting. Moreover, AI tools often encourage iterative refinement, which is key to creative work: students who generated content with AI were willing to delete and rewrite sections more readily, treating it as prototyping rather than one-and-done writing. This iterative mindset is a form of creative risk-taking – not being afraid to scrap a boring idea and try a new direction mid-stream, because the tool can help generate or evaluate the new material rapidly. However, a nuanced finding is that AI can also inadvertently reduce certain risks: if students lean on AI to decide if something is good, they might shy away from ideas the AI doesn’t “like.” For example, if an AI model tends to favor conventional story arcs, a student might abandon a truly unconventional narrative thinking it’s wrong because the AI didn’t support it. There was a case where a student started a nonlinear story, but after AI feedback suggested a chronological order, the student conformed – possibly losing an opportunity to push creative boundaries. This highlights that while AI lowers the fear of technical failure, teachers should ensure it doesn’t enforce conformity in the guise of helpfulness. When guided well, AI scaffolding supports creative risk-taking by acting as a collaborator that catches errors and lends ideas, so students can venture further into the imaginative realm knowing they have backup. The classroom culture also shifts: students become more inclined to share wild ideas because they had a chance to validate or polish them with the AI first, increasing overall creative output in the group.

items.quote: Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son...Who has heard of such as this? Who has seen such things? Shall the earth be made to give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children
items.paragraph: Most significantly, Isaiah 66:7-8 presents a birth metaphor for national redemption in explicitly eschatological language: "Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her pain came, she delivered a son...Who has heard of such as this? Who has seen such things? Shall the earth be made to give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children" (Isaiah 66:7-8). The birth of the nation becomes not merely historical (the Exodus) but prophetic—a future event when Israel will be miraculously "born" in a single moment of divine redemption.[^20]

items.quote: Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that You should say to me, ‘Carry them in your bosom as a nurse carries an infant’?
items.paragraph: Beyond individual stories, biblical language often fuses birth imagery with national deliverance. The prophets, for instance, compare the Exodus from Egypt to a birthing event for Israel. Isaiah evokes the momentous escape from bondage in maternal terms: “Before she was in labor she gave birth… Shall a land be born in one day? Or shall a nation be delivered in one moment? For as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children” (Isa. 66:7–8). Here Zion (representing Israel) is pictured as a woman in labor, miraculously delivering a new nation. Likewise, God likens His rescue of Israel to the work of a midwife or mother: “You yourself drew me from the womb, made me secure at my mother’s breast… From my mother’s womb You have been my God” (Ps. 22:9–10). Such verses connect individual birth with national rebirth. Indeed, later Jewish tradition explicitly describes the Red Sea as a birth canal and the Exodus as the birth of Israel as God’s child[[10]](https://www.lookstein.org/professional-dev/bible/implications-feminine-imagery-bible/#:~:text=Egypt%20and%20the%20birth%20of,over%20you%2C%20and%20I%20covered). Even certain Hebrew terms carry dual meanings in this respect. For example, the word zeraʿ can mean both “seed/offspring” and literal grain seed; God’s promise to “make Hagar’s zeraʿ numerous” (Gen. 16:10) hints at offspring as a crop yielded by God[[11]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/biblically-how-are-babies-conceived#:~:text=Traces%20of%20a%20two,12)[[12]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/biblically-how-are-babies-conceived#:~:text=Z%20era%20%CA%BF%20can%20mean,is%20blessed%20in%20similar%20terms). And when Moses complains about leading Israel, he asks, “Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that You should say to me, ‘Carry them in your bosom as a nurse carries an infant’?” (Num. 11:12). The rhetorical questions show Moses recognizing that it was God, not any human, who “birthed” the nation. In short, the Bible’s pregnancy and birth imagery—especially in difficult birth stories repeatedly highlighted in Genesis—serves to depict Israel’s own genesis. Through pain, struggle, and surprising reversals, a people is born under God’s midwifery. Each birth narrative, from Jacob and Esau to Perez and Zerah, functions as microcosm and metaphor: Israel’s national identity is one of hard-won emergence by God’s design, like a child delivered amid travail yet destined for greatness.

items.quote: the main arena for anti-colonial struggles
items.paragraph: The historical significance of the 1960 Declaration was enormous. It marked the formal delegitimization of colonialism by the international community. Coming from the General Assembly, it lacked the binding force of law that a Security Council resolution under Chapter VII might carry. Yet as an authoritative interpretation of the UN Charter’s principles, it had profound normative weight[[46]](https://legal.un.org/avl/ha/dicc/dicc.html#:~:text=In%20the%20end%2C%20the%20persuasiveness%2C,inclusive%2C%20representative%2C%20pluralist%20world%20community). It affirmed that the era of colonial empires was not just unfortunate but unlawful and contrary to universal values. Colonized peoples fighting for independence drew inspiration and legitimacy from this Declaration, while colonial powers found themselves on the defensive diplomatically. The Declaration also energized the UN’s own efforts: in 1961, the Special Committee on Decolonization (the “Committee of 24”) was established to monitor implementation of the Declaration and push remaining colonies toward freedom[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_list_of_non-self-governing_territories#:~:text=Resolution%201514%20,which%20reviews%20the). Throughout the 1960s, the General Assembly would regularly invoke Resolution 1514 and follow it up with further resolutions – for example, defining criteria for self-government (Resolution 1541 (XV)), condemning policies of apartheid and settler colonialism, and calling for immediate independence of territories like Angola, Mozambique, and Rhodesia. In sum, the UN had become “the main arena for anti-colonial struggles” as newly independent nations used their collective voice to accelerate the end of colonialism[[34]](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1952-54v03/d881#:~:text=,rate%20of%20development%20of%20their). The complexity of this process is worth noting: the UN did not cause decolonization on its own – local liberation movements and Cold War geopolitics were critical drivers – but the organization provided a crucial platform where imperialism was delegitimized and a rules-based decolonization process was encouraged. By the late 1960s, with the exception of Portuguese Africa and a few remaining enclaves, most of the world’s peoples had exercised their right to self-determination and joined the United Nations as sovereign states.

items.quote: a direct and violent attack upon the senses of the audience.
items.paragraph: The theoretical framework suggests that the Qur'an's apocalyptic imagery works not through rational argument but through what Artaud called "a direct and violent attack upon the senses of the audience." Rather than explaining why one should fear divine judgment, the text envelops readers in sensory descriptions of hellfire, the anguish of the damned, the physical transformations of bodies in torment, and the eternal nature of punishment. These descriptions are not metaphorical poetry to be contemplated at distance but visceral stagings of eschatological reality designed to produce an immediate, embodied response.[^20]

items.quote: the mouth that will speak with the Divine Presence should not suckle what is unclean
items.paragraph: One striking example is the infancy of Moses. In Exodus 2, the baby Moses is under mortal threat due to Pharaoh’s decree to kill Hebrew male infants. Through a twist of providence and cleverness, Moses is not only spared but nursed by his own Hebrew mother. After Pharaoh’s daughter rescues Moses from the Nile, Moses’s sister offers to find a wet nurse and brings Jochebed (Moses’s birth mother) to nurse him[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite)[[16]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Then%20said%20his%20sister%20to,Sotah%2012b). The text emphasizes this arrangement: “Take this child and nurse him for me,” says Pharaoh’s daughter, unwittingly returning Moses to his true mother’s breast[[17]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=Then%20his%20sister%20said%20to,%28Exodus%202%3A7%E2%80%939)[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite). This detail carries symbolic weight. Ancient readers and later Jewish tradition understood that nursing an infant could impart lasting identity. The Talmud surmises that God orchestrated Moses’s Hebrew nursing because “the mouth that will speak with the Divine Presence should not suckle what is unclean”[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite). In other words, Moses refused to nurse from an Egyptian woman, so he was given to a Hebrew nurse—ensuring his physical sustenance came from within his own people[[15]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=slave%20of%20Pharaoh%E2%80%99s%20daughter,be%20breastfed%20by%20an%20Israelite). The Midrash adds that this prevented Egyptians from claiming credit for his upbringing[[18]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=mouth%20which%20will%20speak%20with,Sotah%2012b). By drinking Hebrew mother’s milk, Moses would absorb the faith and culture of Israel from his earliest days. Thus, breastfeeding becomes a conduit of covenantal identity: the greatest prophet of Israel was literally nurtured on the milk of an Israelite mother, even while growing up in Pharaoh’s palace. This nurturing not only saved Moses’s life but also constituted a quiet act of resistance against Pharaoh’s genocidal policy – a Hebrew woman nourishing the very child who would one day overthrow Egypt’s oppression.

items.quote: The children struggled together within her womb
items.paragraph: These difficult birth narratives resonate throughout the prophetic literature, where **childbirth becomes the dominant metaphor for national trauma and redemption**. Isaiah employs labor pains to describe Israel's exile and anticipated restoration: "The children struggled together within her womb" finds its echo in the image of Zion in labor pangs, bringing forth not just individual children but the entire reborn nation. Micah declares: "Writhe in agony, O Daughter Zion, like a woman in labor, for now you will leave the city and camp in the open field; you will go to Babylon—there you will be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies" (Micah 4:10).[^18][^19]

Williams blamed money for this: “there’s a lot of money tied up in rock,” she said, implying record companies pushed it at the expense of quality[[73]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-ItsAllGreat-1977.html#:~:text=Because%20there%E2%80%99s%20a%20lot%20of,new%20era%20of%20music%2C%20it). After bebop, she observed, many great players defected to popular styles or were pressured to, and “we almost lost” jazz’s continuity[[39]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,sing%20the%20music%20they%27re%20hearing). She cited this trend as a major reason jazz creativity “stopped” for a time[[41]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,have%20her%20students%20sing%20the).

items.quote: Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them
items.paragraph: **The midwives Shiphrah and Puah** represent another form of maternal resistance through control of birth processes. When Pharaoh commands them to kill all male Hebrew infants, they refuse, claiming that "Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them" (Exodus 1:19). Whether this claim was historically accurate or strategically deployed, the midwives' resistance operates through their control of the birth process itself. They function as guardians of Hebrew reproduction and thus as protectors of the nation's continued existence. Their refusal to perform infanticide becomes an act of proto-political resistance—preserving the people through their maternal care.[^25][^26]

items.quote: Two nations are in your womb… one people shall be stronger than the other, and the older shall serve the younger
items.paragraph: Rebekah’s pregnancy is described as a harrowing ordeal: “the children struggled together within her” to the point she cries out in distress (Gen. 25:22). The Hebrew term for “struggled” can imply crushing or wrestling, indicating how tumultuous this pregnancy was. When Rebekah consults God, the theological meaning of her difficult childbirth is revealed: “Two nations are in your womb… one people shall be stronger than the other, and the older shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). In other words, her womb contains more than babies – it contains nations in miniature. The twins Jacob and Esau represent Israel and Edom, and their prenatal contention foreshadows the historical struggle between these peoples. The Bible explicitly ties an individual birth to national destiny here. Jacob’s birth gripping Esau’s heel (for which he is named) signifies his supplanting of the firstborn. This birth scene prefigures the later ascendancy of Israel (Jacob) over Edom (Esau). Indeed, scholars note that the motif of twins wrestling in utero recurs to dramatize how two kindred nations will diverge, with the divinely chosen one unexpectedly prevailing[[6]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=,Peretz%29%20will%20be%20dominant). The younger twin’s triumph – contrary to normal primogeniture – becomes a theological statement: Israel’s origin involves God’s election of the unlikely, symbolized by the newborn “grabbing the heel” to overtake the elder[[6]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=,Peretz%29%20will%20be%20dominant).

items.quote: all cloud providers are able to offer [such credits] profitably
items.paragraph: Cloud Credit Programs: Another pricing-related practice is the extensive use of cloud credits – essentially free or heavily discounted cloud services for certain customers (often startups, developers, or other prospective high-growth clients). On the surface, credits encourage adoption (and indeed can help startups avoid upfront costs[[34]](https://www.autoritedelaconcurrence.fr/en/press-release/cloud-computing-autorite-de-la-concurrence-issues-its-market-study-competition-cloud#:~:text=)). However, competition reports have raised concerns when credit programs are extremely large or selectively targeted in ways that smaller rivals cannot match. The French Competition Authority noted that top providers offer very high-value credits – sometimes “up to $200,000 for two years” – to startups and other strategic customers[[35]](https://www.autoritedelaconcurrence.fr/en/press-release/cloud-computing-autorite-de-la-concurrence-issues-its-market-study-competition-cloud#:~:text=However%2C%20the%20Autorit%C3%A9%20considers%20that,providers%20to%20offer%20them%20profitably). These go far beyond typical free trials in other industries. Such generous credits can act as loyalty-inducing rebates: a startup that builds on (for example) AWS or Azure using free credits may become deeply embedded in that platform’s ecosystem by the time the credits are exhausted. At that point, the cost (and difficulty) to migrate to a different cloud is high, and the customer is effectively “won over” long-term. The French Autorité pointed out that the “vast ecosystem” benefits the big providers, and questioned whether “all cloud providers are able to offer [such credits] profitably”[[35]](https://www.autoritedelaconcurrence.fr/en/press-release/cloud-computing-autorite-de-la-concurrence-issues-its-market-study-competition-cloud#:~:text=However%2C%20the%20Autorit%C3%A9%20considers%20that,providers%20to%20offer%20them%20profitably). The implication is that only the largest players (with deep pockets and broad product monetization) can sustain these large-scale credit incentives, which smaller cloud firms cannot afford – thereby putting smaller competitors at a disadvantage. In competition terms, massive credit programs can be viewed as a form of predatory pricing or fidelity rebate: they lock in future business by offering services below cost initially, in a manner difficult for rivals to counter. Authorities thus advise close scrutiny of targeted cloud credit offers that might foreclose competition over time[[36]](https://www.autoritedelaconcurrence.fr/en/press-release/cloud-computing-autorite-de-la-concurrence-issues-its-market-study-competition-cloud#:~:text=However%2C%20the%20Autorit%C3%A9%20considers%20that,providers%20to%20offer%20them%20profitably).

items.quote: an art work expresses an emotion if and only if it has the power to arouse that emotion in an appropriate audience
items.paragraph: Definition and Origin: In aesthetic theory, arousalism (also known as the arousal theory of art and emotion) is the view that an artwork’s expressiveness lies in its power to arouse specific emotions or sensory feelings in the audience[[1]](https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/artistic-expression/v-1/sections/arousal-theory#:~:text=Arousalism%20refers%20to%20this%20second,variety%20of%20suitably%20qualified%20perceivers). In other words, a work of art is considered “sad” or “joyful” because it tends to make the audience feel sadness or joy. The emotion is located in the listener or viewer rather than in the artwork itself[[2]](https://www.scribd.com/document/501461621/Ion-Olte%C8%9Beanu-Understanding-Music-Theory-Meaning-Self-conciousness-And-Emotional-Expressiveness-2010#:~:text=hoff%20puts%20it%2C%20music%20listening,of%20the%20composer%20does%20affect). This theory emerged in Western philosophy of art as a response to questions about how art conveys emotion. Notable proponents include Derek Matravers, Aaron Ridley, and Jenefer Robinson, who have defended the idea that art’s emotive meaning is largely a product of the audience’s psychological response[[3]](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110670011-002/html?lang=en&srsltid=AfmBOoptLtVLcLG02aSUhHowodWpIU2VQtNxTEJPpSyuP4jG8htFLtym#:~:text=Chapter%201,theories%20of%20expressive%20experienceisarousalism)[[4]](https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/artistic-expression/v-1/sections/arousal-theory#:~:text=Arousalism%20refers%20to%20this%20second,the%20perceiving%20of%20it%2C%20just). For example, philosopher Stephen Davies summarizes arousalism as the claim that “an art work expresses an emotion if and only if it has the power to arouse that emotion in an appropriate audience”[[1]](https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/artistic-expression/v-1/sections/arousal-theory#:~:text=Arousalism%20refers%20to%20this%20second,variety%20of%20suitably%20qualified%20perceivers). Despite criticism from some (such as Peter Kivy, who argued that music labeled “sad” does not always make listeners feel sad), arousalism remains an influential approach in understanding the link between artistic form and audience affect[[5]](https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/artistic-expression/v-1/sections/arousal-theory#:~:text=The%20arousal%20theory%20faces%20two,sentiments%20might%20permanently%20block%20the).

items.quote: How should we respond and adapt to AI?
items.paragraph: In conclusion, generative AI in education presents a classic double-edged sword: it offers unprecedented opportunities to enrich learning and reduce inequities, yet it also threatens to undermine fundamental aspects of education if misused. Up to May 2023, the dialogue in the education community has shifted from “Should we allow AI?” towards “How should we respond and adapt to AI?”. The prevailing view is that AI is here to stay – banning it outright is neither practical nor beneficial[[34]](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2024/2/15-1#:~:text=Current%20evidence%20suggests%20that%20using,free). Instead, the path forward is to integrate AI thoughtfully: leverage its strengths (personalization, efficiency, access) while actively managing its risks (integrity, accuracy, bias). This requires effort at all levels, from teachers adjusting classroom practices to administrators updating curriculum and assessment policies, and even to policymakers setting frameworks for safe and equitable AI use. If done well, the result could be a transformation in education akin to past technological revolutions – with AI serving as a powerful ally in teaching and learning. Educators are advised to embrace a mindset of continuous learning and adaptation, collaborating with students in this new landscape. By keeping human values at the center and treating AI as a tool, not a replacement, we can shape a future of education that harnesses generative AI’s potential while preserving the core mission of education: to develop knowledgeable, skilled, and ethical human beings[[43]](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2024/2/15-1#:~:text=In%20summary%2C%20AI%20tools%20like,and%20ethical%20use%20in%20educational).

items.quote: if CPU usage exceeds 80%, add another server
items.paragraph: - Threshold-Based Rules: The simplest and most widely used form of reactive scaling. Administrators define static thresholds on metrics (CPU, memory, etc.) that trigger scaling actions. For example, “if CPU usage exceeds 80%, add another server”. This approach is straightforward and easy to implement[[2]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07909v1#:~:text=CPU%20and%20memory%20usage%20,dependencies%20is%20challenging%20%5B21). Its main advantage is simplicity and fast reaction once a trigger fires. However, it requires manually tuning the thresholds, which is challenging in dynamic environments[[2]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07909v1#:~:text=CPU%20and%20memory%20usage%20,dependencies%20is%20challenging%20%5B21). Incorrect thresholds can cause oscillations or SLA violations (too high thresholds delay scaling, too low cause oscillatory scaling). Moreover, in complex applications with interdependent components, finding one-size-fits-all thresholds is difficult[[3]](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.07909v1#:~:text=percent%2C%20then%20scale%20up%20the,dependencies%20is%20challenging%20%5B%2040). In short, threshold rules work for predictable, slowly varying loads, but struggle with sudden spikes[[4]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397316654_Real-Time_Workload_Prediction_and_Dynamic_Autoscaling_A_New_Paradigm_for_Cloud_Performance_Management#:~:text=While%20simple%20%20to%20implement%2C,to%20system%20state%20after%20it).

items.quote: Shall I go and call a woman for you who is nursing from the Hebrew women, so that she may nurse the child for you?
items.paragraph: The **story of Moses and his biological mother Jochebed** illustrates this principle paradigmatically. After Moses's birth during the persecution of Hebrew male infants, his mother places him in a basket on the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter discovers the child and desires to keep him. Crucially, Moses's sister Miriam appears before Pharaoh's daughter and asks: "Shall I go and call a woman for you who is nursing from the Hebrew women, so that she may nurse the child for you?" (Exodus 2:7). Pharaoh's daughter agrees, and "the woman took the baby and nursed him" (Exodus 2:9)—unknowingly, this woman is Moses's biological mother, Jochebed.[^22]

items.quote: IF temperature is high AND humidity is low, THEN open vents 50%
items.paragraph: Basic principle: Fuzzy logic control uses human-like reasoning with “IF-THEN” rules instead of a mathematical model. It defines fuzzy sets (membership functions) for input variables (e.g. “temperature is high/medium/low”) and applies a rule base from expert knowledge (e.g. “IF temperature is high AND humidity is low, THEN open vents 50%”). The controller fuzzifies sensor inputs, applies the fuzzy inference rules, and then defuzzifies the output to a precise actuator command. This approach can naturally express and coordinate complex, nonlinear relationships in the greenhouse climate using linguistic terms and expert insights[[4]](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0472/15/20/2135#:~:text=Unlike%20conventional%20PID%20control%2C%20fuzzy,coordinated%20regulation%20of%20multiple%20variables).

items.quote: what does this story represent or teach?
items.paragraph: - Emphasis on Content over Form: The representational-text approach prioritizes what is depicted (story and content) rather than how it is depicted. The art, animation technique, or industry context tends to be backgrounded; instead, narrative content is foregrounded. Scholars might discuss characters’ psychology, plot outcomes, or moral lessons in great detail, treating anime almost like a novel or live-action film. Thomas Lamarre points out that in these analyses, animation’s moving-image nature is often ignored – anime is handled as if it were static text or illustrated story[[4]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=,treat%20anime%20as%20text%20in). For example, an academic paper might delve into the philosophical questions raised by Ghost in the Shell (such as identity in a cyborg age) while barely mentioning that it is animated, thereby sidestepping the stylistic execution of those ideas[[8]](https://www.animemangastudies.com/2019/01/20/the-shortcomings-and-blind-spots/#:~:text=reviews.%20,of%20the%20materiality%20of%20animation). The focus remains on interpretative meaning (“what does this story represent or teach?”) rather than on cinematic technique.

items.paragraph: 3. Narrative and Content Characteristics: The storytelling and stylistic traits of Japanese TV anime and Nordic Noir are quite distinct, reflecting their genres and cultural origins, yet both have recognizable signatures that appeal globally. Anime is not a single genre but a medium encompassing a vast array of genres (fantasy, science fiction, romance, mecha, etc.), so content varies widely. However, some general characteristics of popular TV anime include imaginative or fantastical premises, complex world-building, and often serial narratives with continuing arcs. Many anime target youth or subculture niches (shōnen action for teen boys, mahō-shōjo magic girl shows for tween girls, etc.), and even those for younger audiences tend to incorporate themes of personal growth, friendship, and moral conflict. A hallmark of anime storytelling is its willingness to blend escapist fantasy with serious themes – for instance, a colorful adventure series might also tackle questions of identity or sacrifice. Notably, anime has a tradition of handling mature or dark topics in animated form, something that Western TV animation historically shied away from. It’s been observed that in Japan, anime is not solely for children; it can deal with “deeper issues like alienation, gender inequality, corruption and teen angst,” often in a metaphorical or sci-fi-inflected way[[29]](https://www.fluxmagazine.com/japanese-anime-on-british-tv/#:~:text=Global%20phenomenon%20Pok%C3%A9mon%20is%20the,homosexuality%2C%20corruption%20and%20teen%20angst). Visually, anime is known for distinctive character designs (large expressive eyes, emblematic costumes), fast-paced and dynamic action sequences, and an interplay of drama and humor (even serious anime often have moments of comic relief or stylized exaggeration). In terms of narrative structure, anime series often follow multi-episode story arcs, sometimes punctuated by “filler” episodes, and they may not always conclude definitively (open endings are common, leaving room for continuation in another season or in manga form). Now, Nordic Noir dramas, as a subgenre of crime drama, have a more unified set of characteristics. These series typically feature gritty, atmospheric crime investigations set against the backdrop of Scandinavian society. Hallmarks of Nordic Noir include: a “murky” or bleak atmosphere, dark and moody cinematography (rain, snow, long winter nights), and a tone of moral complexity[[30]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=Nordic%20Noir%20is%20most%20often,a%20dark%20underbelly%20here%2C%20too). The protagonists are often flawed detectives – brooding, emotionally troubled, but determined – and the narrative delves into their personal lives as much as the crime. Shows like The Killing and The Bridge are structured around a central mystery (often a murder) that unfolds over the entire season, allowing for slow-burn pacing and intricate plotting. Along the way, the story usually uncovers layers of social commentary: Nordic Noir uses the crime plot as a lens to interrogate social issues in the ostensibly well-functioning Nordic welfare states[[31]](https://nordics.info/themes/nordic-noir#:~:text=Opposing%20images%3A%20faultless%20societies%20vs,dysfunctionality). Themes of political corruption, immigration, misogyny, and the erosion of the social safety net frequently surface, contrasting the perceived utopia of Scandinavian society with a darker underbelly. Stylistically, the dialogue tends to be terse and realistic (often avoiding melodrama), and the visuals emphasize stark, realistic settings – think quiet suburban streets or isolated fjord landscapes turned into scenes of unsettling crime. A defining narrative feature is the tension between the calm surface of Nordic life and the violence or moral decay underneath[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordic_noir#:~:text=or%20the%20Nordic%20countries%20,clarification%20needed). The storytelling is tightly integrated (each episode drives the overarching case forward, with cliffhangers maintaining suspense) and typically resolves the main mystery by season’s end, albeit often with ambiguous or bittersweet outcomes. In terms of content appeal, anime offers spectacle, creativity, and emotional highs – giant robots, epic battles, heart-wrenching character moments – whereas Nordic Noir offers realism, psychological depth, and suspense – the thrill of whodunit combined with commentary on society. Each thus scratches a different itch for global audiences: anime often provides imaginative escapism and emotional rollercoasters, and Nordic Noir delivers cerebral, edge-of-seat drama with a “prestige” feel. It’s worth noting that both have influenced others: anime’s visual tropes have appeared in Western animation, and Nordic Noir’s style has inspired crime dramas in other countries (e.g. the UK’s Broadchurch was influenced by the tonal approach of The Killing[[33]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=,Professor%C2%A0Hochscherf%20says)[[34]](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-03/nordic-noir-tv-history-inspires-other-shows/103223036#:~:text=She%20says%20Nordic%20noir%27s%20influence,drew%20inspiration%20from%20the%20genre)).

items.quote: the children struggled together within her
items.paragraph: While some biblical pregnancies proceed without complication, the text gives disproportionate narrative attention to **difficult and conflicted births**, transforming them into symbolic representations of theological truths about covenant, election, and national struggle. Rebecca's pregnancy with Jacob and Esau exemplifies this pattern most strikingly. The text records that "the children struggled together within her" (Genesis 25:22), causing Rebekah such anguish that she cries out: "If it is thus, why do I exist?" (Genesis 25:22). This is not merely medical observation; the struggling within the womb foreshadows the lifelong conflict between the twins and—more theologically significant—represents the struggle between two future nations within a single body.[^12][^13]

items.quote: to ensure verifiers… establish independence… The Committee… guarantee[s] independence of verification activities… [and] publishing a list of accredited verifiers should minimize any potential for conflicts of interest
items.paragraph: Mitigation Measures: Chinese regulators have recognized this risk and taken steps to address it. In late 2017, PBoC and CSRC jointly issued the Guidelines for Green Bond Assessment and Certification (Interim), which established an accreditation and supervision scheme for external reviewers[[9]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=review%20and%20an%20accreditation%20scheme,professional%20credentials%20after%20approval%2C%20establish). The newly formed Green Bonds Standard Committee (GBSC) under PBoC/CSRC requires external review firms to register and demonstrate qualifications, including having “no record of misconduct” and systems to ensure independence[[9]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=review%20and%20an%20accreditation%20scheme,professional%20credentials%20after%20approval%2C%20establish)[[47]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=CSRC%20requires%20external%20reviewers%20to,20). Importantly, the GBSC has a mandate to supervise verifiers on an ongoing basis, ensuring they maintain professional standards and “establish independence from issuers, and engage in fair pricing”[[48]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=clean%20legal%20record%2C%20professional%20liability,for%20green%20bond%20verifiers%20%E2%80%93)[[49]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=The%20Green%20Bonds%20Standard%20Committee,20). The Committee can conduct spot-checks on verification reports and even punish verifiers or issuers in cases of misbehavior – it has the power to “revoke the green bond label of issuers that fail to correct non-compliance… highlighted in verification reports” and to sanction verifiers for improper conduct[[50]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=green,While%20the%20practice)[[51]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=The%20Committee%20is%20granted%20the,widespread%2C%20regulators%20should%20ensure%20that). According to CPI’s analysis, the Committee’s authority is designed “to ensure verifiers… establish independence… The Committee… guarantee[s] independence of verification activities… [and] publishing a list of accredited verifiers should minimize any potential for conflicts of interest”[[44]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=issuers%20that%20fail%20to%20correct,publishing%20a%20list%20of%20accredited)[[10]](https://climatepolicyinitiative.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/MRV-System-Design-Recommendations-for-Green-Bonds-in-China.pdf#:~:text=authority%20has%20great%20to%20minimize,the%20Committee%20has%20already%20made). In other words, by vetting and monitoring the reviewers, and by holding the ultimate stick of withdrawing an issuer’s green label if things are misrepresented, regulators aim to realign incentives. Reviewers are aware that overly lax opinions could not only harm their reputation but also risk regulatory penalties or loss of accreditation.

This head start, combined with continuous innovation, has given MindBridge a strong reputation in the industry. Independent evaluations have described MindBridge as “the global leader in AI-powered financial risk discovery and anomaly detection”, highlighting how it helps professionals identify and analyze risk across broad datasets[[27]](https://www.mindbridge.ai/#:~:text=MindBridge%20,risk%20across%20broad%20financial%20datasets). Since its founding, MindBridge has accumulated a number of accolades that reflect its position: for instance, it was named a Gartner “Cool Vendor” in Finance in 2022[[28]](https://www.mindbridge.ai/company/#:~:text=MindBridge%20named%20a), and it has appeared in Gartner’s 2024 Hype Cycle report for emerging autonomous accounting technologies[[29]](https://www.mindbridge.ai/company/#:~:text=According%20to%20Gartner%C2%AE%2C%20%E2%80%9CA%20new,%E2%80%9D). It also earned a spot on Deloitte’s “Companies-to-Watch” list early on and more recently made the 2024 Deloitte Fast 500 as one of North America’s fastest-growing tech companies[[30]](https://www.mindbridge.ai/news/mindbridge-named-one-of-the-fastest-growing-technology-companies-in-north-america/#:~:text=MindBridge%20Named%20One%20of%20the,assessment%20in%20finance%20and%20auditing). These honors underscore MindBridge’s status as a leading innovator in audit tech.

items.quote: absorbed the changes of each period,
items.paragraph: In outlining jazz’s historical trajectory, Williams highlighted a continuous evolution through distinct eras, rather than sharp breaks. She experienced these eras firsthand and viewed each as a building block. In her narrative: Spirituals (and the blues) gave birth to Ragtime, which led to the early jazz of New Orleans and the swing era (epitomized for her by the Kansas City style), which in turn culminated in Bebop[[33]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=students%20the%20four%20major%20eras,the%20forces%20she%20believes%20have)[[49]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=Down%20into%20the%20earth%20of,magic%2C%E2%80%9D%20%E2%80%9Cmere%20exercises%2C%E2%80%9D%20and%20%E2%80%9Cclassical). She often noted she was “there when it began” – taught spirituals and ragtime by her mother, playing pro in the 1920s, composing for swing bands in the ’30s, and hosting bop jam sessions in the ’40s[[50]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=sneak%20her%20into%20,and%20write%20music). She took pride in “chang[ing] her style with each period” of jazz while always maintaining her own voice[[50]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=sneak%20her%20into%20,and%20write%20music)[[51]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=to%20it,brilliant%20flashes%20of%20modern%20dissonance). An Ebony magazine writer observed that Williams’s playing “absorbed the changes of each period,” blending elements of Fats Waller and Earl Hines (stride and swing) with touches of Monk and Bud Powell (bebop modernism), all unified by blues and her unique imagination[[51]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=to%20it,brilliant%20flashes%20of%20modern%20dissonance). This encapsulates Williams’s belief that innovation and tradition were not opposites in jazz, but complementary. She cherished innovators – she was an early champion of bebop’s radicals – but only when their innovations built on the soulful foundation laid by earlier generations.

items.quote: are designed very specifically for their intended installation and use a complicated valve system,
items.paragraph: Design and Operational Complexity: Conventional micro-hydroturbines are typically engineered specifically for a site’s head and flow conditions, which makes their design and selection more involved. Technologies like Francis turbines, for instance, “are designed very specifically for their intended installation and use a complicated valve system,” and thus are not commonly used at micro scale due to this complexity[[13]](https://attra.ncat.org/publication/micro-hydro-power-a-beginners-guide-to-design-and-installation/#:~:text=Francis%20turbines%20are%20typically%20installed,around%20it%20and%20then%20falls). Designing a micro-hydro installation often requires custom turbine sizing, fabrication, and tuning of control systems (governors, electrical controllers), which increases project complexity. Operating these systems may require skilled oversight to adjust settings or perform regular maintenance on specialized components (like needle valves or governors). PATs, on the other hand, are valued for their low complexity and ease of installation[[8]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369627595_Small_hydropower_generation_using_pump_as_turbine_a_smart_solution_for_the_development_of_Pakistan's_energy#:~:text=expensive%20electricity,stage%20etc.%20for%20power). Selecting a PAT largely involves picking a standard pump that matches the desired operating point, and installation is akin to installing a pump – often simpler than a custom turbine assembly. PAT units come as off-the-shelf products (centrifugal pumps) that are widely understood by technicians, and they typically use standard induction motors as generators, which are durable and straightforward to integrate[[14]](https://attra.ncat.org/publication/micro-hydro-power-a-beginners-guide-to-design-and-installation/#:~:text=A%20PAT%20usually%20includes%20an,the%20end%20of%20this%20publication). Overall, PAT technology offers a simpler “plug-and-play” approach with fewer bespoke design elements. The trade-off is that accurately predicting PAT performance can be tricky (since pump catalogs don’t directly give turbine-mode curves)[[15]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369627595_Small_hydropower_generation_using_pump_as_turbine_a_smart_solution_for_the_development_of_Pakistan's_energy#:~:text=Pumps%20as%20Turbines%20,the%20findings%20of%20performance%20prediction), and achieving optimal performance may require some testing or empirical adjustment. In summary, micro-turbines involve higher design and operational complexity, whereas PATs are simpler to deploy but may need iterative selection/tuning to hit performance targets[[15]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369627595_Small_hydropower_generation_using_pump_as_turbine_a_smart_solution_for_the_development_of_Pakistan's_energy#:~:text=Pumps%20as%20Turbines%20,the%20findings%20of%20performance%20prediction).

items.quote: his nurse took him up and fled
items.paragraph: Similarly, the brief mention of Mephibosheth’s nurse in 2 Samuel highlights a nurse’s loyalty in the face of political turmoil. Mephibosheth, a son of Prince Jonathan and grandson of King Saul, was only five when his father and grandfather died in battle. In the chaos following Saul’s fall, “his nurse took him up and fled” to protect him from potential violence (2 Sam. 4:4). This unnamed nurse’s maternal instinct saved the last heir of Saul’s line, though the boy was accidentally dropped in haste and became lame. While Mephibosheth’s nursing days were likely over by age five, the text pointedly uses the term “omenet” (nurse/caregiver) for her[[19]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=The%20Hebrew%20term%20meneket%2C%20nurse%2C,Kings%2010%3A1%3B%20Esther%202%3A7%2C%2020)[[20]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=The%20Hebrew%20term%20meneket%2C%20nurse%2C,Kings%2010%3A1%3B%20Esther%202%3A7%2C%2020). This same term is used for only one other woman – Naomi, who lovingly nursed her grandson Obed, the ancestor of David[[21]](https://www.jewishideas.org/article/identity-royalty-and-contentment-breastfeeding-tanakh#:~:text=4%3A16%E2%80%9317). By preserving Jonathan’s son, Mephibosheth’s nurse ensured the continuity of Saul’s family and provided David an opportunity to later show covenant kindness to Jonathan’s offspring (2 Sam. 9). In effect, her nurturing care thwarted the complete annihilation of Saul’s house. This can be seen as another form of resistance to the destructive tide of power struggles: a caregiver’s devotion shelters a remnant of the former royal family. Although Mephibosheth never claims the throne, his survival carries forward a story of mercy and memory in Israel’s royal history. The nurse’s act is thus a quiet echo of other biblical women who defy royal edicts or violence to safeguard a child (much as the Hebrew midwives and Moses’s mother did in Egypt).

items.quote: Forecasting Workload in Cloud Computing: Towards Uncertainty-Aware Predictions and Transfer Learning
items.paragraph: "Forecasting Workload in Cloud Computing: Towards Uncertainty-Aware Predictions and Transfer Learning" addresses workload prediction uncertainty through Bayesian deep learning models that provide both predictions and uncertainty quantification. The research proposes univariate and bivariate Bayesian deep learning architectures yielding predicted workload demand along with uncertainty bounds. Extensive experiments on Google and Alibaba clusters demonstrate that modelling prediction uncertainty positively impacts performance, particularly on service level metrics. The uncertainty quantification can be tailored to desired target service levels critical in cloud applications, enabling resource decisions informed by confidence intervals rather than point estimates. The work investigates transfer learning capabilities across different cloud provider domains, revealing that acceptable transfer performance is achievable within the same provider where data distributions are more similar, providing a pathway for more rapid model deployment on new services.[^16]

items.quote: Musicians started playing commercial rock and what they call ‘free music,’ and all the feeling went out of it,
items.paragraph: In Williams’s eyes, bebop was the last great unifying era of jazz, and she regarded it with particular reverence. She herself had been a mentor to bop players (like Monk, Parker, Gillespie) and embraced their advances. “Personally, I have always believed that bebop was here to stay,” she wrote in 1954, insisting that new styles like Dave Brubeck’s cool jazz, while interesting, “are not bop.”[[52]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-MyLifewKoJ-1954.html#:~:text=the%20phrasing%20been%20like%20it,to%20continue%20writing%20and%20experimenting) She saw bop’s complex phrasing and harmonies as a natural evolution of jazz’s language without discarding its roots. Indeed, she encouraged the original modernists “to continue writing and experimenting” back then[[52]](https://daveratcliffepiano.com/MaryLouWilliams/MLW-MyLifewKoJ-1954.html#:~:text=the%20phrasing%20been%20like%20it,to%20continue%20writing%20and%20experimenting). By the 1970s, however, Williams felt jazz history had hit a crisis after the bebop era. In her words, “after the bop era it just all went to pot.”[[41]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,have%20her%20students%20sing%20the) She believed that the late 1950s and 1960s brought a fragmentation where some musicians lost touch with the core lineage. Two main culprits she cited were the rise of commercial popular music (rock & roll) and certain forms of avant-garde jazz. Williams saw many jazz players in the ’60s chasing commercial success by playing rock or funk, or going to the opposite extreme of playing an “free” avant-garde that eschewed melody and blues. “Musicians started playing commercial rock and what they call ‘free music,’ and all the feeling went out of it,” she lamented of that period[[41]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,have%20her%20students%20sing%20the). To her, these trends broke the once-continuous evolution of the music. She would tell students that if a creative musician listens only to such music lacking the great traditions, “he can’t ever get off the ground. You have to hear great music in order to…create something new.”[[39]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,sing%20the%20music%20they%27re%20hearing) In other words, without the grounding of Armstrong, Ellington, Basie, Parker, etc., there can be no meaningful innovation – only chaos or commercial dilution.

items.quote: Shall the earth be made to give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children.
items.paragraph: **At the eschatological and redemptive level**, the prophets appropriate maternal imagery to describe Israel's ultimate national redemption and restoration. Isaiah 66:7-8 presents a vision in which Zion (representing the covenant people and their restoration) will give birth to an entire nation in a single moment: "Shall the earth be made to give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children." This prophecy mirrors and spiritualizes the birth of Israel during the Exodus, suggesting that national redemption is fundamentally a reproductive event—the birth or rebirth of the people.[^40]

items.quote: Not someone who’s always telling them, ‘Do this, do that,’... but somebody they want to pay attention to
items.paragraph: Underlying Mary Lou Williams’s pedagogy was a kind of tough love and deep faith in jazz’s value. She believed young musicians needed heroes and role models from the past: “How can anyone advance without listening to someone older?” she asked, lamenting that modern kids “no longer have heroes – like Babe Ruth” in music[[5]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=music%2C%20and%20a%20new%20pianist%2C,They%27re%20looking)[[17]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,Jazz%20has%20healing%20in%20it). Rather than scold or dictate, she felt a master’s inspiring example was key: “Not someone who’s always telling them, ‘Do this, do that,’... but somebody they want to pay attention to”[[17]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,Jazz%20has%20healing%20in%20it). Williams happily filled that mentor role. Her students, she said, were “great kids. They’re looking for love, and that’s what’s in the music I’m teaching. Jazz has healing in it, and a lot of love.”[[18]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=%3E%20%20%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0%C2%A0,Arts%2C%20is%20a%20freelance) This almost spiritual view of teaching jazz – as passing on “healing” and “love” – flowed from her own mid-life religious conversion (to Catholicism in 1957) and charity work[[19]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=The%20importance%20of%20the%20blues,technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling)[[20]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling). She truly saw jazz as a positive force for the soul. Indeed, Williams often referred to jazz as “music with healing in it and spiritual feeling,” and she worked “in defiance of those who would call jazz ‘the devil’s music’”[[19]](https://folkways.si.edu/artists/mary-lou-williams#:~:text=The%20importance%20of%20the%20blues,technique%20but%20very%20little%20feeling)[[21]](https://angelusnews.com/arts-culture/mary-lou-williams-pioneer-of-sacred-jazz/#:~:text=According%20to%20Father%20Peter%20O%E2%80%99Brien%2C,%E2%80%9D). Whether leading a jazz Mass in a cathedral or a bebop choir in a classroom, her goal was the same: to “open ears” and let people “hear and feel jazz” in its authentic form[[22]](https://ratical.org/MaryLouWilliams/Mission.html#:~:text=Mary%20Lou%20and%20the%20bassist,out%20the%20parts%20I%20had). By all accounts, Mary Lou Williams in her final decade became a fervent jazz evangelist, intent on “saving” the music by educating new listeners and players in its rich heritage[[23]](https://music.unc.edu/event/kernodle-pruettlecture24/#:~:text=decades%20that%20followed%20World%20War,movement%20and%20jazz%2C%20her%20work)[[24]](https://music.unc.edu/event/kernodle-pruettlecture24/#:~:text=pianist%2Fcomposer%2Farranger%20Mary%20Lou%20Williams%20during,and%20provide%20another%20means%20for).

items.quote: Provisions to form a new UN agency to oversee the decolonization of dependent territories were included in Chapter XII of the Charter,
items.paragraph: Continuity and Change: From League Mandates to UN Trusteeships: The UN Charter also created a new system to manage certain colonies – the International Trusteeship System – building on the League of Nations mandates idea but with the explicit aim of eventual self-government or independence. “Provisions to form a new UN agency to oversee the decolonization of dependent territories were included in Chapter XII of the Charter,” effectively as a successor to the League’s mandate system[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Trusteeship_Council#:~:text=Provisions%20to%20form%20a%20new,the%20eleventh%20was%20Italian%20Somaliland). Former League mandates and some other territories (mostly those taken from the defeated Axis powers) were eligible to be placed under UN trusteeship. In practice, 11 territories were placed under UN trusteeship in the late 1940s: these included 10 former League mandates (for example, Tanganyika, Cameroon, Togoland, Ruanda-Urundi in Africa; New Guinea and islands in the Pacific; Western Samoa; etc.) and Italian Somaliland in the Horn of Africa[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Trusteeship_Council#:~:text=territories%20,the%20eleventh%20was%20%20119). Administering countries (such as Britain, France, New Zealand, Belgium, Australia, and later Italy for Somaliland) agreed to govern these Trust Territories under UN supervision. The Trusteeship Council, one of the UN’s principal organs, was established in 1945 to supervise this process[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Trusteeship_Council#:~:text=Under%20the%20Charter%2C%20the%20Trusteeship,attained%20independence%2C%20the%20size%20and). The objective was clear: unlike the open-ended League mandates, the UN Trusteeship System aimed to prepare territories for full independence or free self-government. Article 76 of the Charter set this goal, and over the next decades the promise was largely fulfilled – all Trust Territories achieved self-rule by 1994, when the last, Palau, became independent[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Trusteeship_Council#:~:text=international%20peace%20and%20security)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Trusteeship_Council#:~:text=With%20the%20independence%20of%20Palau,independence%20as%20a%20sovereign%20nation). This represented a significant step toward decolonization within an international legal framework. However, it’s important to note that not all colonies were covered by the trusteeship system – only those volunteered by the administering powers or inherited from League mandates. The vast remainder of the colonial world (e.g. the British and French empires in Asia and Africa) remained under direct imperial control, albeit now subject to the general obligations of Chapter XI and international scrutiny through the UN General Assembly.

items.quote: Schedule a meeting next week with team X
items.paragraph: Beyond new data modalities, functional expansion includes enabling the AI to take actions in the world. For example, tool components could let it control software or IoT devices, automate workflows, or execute code. A Big Loop system might integrate with an email-sending API, a database interface, or a robotics controller. One scenario: the AI agent can break down a user’s high-level request (say, “Schedule a meeting next week with team X”) into actions like querying participants’ calendars (via a calendar API), finding a common slot, and sending out invites. This kind of workflow automation is achievable because the Big Loop can incorporate project management and workflow tools to manage tasks and processes[[18]](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/17/9466#:~:text=,65%5D%3B%20integrate%20online). In contrast, a standalone LLM can only describe what to do, not actually execute it. By using tools as extensions of itself, the AI becomes far more actionable. It can not only output answers, but also interact with external systems on the user’s behalf (under appropriate safeguards).

items.quote: a Taoist xian who lives on Kunlun, serving as the film’s comic relief
items.paragraph: - Taiyi Zhenren (Master and Mentor): Taiyi Zhenren – the immortal mentor of Nezha – has appeared in many forms across adaptations. The 1979 film presented Taiyi as a rotund, elderly Taoist immortal (often riding a flying beast), who resurrects Nezha using the lotus flowers. The 2003 series made him a comedic, jovial teacher figure guiding Nezha. In Ne Zha 2, Taiyi retains his traditional role as Nezha’s guide and comic relief, but his capabilities and personality get some updates. He is portrayed as a somewhat bumbling yet wise master – “a Taoist xian who lives on Kunlun, serving as the film’s comic relief”[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_Zha_2#:~:text=Vincent%20Rodriguez%20III%20,Zhang%20Jiaming%20%20Rick%20Zeiff) – very much in line with past depictions. However, Taiyi’s heroism is enhanced: at the film’s start he performs a grand ritual with the Seven-Colored Sacred Lotus to rebuild Nezha and Ao Bing’s bodies, an act that nearly exhausts his powers[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_Zha_2#:~:text=Jiaozi%20,his%20fight%20against%20Master%20Shen). This is an inventive expansion on the lotus-resurrection from myth (in the novel Investiture of the Gods, Taiyi uses lotus roots to remake Nezha after Nezha’s suicide). In Ne Zha 2, Taiyi basically kickstarts the plot by saving the two boys, showing his resourcefulness and dedication. Throughout the trials, he accompanies Nezha (often arriving on his quirky mount) and provides guidance – but notably, he is not the infallible authority figure. Taiyi even listens to Nezha and Ao Bing, and at times is outwitted by the scheming villain (Wuliang). His depiction has a modern sensibility: a mentor who is humorous and endearing rather than remote or didactic. By preserving Taiyi’s famous attributes (his portly appearance, earthy humor, and magical skills) while also making him more actively involved in battles and plot twists, Ne Zha 2 successfully refreshes this classic character. The essence of Taiyi – a benevolent trickster-teacher – remains, but he’s given more depth (such as being Shen Gongbao’s senior fellow apprentice, hinting at past connections) and greater responsibility in the story’s outcome.

items.quote: the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah
items.paragraph: Similarly, the birth of Perez and Zerah from Tamar is laden with symbolic import for Israel’s story. Tamar, a Canaanite daughter-in-law of Judah, secures Judah’s lineage by courageously bearing his heirs – twins – after a scandalous deception. Her labor is described in almost fantastical terms: one twin (Zerah) extends a hand out of the womb, upon which the midwife ties a red thread to mark him as firstborn, but he then retracts his hand and his brother (Perez) is actually born first (Gen. 38:27–30). This “impossible” birth scenario (twins trading places mid-delivery) is not mere oddity; it functions as allegory[[7]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=The%20Meaning%20of%20the%20Story). The struggle between Perez and Zerah, like that of Jacob and Esau, signifies a conflict over birthright and preeminence. In Judah’s tribe, two clans descended from these twins would later coexist, but the line of Perez would produce King David – and thus ultimately “win” the primacy. The story frankly declares Perez’s name to mean “breach” or “breakthrough,” as the midwife exclaims, “What a breach you have made for yourself!”[[8]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/why-does-the-torah-describe-babies-born-hands-first#:~:text=birthright.,in%20favor%20of%20his%20brother). Generations later, this line “breaches” into leadership of Israel. In fact, the Book of Ruth explicitly links Tamar’s arduous childbirth to the founding of the House of David, blessing Boaz that his house be like “the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah” (Ruth 4:12). Thus, Tamar’s difficult twin birth carries symbolic significance for the nation’s origin, illustrating how a threatened family line was dramatically preserved to yield Israel’s royal dynasty[[9]](https://www.thetorah.com/article/the-protective-red-thread#:~:text=Moreover%2C%20the%20biblical%20narratives%20of,enables%20them%20to%20conquer%20Canaan). These repeated tales of twins and tumultuous deliveries stress a common theme: the nation of Israel is born out of struggle, divine election, and reversal of human norms. Just as a baby’s birth can be fraught with danger yet culminate in joy, Israel’s emergence as a people involves peril and providence in equal measure.

items.quote: the so-called donation from death-row prisoners doesn't exist any longer
items.paragraph: This interpretation was explicitly stated by Huang in his March 2014 interview: "Once the organs from willing death-row prisoners are enrolled into our unified allocation system, they are then treated as voluntary donation from citizens; the so-called donation from death-row prisoners doesn't exist any longer." The critical phrase here is "the so-called donation from death-row prisoners doesn't exist any longer"—a purely administrative reclassification rather than an end to the actual use of prisoner organs.[^18]

items.quote: The sky turned dark and cloudy in the story – what do you think might happen?
items.paragraph: - Explicitly Teach Cause-and-Effect and Inference Skills: Some autistic students may benefit from direct instruction in how to use clues and past information to make predictions. This can be done through academic exercises that double as life skills. For example, in reading comprehension lessons, teachers often ask students to predict what will happen next in a story. For an autistic student, this is not just a literacy skill but also a practice in real-world prediction. Teachers can scaffold this by pointing out obvious cues (“The sky turned dark and cloudy in the story – what do you think might happen?”) and guiding the student to form a prediction (“Maybe it will rain”). Connecting these dots explicitly can translate to the student’s daily life (dark clouds mean rain is likely, so they can predict indoor recess). Likewise, science experiments offer a chance to hypothesize (“If we drop two objects, which will hit the ground first?”) and then observe outcomes – a concrete way to see that making guesses and seeing them corrected is a normal process. By training the brain’s prediction muscles in low-stakes contexts, we help the student build confidence and skill in anticipating and updating expectations. This reduces anxiety because the student gradually learns that uncertainty can be approached systematically rather than avoided – they start engaging in the same “automatic process we go through when decision making” but in a more deliberate, practiced manner[[28]](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/13/6/575#:~:text=,making%2C%20and%20modelling%20this).
